knowledge_statements.title: Convex Optimization Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order inclusion and variational-inequality representations of constrained convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Then \[x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\partial f(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star),\] provided the subdifferential sum rule applies at \(x^\star\). If \(f\) is differentiable near \(C\), this is equivalently \(\langle\nabla f(x^\star),x-x^\star\rangle\ge0\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constrained convex minimizers are zeros of the objective subdifferential plus the constraint normal cone, or solutions of the gradient VI when differentiable.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
A qualification ensuring \(\partial(f+\delta_C)=\partial f+N_C\) holds at the candidate point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{C}f\iff0\in\partial f(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Potential–Operator Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional criterion and path-integral construction for a gradient potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and simply connected, and let \(F:U	o\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable. There exists \(\Phi\in C^2(U)\) with \(F=
abla\Phi\) if and only if the Jacobian is symmetric everywhere: \[
abla F(x)=
abla F(x)^{\mathsf T}\quad	ext{for every }x\in U.\] For a fixed \(x_0\in U\), the potential is determined up to an additive constant by \[\Phi(x)-\Phi(x_0)=\int_{\gamma_{x_0,x}}\langle F(u),duangle,\] where the integral is independent of the piecewise smooth path \(\gamma_{x_0,x}\subset U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a simply connected domain, a continuously differentiable operator is a gradient exactly when its Jacobian is symmetric; path integration recovers the potential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(F=
abla\Phi\) for some \(\Phi\in C^2(U)\iff
abla F(x)=
abla F(x)^{\mathsf T}\) for all \(x\in U\).

notation.meaning: Piecewise smooth path from the base point to x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional integrability criterion and path-integral construction are standard under the stated hypotheses, but no source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT-System Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex differentiable program represented by its primal–dual KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_x f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(Ax=b\), where \(f,g_i:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) are differentiable and convex and the affine constraints satisfy Slater's condition. A triple \((x^\star,\lambda^\star,
u^\star)\) is primal–dual optimal if and only if it satisfies \[
abla f(x^\star)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i^\star
abla g_i(x^\star)+A^{\mathsf T}
u^\star=0,\] \[g(x^\star)\le0,\quad Ax^\star=b,\quad\lambda^\star\ge0,\quad\lambda_i^\star g_i(x^\star)=0\ 	ext{for all }i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under convexity and Slater’s condition, primal–dual optimal solutions are exactly the triples satisfying stationarity, feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and every \(g_i\) are differentiable and convex.
A Slater point satisfies \(g_i(x)<0\) for all \(i\) and \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^\star,\lambda^\star,\nu^\star)\) is primal–dual optimal if and only if it satisfies the displayed KKT system.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex KKT equivalence is standard under Slater's condition, but it has no citation. A sourced version should also explicitly introduce the dimensions of A and b.

knowledge_statements.title: Nash Variational-Inequality Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational-inequality representation of a differentiable convex game on a product strategy set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) players choose \(x_i\in X_i\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\), where each \(X_i\) is nonempty, closed, and convex. Suppose each cost \(J_i(x_i,x_{-i})\) is differentiable and convex in \(x_i\) for every fixed \(x_{-i}\). Set \(X=\prod_iX_i\) and \(F(x)=\operatorname{col}(\nabla_{x_i}J_i(x))_{i=1}^N\). Then \(x^\star\in X\) is a Nash equilibrium if and only if \[\langle F(x^\star),x-x^\star\rangle\ge0\quad\text{for every }x\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a differentiable game with convex individual problems, Nash equilibria are exactly solutions of the VI formed from players’ partial gradients.
assumptions_latex: Each strategy set \(X_i\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Each \(J_i(\cdot,x_{-i})\) is differentiable and convex on \(X_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) is a Nash equilibrium if and only if \(x^\star\in\operatorname{VI}(X,F)\).

notation.meaning: Strategy profile of all players except player i.
Game pseudo-gradient formed from players’ partial gradients.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Nash-equilibrium VI representation is mathematically standard for fixed product strategy sets and playerwise convex differentiable costs, but no citation or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite normal-form game and mixed-strategy profile
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses losses rather than payoffs and assumes independent randomization in a mixed-strategy profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite $K$-person normal-form game consists of finite action sets $A_k=\{1,\ldots,N_k\}$ and loss functions $\ell^{(k)}:\prod_{r=1}^K A_r\to[0,1]$. A mixed strategy of player $k$ is $p^{(k)}\in\Delta(A_k)$. Under independent randomization, the mixed-strategy profile is the product distribution $\pi=\bigotimes_{r=1}^Kp^{(r)}$, with $\pi(i_1,\ldots,i_K)=\prod_{r=1}^Kp^{(r)}_{i_r}$, and player $k$ has expected loss $\mathbb E_\pi[\ell^{(k)}(I)]=\sum_{i\in\prod_rA_r}\pi(i)\ell^{(k)}(i)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite normal-form game specifies a finite action set and a bounded loss function for each player. A mixed strategy is a distribution over one player's actions; independent mixed strategies form a product distribution, under which each player's expected loss is the probability-weighted sum of that player's losses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi(i)=\prod_{r=1}^Kp^{(r)}_{i_r},\qquad \mathbb E_\pi[\ell^{(k)}(I)]=\sum_i\pi(i)\ell^{(k)}(i).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence and Solvability of the Symmetric Differential Nash Game
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the equilibrium-equivalence, existence, conditional uniqueness, and computational conclusions stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated symmetric-coupling assumption and the conditions imposed on every player's problem in Lecture IV: (i) $(\mathbf x^*,\mathbf u^*)$ is a Nash equilibrium if and only if it is an optimal solution of the aggregate optimal-control problem (2.36); (ii) a Nash equilibrium exists with $\mathbf x^*$ absolutely continuous and $\mathbf u^*\in L^2([0,\mathcal T])$; (iii) if additionally $\mathbf S\succ0$, there is a unique Nash equilibrium among pairs for which $\mathbf x^*$ is continuously differentiable and $\mathbf u^*$ is Lipschitz continuous on $[0,\mathcal T]$; and (iv) a Nash equilibrium can be obtained as the limit of numerical trajectories produced by discretizing (2.36) as in Lecture IV.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the symmetric coupling and individual-player hypotheses, Nash equilibria are exactly the optima of the aggregate optimal-control problem. Such an equilibrium exists with absolutely continuous states and square-integrable controls. Positive definiteness of S gives uniqueness in the continuously differentiable-state, Lipschitz-control class, and discretizations of the aggregate problem converge to an equilibrium.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each player's problem satisfies the conditions stated in Lecture IV}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{NE}=\operatorname*{argmin}\text{ of (2.36)},\quad \operatorname{NE}\ne\varnothing;\qquad \mathbf S\succ0\Rightarrow\text{uniqueness in the stated regularity class, with discretization-based recovery}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uncoupled pure-Nash search procedure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract specifies the procedure but contains no convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each player \(k\) and each \(t\ge 1\): if \(t\) is odd, sample \(I_t^{(k)}\) uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,N_k\}\). If \(t\) is even, set \(I_t^{(k)}=1\) when \(\ell^{(k)}(\mathbf I_{t-1})\le \min_{i_k\in\{1,\ldots,N_k\}}\ell^{(k)}(\mathbf I_{t-1}^{-},i_k)\), and set \(I_t^{(k)}=2\) otherwise. If, at an even time, every player reports action \(1\), each player thereafter repeats forever the action played in the preceding odd period.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every odd time, each player independently samples a uniformly random action. At the following even time, the player reports 1 exactly when its preceding action was a best response to the other preceding actions, and reports 2 otherwise. If every player reports 1, all players permanently repeat the preceding odd-period action profile.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\forall k,\ I_t^{(k)}=1\text{ at an even }t\bigr)\Longrightarrow \mathbf I_s=\mathbf I_{t-1}\quad\forall s>t.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric Positive-Semidefinite Aggregate Coupling Assumption
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the aggregate coupling matrices and imposes symmetry and positive semidefiniteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define $$\mathbf W:=\bigl[W_{ii'}\bigr]_{i,i'=1}^N+\operatorname{diag}(W_{ii})_{i=1}^N$$ and $$\mathbf\Xi:=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf P&\mathbf Q\\ \mathbf R&\mathbf S\end{bmatrix},$$ where each block $\mathbf P,\mathbf Q,\mathbf R,\mathbf S$ is formed from the corresponding cross-player blocks $[P_{ii'}],[Q_{ii'}],[R_{ii'}],[S_{ii'}]$ plus its diagonal-block correction. The symmetric-coupling assumption is $$\mathbf W=\mathbf W^\top\succeq0,\qquad \mathbf\Xi=\mathbf\Xi^\top\succeq0.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The aggregate state-coupling matrix W and the aggregate block state-control coupling matrix Xi are assumed symmetric positive semidefinite, with each formed from the players' cross-coupling blocks and diagonal corrections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf W=\mathbf W^\top\succeq0\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbf\Xi=\mathbf\Xi^\top\succeq0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Periodized regret-testing procedure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Playerwise procedure with period length T and acceptance tolerance ρ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each player \(k\), choose \(\pi_0^{(k)}\) uniformly from the simplex \(\mathcal D_k\). In period \(m\), sample actions from \(\pi_m^{(k)}\) for its first \(T-1\) stages. At stage \(t=mT\), report \(1\) if \[\frac1{T-1}\sum_{s=(m-1)T+1}^{mT-1}\ell^{(k)}(\mathbf I_s)\le \min_{i_k\in\{1,\ldots,N_k\}}\frac1{T-1}\sum_{s=(m-1)T+1}^{mT-1}\ell^{(k)}(\mathbf I_s^{-},i_k)+\rho,\] and report \(2\) otherwise. If every player reports \(1\), retain and play the preceding mixed strategy forever; otherwise independently resample the next mixed strategy uniformly from \(\mathcal D_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each player samples from a fixed mixed strategy for T minus one stages, then tests whether its empirical loss is within rho of its best fixed unilateral action in that period. If every player passes, the current mixed profile is retained forever; otherwise new mixed strategies are sampled uniformly from the players' simplices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{All tests accept at period }m\Longrightarrow \pi_r^{(k)}=\pi_{m-1}^{(k)}\text{ is played forever for every }k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Open-Loop Differential Nash Equilibrium
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by playerwise optimality with all other state-control trajectories fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An aggregate trajectory pair $(\mathbf{x}^*,\mathbf{u}^*)$, with $\mathbf{x}^*=(x_i^*)_{i=1}^N$ and $\mathbf{u}^*=(u_i^*)_{i=1}^N$, is a Nash equilibrium if, for every $i=1,\ldots,N$, $$ (x_i^*,u_i^*)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x_i,u_i)}\theta_i(x_i,x_{-i}^*,u_i,u_{-i}^*) $$ subject to $(x_i,u_i)$ being feasible for player $i$'s dynamic problem (2.35).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An aggregate state-control trajectory is an open-loop Nash equilibrium exactly when every player's trajectory minimizes that player's objective over its feasible dynamic trajectories while all other players' trajectories are fixed at their equilibrium values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\},\quad (x_i^*,u_i^*)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x_i,u_i)\ \mathrm{feasible}}\theta_i(x_i,x_{-i}^*,u_i,u_{-i}^*)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed Nash equilibrium and finite-game existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers product mixed strategies in finite loss-minimization games.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A product profile $\pi=\bigotimes_{r=1}^Kp^{(r)}$ is a Nash equilibrium if, for every player $k$ and every alternative $q^{(k)}\in\Delta(A_k)$, $\mathbb E_\pi[\ell^{(k)}(I)]\leq\mathbb E_{\pi'_k}[\ell^{(k)}(I)]$, where $\pi'_k=p^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes q^{(k)}\otimes\cdots\otimes p^{(K)}$. Every finite game has at least one mixed Nash equilibrium, although it may have multiple equilibria.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-strategy profile is a Nash equilibrium when no player can lower their expected loss by changing only their own mixed strategy. Every finite game has at least one such equilibrium, but uniqueness is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall k\;\forall q^{(k)},\quad \mathbb E_\pi\ell^{(k)}\leq\mathbb E_{\pi'_k}\ell^{(k)};\qquad \mathcal N\neq\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additive ε-Nash equilibrium
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite mixed-strategy games with losses, where smaller values are preferred.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\pi=\mathbf p^{(1)}\times\cdots\times\mathbf p^{(K)}\). Then \(\pi\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-Nash equilibrium if, for every player \(k\) and every mixed strategy \(\mathbf q^{(k)}\), \[\pi\ell^{(k)}\le \pi_k'\ell^{(k)}+\varepsilon,\qquad \pi_k'=\mathbf p^{(1)}\times\cdots\times\mathbf q^{(k)}\times\cdots\times\mathbf p^{(K)}.\] It is sufficient to verify this inequality for deviations \(\mathbf q^{(k)}\) concentrated on a single action. The set of such profiles is denoted \(\mathcal N_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed profile is an epsilon-Nash equilibrium when no player can lower its expected loss by more than epsilon through any unilateral mixed-strategy deviation. It suffices to check unilateral deviations to pure actions; the resulting set is denoted N-epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi\in\mathcal N_\varepsilon\iff \forall k\ \forall\mathbf q^{(k)},\ \pi\ell^{(k)}\le\pi_k'\ell^{(k)}+\varepsilon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stabilization and approximate-Nash guarantee for regret testing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The guarantee allows a small positive probability of stabilizing outside the target approximate-equilibrium set; the stated typical stopping time grows exponentially with the mixed-profile dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every player runs the regret-testing procedure with \(\rho\le\tfrac12\) and \((T-1)\rho^2\ge2\ln(\sum_{k=1}^K N_k)\). With probability one, there exists a mixed profile \(\pi\) that is played in every sufficiently large period. Writing \(d=\sum_{k=1}^K(N_k-1)\), \[\Pr\{\pi\notin\mathcal N_{2\rho}\}\le 8T\rho^{2-d}\ln(T\rho^{2-d})e^{-2(T-1)\rho^2}.\] For sufficiently large \(T\), this failure probability can be made arbitrarily small for fixed arbitrarily small \(\rho>0\); when \(T\rho^2\) is significantly larger than \(d\ln d\), it is further bounded by \(e^{-T\rho^2}\). The typical stopping time is of order \(T\rho^{-d}\). Nevertheless, no choice of \(T\) and \(\rho\) makes this method almost surely reach an arbitrarily prescribed \(\varepsilon\)-Nash equilibrium, because erroneous acceptance retains positive probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated period-length and tolerance condition, regret testing almost surely stabilizes at a mixed profile. The probability that the stabilized profile is not a 2-rho Nash equilibrium satisfies the displayed exponentially decreasing bound. The typical stabilization time is of order T times rho to the minus d, and the method retains a positive failure probability, so it does not ensure almost-sure convergence to arbitrarily accurate epsilon-Nash equilibria.
assumptions_latex: \text{Every player uses the stated regret-testing procedure with common }T\text{ and }\rho
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr\{\exists M\ \forall m\ge M:\pi_m=\pi\}=1,\qquad \Pr\{\pi\notin\mathcal N_{2\rho}\}\le8T\rho^{2-d}\ln(T\rho^{2-d})e^{-2(T-1)\rho^2}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementarity representation of the multivalued signum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the scalar multivalued signum graph through two complementarity pairs and an auxiliary scalar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,\widehat a\in\mathbb{R}\), where \(\operatorname{sgn}(a)=1\) if \(a>0\), \(\operatorname{sgn}(0)=[-1,1]\), and \(\operatorname{sgn}(a)=-1\) if \(a<0\), one has \(\widehat a\in\operatorname{sgn}(a)\) if and only if there exists \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(0\le 1+\widehat a\perp -a+\lambda\ge0\) and \(0\le\lambda\perp1-\widehat a\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar belongs to the multivalued signum of a exactly when an auxiliary scalar exists satisfying the two stated complementarity conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat a\in\operatorname{sgn}(a)\iff\exists\lambda\in\mathbb{R}:\ 0\le1+\widehat a\perp-a+\lambda\ge0,\quad 0\le\lambda\perp1-\widehat a\ge0.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear complementarity representation of a variational inequality on the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\). A point \(x^\star\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(\mathbb{R}_+^n,F)\) if and only if it solves the nonlinear complementarity problem \[x^\star\ge0,\qquad F(x^\star)\ge0,\qquad \langle x^\star,F(x^\star)\rangle=0.\] Equivalently, the componentwise relations \(x_i^\star F_i(x^\star)=0\) hold for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\), together with nonnegativity of both complementary vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VI on the nonnegative orthant is equivalent to nonnegativity of the point and operator value together with componentwise complementarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname{VI}(\mathbb{R}_+^n,F)\iff 0\le x^\star\perp F(x^\star)\ge0\).

notation.meaning: The vectors have zero inner product.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orthant VI and nonlinear-complementarity equivalence is correct, but the record has no supporting source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-map equation equivalent to a variational inequality over a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and fix \(\gamma>0\). Define the normal map by \[F^{\mathrm{nor}}_\gamma(z)=\gamma F(P_Cz)+z-P_Cz.\] If \(F^{\mathrm{nor}}_\gamma(z^\star)=0\), then \(x^\star=P_Cz^\star\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\), and \(z^\star=x^\star-\gamma F(x^\star)\). Conversely, if \(x^\star\in\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\), then \(z^\star=x^\star-\gamma F(x^\star)\) satisfies \(P_Cz^\star=x^\star\) and \(F^{\mathrm{nor}}_\gamma(z^\star)=0\). Thus \[\{P_Cz:F^{\mathrm{nor}}_\gamma(z)=0\}=\operatorname{VI}(C,F).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting any zero of the normal map gives a variational-inequality solution, and every such solution has the normal-map zero obtained by subtracting its scaled operator value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{P_Cz:F^{\mathrm{nor}}_\gamma(z)=0\}=\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\), with \(z=x-\gamma F(x)\) for each corresponding solution \(x\).

notation.meaning: Scaled normal map associated with F and C.

knowledge_statements.title: NCP-Function Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equation representation of complementarity using the Fischer–Burmeister NCP function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Fischer–Burmeister function by \(\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b\). For real \(a,b\), \[\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ ab=0.\] Hence, for \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) componentwise by \((\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x))_i=\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x_i,F_i(x))\). Then \[\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\le x\perp F(x)\ge0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying the Fischer–Burmeister function componentwise converts a nonlinear complementarity problem into an equivalent system of nonsmooth equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=0\iff0\le x\perp F(x)\ge0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Fischer–Burmeister equivalence and componentwise equation representation are correct, but no authoritative citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Primal–Dual Value Relations
children.top_down_role: Value correspondences linking primal, dual, saddle, and variational formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Value Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak and saddle-point strong duality for a convex–concave Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty sets and let \(L:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). Define \[p^\star=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y),\qquad d^\star=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y).\] Weak duality always gives \(d^\star\le p^\star\). If \((x^\star,y^\star)\) is a saddle point, meaning \(L(x^\star,y)\le L(x^\star,y^\star)\le L(x,y^\star)\) for all \((x,y)\in X\times Y\), then \[d^\star=p^\star=L(x^\star,y^\star),\] and both outer extrema are attained at \(y^\star\) and \(x^\star\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual value never exceeds the primal value; a saddle point makes them equal to its Lagrangian value and attains both.
assumptions_latex: The displayed infima and suprema are interpreted in the extended-real sense.
For the equality conclusion, \((x^\star,y^\star)\) satisfies the saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^\star\le p^\star\), and a saddle point implies \(d^\star=p^\star=L(x^\star,y^\star)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Values, Attainment, and Saddle Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's problem labels because the extracted item does not include the definitions of problems (7.28) and (7.29).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_{28}\) and \(v_{29}\) be the optimal values of problems (7.28) and (7.29), respectively. Then: (i) \(v_{28}\ge v_{29}\); (ii) the two problems have the same optimal value and both attain it if and only if a saddle point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) exists, in which case \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\) solve (7.28) and (7.29), respectively; and (iii), whenever \(v_{28}=v_{29}\), \[\operatorname{Saddle}=\operatorname{Sol}(7.28)\times\operatorname{Sol}(7.29).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value of problem (7.28) is at least that of problem (7.29). Equality with attainment by both problems is equivalent to existence of a saddle point, whose components solve the respective problems. Under equality of values, all saddle points are exactly the Cartesian product of the two optimal-solution sets.
assumptions_latex: \text{Problems (7.28) and (7.29) and their associated saddle-point relation are as defined in the surrounding formulation.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v_{28}\ge v_{29};\quad [v_{28}=v_{29}\text{ and both optima are attained}]\iff\operatorname{Saddle}\neq\varnothing;\quad v_{28}=v_{29}\Rightarrow\operatorname{Saddle}=\operatorname{Sol}(7.28)\times\operatorname{Sol}(7.29).

knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Gap Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual gap as a nonnegative saddle-point residual and optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). For \((x,y)\in X\times Y\), define the primal–dual gap \[G(x,y)=\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y),\] whenever both terms are finite. Then \(G(x,y)\ge0\). Moreover, \(G(x,y)=0\) if and only if \[L(x,v)\le L(x,y)\le L(u,y)\quad\text{for every }u\in X,v\in Y,\] so zero gap is equivalent to \((x,y)\) being a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal–dual gap is nonnegative, and—when finite—it vanishes exactly at saddle points, providing a directly checkable optimality residual.
assumptions_latex: The supremum and infimum defining \(G(x,y)\) are finite at the evaluated pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x,y)\ge0\), and \(G(x,y)=0\iff(x,y)\) is a saddle point of \(L\) on \(X\times Y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Homogeneous pairwise inequalities imply SRG-fullness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for an operator class to be completely characterized by its scaled relative graph; no smoothness of the representing function is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R\) be nonnegative homogeneous, meaning \[h(\theta a,\theta b,\theta c)=\theta h(a,b,c)\qquad(\theta\ge0).\] Suppose an operator class \(\mathcal A\) is defined by \[\mathbb A\in\mathcal A\iff h\!\left(\|u-v\|^2,\|x-y\|^2,\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\right)\le0\] for all \(x,y\) and all \(u\in\mathbb A x\), \(v\in\mathbb A y\). Then \(\mathcal A\) is SRG-full. In particular, this applies to the monotone, \(\mu\)-strongly monotone, \(\beta\)-cocoercive, \(L\)-Lipschitz, and \(\theta\)-averaged/nonexpansive operator classes represented in this form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any operator class defined by a nonnegatively homogeneous inequality involving the squared output difference, squared input difference, and their inner product is SRG-full. Smoothness of the representing function is unnecessary; the result includes standard monotone, strongly monotone, cocoercive, Lipschitz, and averaged operator classes.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(h(\theta a,\theta b,\theta c)=\theta h(a,b,c)\) for every \(\theta\ge0\).
\(\mathbb A\in\mathcal A\) is equivalent to the stated inequality holding for all \(x,y\), \(u\in\mathbb A x\), and \(v\in\mathbb A y\).
No smoothness assumption is imposed on \(h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\text{ is SRG-full}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: SRG-full operator class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines when scaled relative graphs completely characterize membership in an operator class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operator class \(\mathcal A\) is SRG-full if, for every operator \(\mathbb A\), \[\mathbb A\in\mathcal A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal G(\mathbb A)\subseteq\mathcal G(\mathcal A).\] Since membership already implies this containment by the definition of the class SRG, the substantive condition is \[\mathcal G(\mathbb A)\subseteq\mathcal G(\mathcal A)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbb A\in\mathcal A.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator class is SRG-full when an operator belongs to the class exactly when its scaled relative graph is contained in the scaled relative graph of the class.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a class of operators.
\(\mathcal G(\mathbb A)\) and \(\mathcal G(\mathcal A)\) denote the scaled relative graphs of an operator and of the class, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall\mathbb A,\;\mathbb A\in\mathcal A\iff\mathcal G(\mathbb A)\subseteq\mathcal G(\mathcal A)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Operator Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued monotonicity on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). The operator \(A\) is monotone when
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq 0
\]
for every \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\). The monotone operator regime consists of inclusion problems \(0\in A x\) for which this inequality is available, without assuming maximality, strong monotonicity, single-valuedness, or continuity of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is monotone when every pair of graph points has a nonnegative primal–dual displacement pairing; no maximality or quantitative modulus is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0\) for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jacobian tests for differentiable operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All tests are global on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The convex-subdifferential characterization additionally assumes monotonicity and continuity of the Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be differentiable. Then
\[
T\text{ is monotone}\iff DT(x)+DT(x)^\top\succeq0\quad\forall x,
\]
\[
T\text{ is }\mu\text{-strongly monotone}\iff DT(x)+DT(x)^\top\succeq2\mu I\quad\forall x,
\]
and
\[
T\text{ is }L\text{-Lipschitz}\iff\sigma_{\max}(DT(x))\le L\quad\forall x.
\]
If, moreover, \(T\) is monotone and \(DT\) is continuous, then \(T\) is the subdifferential of a closed proper convex function if and only if \(DT(x)=DT(x)^\top\) for every \(x\). For \(n=3\), this symmetry condition is equivalent to vanishing curl.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable Euclidean operator, the symmetric part of its Jacobian characterizes monotonicity and strong monotonicity, while the largest singular value characterizes Lipschitz continuity. If the operator is monotone and its Jacobian is continuous, it is a convex subdifferential exactly when the Jacobian is symmetric everywhere; in three dimensions this is the curl-free condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}T\text{ monotone}&\iff DT(x)+DT(x)^\top\succeq0\ \forall x,\\T\text{ }\mu\text{-strongly monotone}&\iff DT(x)+DT(x)^\top\succeq2\mu I\ \forall x,\\T\text{ }L\text{-Lipschitz}&\iff\sigma_{\max}(DT(x))\le L\ \forall x;\end{aligned}\quad\text{and if }T\text{ is monotone and }DT\text{ continuous, }T=\partial f\iff DT(x)=DT(x)^\top\ \forall x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Set-Valued Operators, Their Calculus, and Inverses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary properties for operators on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operator \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) assigns each \(x\) a possibly empty subset \(Tx\). Define \(\operatorname{Gra}T=\{(x,u):u\in Tx\}\), \(\operatorname{dom}T=\{x:Tx\ne\varnothing\}\), \(\operatorname{ran}T=\{y:\exists x,\ y\in Tx\}\), and \(T(C)=\bigcup_{c\in C}Tc\). For operators \(S,T\), \((T\circ S)x=T(Sx)\) and \((T+S)x=Tx+Sx\), with set-valued composition and Minkowski sum. The identity and zero operators have graphs \(\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb{R}^n\}\) and \(\{(x,0):x\in\mathbb{R}^n\}\). For \(L>0\), \(T\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz when \(\|u-v\|\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{Gra}T\); such an operator is single-valued on its domain. Its inverse is \(T^{-1}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{Gra}T\}\), so \((T^{-1})^{-1}=T\) and \(\operatorname{dom}T^{-1}=\operatorname{ran}T\), although generally \(T^{-1}T\ne I\). If \(T^{-1}\) is single-valued, then \(T^{-1}Tx=x\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued operator assigns each point a possibly empty set and is equivalently represented by its graph. Its domain, range, set image, composition, Minkowski sum, identity, zero operator, Lipschitz property, and graph-reversing inverse are defined as stated. Lipschitz set-valued operators are single-valued on their domains. Inversion is involutive and exchanges range with inverse domain, but it need not give a two-sided functional inverse; if the inverse is single-valued, applying it after the operator returns every point in the operator's domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is represented equivalently by }\operatorname{Gra}T;\quad T\text{ Lipschitz}\Rightarrow T\text{ single-valued on }\operatorname{dom}T;\quad (T^{-1})^{-1}=T,\ \operatorname{dom}T^{-1}=\operatorname{ran}T,\quad T^{-1}\text{ single-valued}\Rightarrow T^{-1}Tx=x\ \forall x\in\operatorname{dom}T.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity and maximal monotonicity of convex subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-analytic classification of subdifferential operators, including the necessity of the closedness hypothesis for the stated maximality guarantee and the failure of the converse representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] is proper and convex, then \partial f is monotone. If f is closed, proper, and convex, then \partial f is maximal monotone. Not every maximal monotone operator is the subdifferential of a closed proper convex function, and a proper convex function without the closedness assumption can have a nonmaximal subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a proper convex function is monotone. Closedness, properness, and convexity guarantee that it is maximal monotone. The converse representation fails: some maximal monotone operators are not convex subdifferentials. Closedness also cannot simply be omitted from the maximality guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the maximality conclusion, }f\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f\text{ is monotone};\qquad f\text{ closed, proper, and convex}\Longrightarrow\partial f\text{ is maximal monotone};\qquad \{\partial f:f\text{ closed, proper, convex}\}\subsetneq\{T:T\text{ maximal monotone}\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Demipositive Maximal Monotone Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition together with sufficient subclasses and a skew-symmetric counterexample showing that monotonicity alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A maximal monotone operator \(\mathbb A:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) is demipositive if there exists \(x^\star\in\operatorname{Zer}\mathbb A\) such that \[\langle a,x-x^\star\rangle>0\qquad\forall x\notin\operatorname{Zer}\mathbb A,\ \forall a\in\mathbb A(x).\] Strongly monotone operators, cocoercive operators, subdifferentials of closed proper convex functions, and maximal monotone operators satisfying \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{Zer}\mathbb A)\ne\varnothing\) are demipositive. Monotonicity alone is insufficient: \(\mathbb A(x,y)=(y,-x)\) is monotone but not demipositive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal monotone operator is demipositive when some zero has strictly positive pairing with every operator value at every point outside its zero set. Strongly monotone and cocoercive operators, convex subdifferentials, and maximal monotone operators with a zero set having nonempty interior satisfy the property. The planar rotation mapping is monotone but not demipositive.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb A:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\text{ is maximal monotone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb A\text{ is demipositive}\iff\exists x^\star\in\operatorname{Zer}\mathbb A:\ \langle a,x-x^\star\rangle>0\ \forall x\notin\operatorname{Zer}\mathbb A,\ \forall a\in\mathbb A(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resolvent and reflected resolvent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines both mappings and records their full-domain averagedness and nonexpansiveness under maximal monotonicity in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an operator \(\mathbb A\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), its resolvent and reflected resolvent are \(J_{\mathbb A}=(I+\mathbb A)^{-1}\) and \(R_{\mathbb A}=2J_{\mathbb A}-I\). Scaled versions \(J_{\alpha\mathbb A}\) and \(R_{\alpha\mathbb A}\) are defined analogously for \(\alpha>0\). If \(\mathbb A\) is maximal monotone, then \(J_{\mathbb A}\) and \(R_{\mathbb A}\) are single-valued on all of \(\mathbb R^n\), \(R_{\mathbb A}\) is nonexpansive, and \(J_{\mathbb A}\) is \(1/2\)-averaged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of an operator A is the inverse of I+A, and its reflected resolvent is twice the resolvent minus the identity. Positive scalar multiples are handled analogously. For a maximal monotone operator on finite-dimensional Euclidean space, both mappings are single-valued and everywhere defined; the reflected resolvent is nonexpansive and the resolvent is one-half averaged.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb A\text{ is maximal monotone for the mapping properties}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) and \(S:\mathbb R^m\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\), define \(T:\mathbb R^{n+m}\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^{n+m}\) by \(T(x,y)=\{(u,v):u\in R(x),\ v\in S(y)\}=R(x)\times S(y)\). This operator is called the concatenation of \(R\) and \(S\). If both component operators are monotone, then \(T\) is monotone; if both are maximal monotone, then \(T\) is maximal monotone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transformation rules for strong-monotonicity and Lipschitz moduli
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative rules for sums, positive scaling, and linear pullbacks in finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathbb T\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone and \(\mathbb S\) is monotone, then \(\mathbb T+\mathbb S\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone. For \(\alpha>0\), \(\alpha\mathbb T\) is \(\alpha\mu\)-strongly monotone. If \(\mathbb T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone and \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) has rank \(m\), then \(M^\top\mathbb T M\) is \(\mu\sigma_{\min}^2(M)\)-strongly monotone. If \(\mathbb T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), then \(M^\top\mathbb T M\) is \(L\sigma_{\max}^2(M)\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a monotone operator preserves a strong-monotonicity modulus, and positive scaling scales that modulus. A full-column-rank pullback scales strong monotonicity by the squared smallest singular value, while a pullback scales a Lipschitz bound by the squared largest singular value.
assumptions_latex: For the sum rule, \(\mathbb T\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone and \(\mathbb S\) is monotone.
For the strong-monotonicity pullback, \(\mathbb T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\), \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), and \(\operatorname{rank}M=m\).
For the Lipschitz pullback, \(\mathbb T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting strong-monotonicity moduli are respectively \(\mu\), \(\alpha\mu\), and \(\mu\sigma_{\min}^2(M)\), while the pullback Lipschitz constant is \(L\sigma_{\max}^2(M)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Operations preserving monotonicity and maximal monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closure properties, with the qualification conditions required for maximality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\). If \(\mathbb T\) is monotone, respectively maximal monotone, then \(x\mapsto y+\alpha\mathbb T(x+z)\), for \(\alpha>0\) and \(y,z\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\mathbb T^{-1}\) are monotone, respectively maximal monotone. If \(\mathbb T\) and \(\mathbb S\) are monotone, then \(\mathbb T+\mathbb S\) is monotone. If they are maximal monotone and \(\operatorname{dom}\mathbb T\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\mathbb S)\neq\varnothing\), then their sum is maximal monotone. If \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), monotonicity of \(\mathbb T\) implies monotonicity of \(M^\top\mathbb T M\) on \(\mathbb R^m\). If additionally \(\mathbb T\) is maximal monotone and \(\mathcal R(M)\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\mathbb T)\neq\varnothing\), then \(M^\top\mathbb T M\) is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive affine scaling and translation, inversion, addition, and linear pullback preserve monotonicity. The corresponding maximal-monotonicity claims hold under the stated interior-domain qualifications.
assumptions_latex: Each operator has the monotonicity or maximal-monotonicity property specified for its claim.
For maximality of \(\mathbb T+\mathbb S\), \(\operatorname{dom}\mathbb T\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\mathbb S)\neq\varnothing\).
For maximality of \(M^\top\mathbb T M\), \(\mathcal R(M)\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\mathbb T)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated affine transformation, inverse, sum, and linear pullback are monotone, and they are maximal monotone under the corresponding additional hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fitzpatrick function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a set-valued operator on finite-dimensional Euclidean space; monotonicity is not required for the formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathbb A:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\), define \[\mathbf F_{\mathbb A}(x,u)=\langle x,u\rangle-\inf_{(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}\mathbb A}\langle x-y,u-v\rangle=\sup_{(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}\mathbb A}\bigl\{\langle y,u\rangle+\langle x,v\rangle-\langle y,v\rangle\bigr\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fitzpatrick function of a set-valued operator is the canonical pairing minus an infimum over the operator graph, equivalently the displayed supremum over that graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf F_{\mathbb A}:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ is defined by the equivalent infimum and supremum formulas.}

knowledge_statements.title: Maximally Monotone Operator Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-maximal monotonicity on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be monotone. The operator \(A\) is maximally monotone if no monotone operator \(B:H\rightrightarrows H\) has \(\operatorname{gra}A\subsetneq\operatorname{gra}B\). Equivalently, whenever \((x,u)\in H\times H\) satisfies \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0\) for every \((y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), one has \(u\in Ax\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone operator is maximally monotone when its graph admits no proper monotone enlargement, equivalently every point monotonically related to its graph already belongs to it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone exactly when every point monotonically related to \(\operatorname{gra}A\) lies in \(\operatorname{gra}A\).

notation.meaning: The graph of the set-valued operator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of projected Tseng forward-backward-forward splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence under monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity, with strong convergence under uniform monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathcal H\) be nonempty, let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone with \(\operatorname{dom}A\subset D\), and let \(B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be monotone and single-valued on \(D\). Suppose \(A+B\) is maximally monotone. Let \(\beta>0\), and let \(C\subset D\) be closed and convex with \(C\cap\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\ne\varnothing\), such that \(B\) is \(1/\beta\)-Lipschitz on \(C\cup\operatorname{dom}A\). For \(x_0\in C\) and \(0<\gamma<\beta\), define, for every \(n\ge0\), \[y_n=x_n-\gamma Bx_n,\qquad z_n=J_{\gamma A}y_n,\qquad r_n=z_n-\gamma Bz_n,\qquad x_{n+1}=P_C(x_n-y_n+r_n).\] Then \(x_n-z_n\to0\) strongly, and both \((x_n)\) and \((z_n)\) converge weakly to a point of \(C\cap\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\). If either \(A\) or \(B\) is uniformly monotone on every nonempty bounded subset of \(\operatorname{dom}A\), then both sequences converge strongly to the unique point of \(C\cap\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let A be maximally monotone, B be monotone and single-valued, and A+B be maximally monotone. Assume a nonempty closed convex constraint set C contains a zero of A+B and B is 1/beta-Lipschitz on C together with dom A. For any starting point in C and step size strictly between zero and beta, the projected Tseng forward-backward-forward iteration has vanishing x_n−z_n residual, and both sequences converge weakly to a zero in C. If A or B is uniformly monotone on every nonempty bounded subset of dom A, the convergence is strong and the zero in C is unique.
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) is maximally monotone and \(\operatorname{dom}A\subset D\).
\(B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) is monotone and single-valued on \(D\).
\(\beta>0\), and \(C\subset D\) is closed and convex with \(C\cap\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n-z_n\to0\) strongly, while \(x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\) and \(z_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\) for some \(\bar x\in C\cap\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\); if \(A\) or \(B\) is uniformly monotone on every nonempty bounded subset of \(\operatorname{dom}A\), then \(x_n\to\bar x\) and \(z_n\to\bar x\) strongly and \(C\cap\operatorname{zer}(A+B)=\{\bar x\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone and maximal monotone operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a possibly set-valued operator on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operator T:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n is monotone if \langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge 0 for all (x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{Gra}T. knowledge_statements.title: Maximality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minty surjectivity separates maximal monotonicity from mere monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be monotone, and let \(\lambda>0\). Then \(A\) is maximally monotone if and only if
\[
\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)=H.
\]
Thus failure of maximality is witnessed by some \(z\in H\) for which \(z\notin x+\lambda Ax\) for every \(x\in H\); at such a point the resolvent \((I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is not defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone operator crosses the maximality boundary exactly when its shifted range fills the space; otherwise its resolvent is undefined at some point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone if and only if \(\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)=H\).

notation.meaning: The resolvent associated with \(A\) and parameter \(\lambda\).

A monotone operator is maximal monotone if it has no proper monotone extension. If \(\mathbb A\) is maximal monotone, then \(\operatorname{dom}\mathbb J_{\mathbb A}=\mathbb R^n\).

A monotone operator is maximal monotone when it has no proper monotone extension. In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the resolvent of a maximal monotone operator has full domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P be a property of operators and let \mathbb{A}:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n have property P. The operator \mathbb{A} is maximal P if there is no operator \overline{\mathbb{A}} with property P such that \operatorname{gra}\mathbb{A}\subsetneq\operatorname{gra}\overline{\mathbb{A}}. Consequently, any maximal P extension of an already maximal P operator equals the original operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator having property P is maximal P when its graph admits no proper extension that still has property P. Thus, a maximal P extension of an operator already maximal P is the operator itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\,\overline{\mathbb{A}}\text{ with property }P\text{ such that }\operatorname{gra}\mathbb{A}\subsetneq\operatorname{gra}\overline{\mathbb{A}}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-domain continuous monotone operators are maximal monotone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The source defines continuity for an operator to include full domain and single-valuedness; the final boundary statement is not a converse characterization of maximality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operator \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) is called continuous when \(\operatorname{dom}T=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(T\) is single-valued, and the induced map \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuous. If such an operator is monotone, then it is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Here a continuous operator is full-domain, single-valued, and continuous as a function. Every such monotone operator is maximal monotone. Thus nontrivial maximality questions arise outside this class, notably for discontinuous or set-valued operators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is maximal monotone}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximal Lipschitz extensions and domain characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension existence and maximality criterion at a fixed positive Lipschitz constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let L>0. Every L-Lipschitz operator admits a maximal L-Lipschitz extension. Moreover, if \mathbb{A}:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n is L-Lipschitz, then \mathbb{A} is maximal L-Lipschitz if and only if \operatorname{dom}\mathbb{A}=\mathbb{R}^n.

children.top_down_role: Operator geometry governed by a fixed strong-monotonicity modulus.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Monotone Operator Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic monotonicity modulus on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). For \(\mu>0\), the operator \(A\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone if
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq \mu\lVert x-y\rVert^2
\]
for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\). The strongly monotone regime assumes that at least one such positive modulus \(\mu\) is known or exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity strengthens monotonicity by lower-bounding the graph pairing with a positive quadratic function of the input separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\mu\lVert x-y\rVert^2\) for all graph pairs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Step Estimate for Modified Forward–Backward Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fejér-type distance estimate for the projected forward-corrected resolvent step, with a strong-monotonicity refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) be maximal monotone, with \(\operatorname{dom}A\subseteq\operatorname{dom}B\), and let \(B\) be single-valued. Let \(X\subseteq\operatorname{dom}B\) be closed and convex with \(X\cap(A+B)^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing\). For \(c>0\) and \(x\in\operatorname{dom}B\), define \[x^+=J_{cA}((I-cB)(x)),\qquad z=x^+-c(B(x^+)-B(x)).\] For every \(x^*\in X\cap(A+B)^{-1}(0)\), there is \(\eta\ge0\) such that \[\|\Pi_X(z)-x^*\|^2\le\|z-x^*\|^2=\|x-x^*\|^2+c^2\|B(x^+)-B(x)\|^2-\|x^+-x\|^2-2c\eta.\] If \(A+B\) is strongly monotone on \(\operatorname{dom}A\) with modulus \(\sigma>0\), then \(\eta\ge\sigma\|x^+-x^*\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected correction step satisfies an exact one-step squared-distance identity and a projection inequality relative to every solution in X. Strong monotonicity of A+B supplies an additional nonnegative decrease term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\Pi_X(z)-x^*\|^2\le\|z-x^*\|^2=\|x-x^*\|^2+c^2\|B(x^+)-B(x)\|^2-\|x^+-x\|^2-2c\eta,\quad \eta\ge0;\quad (A+B)\text{ strongly monotone with modulus }\sigma\implies\eta\ge\sigma\|x^+-x^*\|^2.

children.title: Uniformly Monotone Operator Regime
children.top_down_role: Operator geometry governed by a general uniform growth modulus.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniformly Monotone Operator Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive distance-dependent monotonicity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). The operator \(A\) is uniformly monotone if there exists an increasing function \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]\) satisfying \(\phi(0)=0\) and \(\phi(t)>0\) for every \(t>0\), such that
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\phi(\lVert x-y\rVert)
\]
for every \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform monotonicity supplies a strictly positive lower bound, depending only on input distance, for the pairing of any two distinct graph points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\phi(\lVert x-y\rVert)\) for all graph pairs.

children.title: Monotonicity-Modulus Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions induced by linear, nonlinear, or local monotonicity moduli.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity-Modulus Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified representation of quantitative monotonicity classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). A monotonicity-modulus regime is represented by a function \(\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]\) with \(\omega(0)=0\) through
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\omega(\lVert x-y\rVert)
\]
for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\). Ordinary monotonicity corresponds to \(\omega\equiv0\); uniform monotonicity requires \(\omega(t)>0\) for \(t>0\); and \(\mu\)-strong monotonicity corresponds to \(\omega(t)=\mu t^2\) with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single distance modulus organizes ordinary, uniform, and strong monotonicity by changing the lower bound imposed on graph-point pairings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The choices \(\omega\equiv0\), \(\omega(t)>0\) for \(t>0\), and \(\omega(t)=\mu t^2\) encode monotone, uniformly monotone, and strongly monotone regimes, respectively.

knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercive Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued inverse-strong monotonicity on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(A:C\to H\). For \(\beta>0\), the operator \(A\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive if
\[
\langle Ax-Ay,x-y\rangle\geq\beta\lVert Ax-Ay\rVert^2
\]
for all \(x,y\in C\). In particular, every cocoercive operator is monotone and \(1/\beta\)-Lipschitz continuous on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocoercivity lower-bounds the input–output pairing by the squared output change; it implies both monotonicity and a reciprocal Lipschitz bound.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle Ax-Ay,x-y\rangle\geq\beta\lVert Ax-Ay\rVert^2\) for all \(x,y\in C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudomonotone Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Karamardian pseudomonotonicity for single-valued variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(A:C\to H\). The operator \(A\) is pseudomonotone in the Karamardian sense if, for every \(x,y\in C\),
\[
\langle Ax,y-x\rangle\geq0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\langle Ay,y-x\rangle\geq0.
\]
This regime is weaker than monotonicity and is distinct from sequential pseudomonotonicity definitions used for set-valued operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Karamardian pseudomonotonicity transfers a nonnegative variational-inequality pairing at one endpoint to the corresponding pairing evaluated at the other endpoint.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all \(x,y\in C\), \(\langle Ax,y-x\rangle\geq0\) implies \(\langle Ay,y-x\rangle\geq0\).

notation.meaning: The feasible domain of the variational inequality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated Karamardian implication is standard and internally consistent, but no citation is supplied. Because pseudomonotonicity has several inequivalent variants, an authoritative source with a definition-level locator is required.

children.title: Weakly Monotone Operator Regime
children.top_down_role: Operator structures admitting bounded departure from monotonicity.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Monotone Operator Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypomonotonicity with a quadratic negative allowance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). For \(\rho\geq0\), the operator \(A\) is \(\rho\)-weakly monotone if
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq-\rho\lVert x-y\rVert^2
\]
for every \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\). The case \(\rho=0\) is ordinary monotonicity; positive \(\rho\) quantifies the permitted loss of monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak monotonicity permits negative graph pairings, but bounds their magnitude by a quadratic penalty with parameter rho.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq-\rho\lVert x-y\rVert^2\) for all graph pairs.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Operator Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the graph monotonicity inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). The operator \(A\) is nonmonotone when monotonicity fails, namely when there exist \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) such that
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle<0.
\]
This designation alone supplies no finite lower quadratic bound, continuity property, or restoration parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is nonmonotone when at least one pair of graph points has a negative displacement pairing; no quantitative lower bound follows automatically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) with \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle<0\).

children.title: Monotonicity-Restoration Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of regularization or reformulation for recovering monotone structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity-Restoration Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp quadratic shift restoring monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), and let \(\rho\geq0\). Then \(A\) is \(\rho\)-weakly monotone if and only if the shifted operator \(A+\rho I\) is monotone. Consequently, the smallest restoration threshold is
\[
\rho_\star=\inf\{\rho\geq0:A+\rho I\text{ is monotone}\}.
\]
If this set is empty, no finite scalar identity shift restores monotonicity; otherwise every \(\rho>\rho_\star\) restores it, while every \(\rho<\rho_\star\) fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding rho times the identity restores monotonicity exactly when rho bounds the operator's quadratic monotonicity loss; the infimum is the sharp restoration threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is \(\rho\)-weakly monotone if and only if \(A+\rho I\) is monotone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local max–min saddle point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The inequality orientation in the extract makes \(x^0\) locally maximizing in the first block and \(y^0\) locally minimizing in the second block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}^q\to\mathbb{R}\). A point \((x^0,y^0)\) is a local max–min saddle point if there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, whenever \(\lVert x-x^0\rVert_2<\varepsilon\) and \(\lVert y-y^0\rVert_2<\varepsilon\), \[f(x,y^0)\le f(x^0,y^0)\le f(x^0,y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near the reference point, fixing the second block makes the reference first block locally maximizing, while fixing the first block makes the reference second block locally minimizing.

children.title: Convex–Concave Saddle Regime
children.top_down_role: Saddle structures with convex primal curvature and concave dual curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex–Concave Saddle Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity in the primal variable and concavity in the dual variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty convex subsets of real vector spaces, and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(L\) is convex–concave if \(x\mapsto L(x,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\), while \(y\mapsto L(x,y)\) is concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). A point \((x^\star,y^\star)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point when
\[
L(x^\star,y)\leq L(x^\star,y^\star)\leq L(x,y^\star)
\]
for all \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The saddle regime is convex in the minimizing variable and concave in the maximizing variable; a saddle point simultaneously satisfies both one-sided optimality inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex, \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave, and saddle points satisfy \(L(x^\star,y)\leq L(x^\star,y^\star)\leq L(x,y^\star)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Saddle subdifferential and saddle-point zeros
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness and properness are required for the stated maximal-monotonicity conclusion, not for the basic definition or zero correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}\) be convex in \(x\) for every fixed \(u\) and concave in \(u\) for every fixed \(x\). Its saddle subdifferential is
\[
\partial L(x,u)=\begin{bmatrix}\partial_xL(x,u)\\ \partial_u(-L(x,u))\end{bmatrix}.
\]
It is nonempty exactly when both component subdifferentials are nonempty, and
\[
0\in\partial L(x^\star,u^\star)\iff(x^\star,u^\star)\text{ is a saddle point of }L.
\]
If \(L\) is a closed proper convex–concave saddle function, then \(\partial L\) is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The saddle subdifferential combines the primal-variable subgradient with the subgradient of the negated function in the dual variable. Its zeros are exactly the saddle points. For a closed proper convex–concave saddle function, the resulting operator is maximal monotone.
assumptions_latex: L:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}\text{ is convex in }x\text{ and concave in }u
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial L(x,u)=\begin{bmatrix}\partial_xL(x,u)\\\partial_u(-L(x,u))\end{bmatrix},\qquad \operatorname{zer}(\partial L)=\operatorname{Saddle}(L),\qquad L\text{ closed and proper}\implies\partial L\text{ maximal monotone}.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex–Strongly Concave Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional saddle objectives with uniform curvature in both variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty convex sets. A function \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) is \((\mu_x,\mu_y)\)-strongly convex–strongly concave, where \(\mu_x,\mu_y>0\), if for every \(y\in Y\), \(x\mapsto L(x,y)-(\mu_x/2)\lVert x\rVert^2\) is convex on \(X\), and for every \(x\in X\), \(y\mapsto L(x,y)+(\mu_y/2)\lVert y\rVert^2\) is concave on \(Y\). The associated regime is the minimax problem \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\) under these two curvature conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both the minimizing and maximizing variables have positive uniform curvature: strong convexity in the first variable and strong concavity in the second.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\) belongs to the strongly convex–strongly concave saddle regime with moduli \((\mu_x,\mu_y)\).

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Strong Curvature Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saddle objectives for which strong curvature is assumed in one variable block and ordinary convexity or concavity in the other, without excluding additional curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty convex sets, and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). The convex–strongly concave regime holds if, for every \(y\in Y\), the map \(x\mapsto L(x,y)\) is convex on \(X\), and there exists \(\mu_y>0\) such that, for every \(x\in X\), the map \(y\mapsto L(x,y)+(\mu_y/2)\lVert y\rVert^2\) is concave on \(Y\). Symmetrically, the strongly convex–concave regime holds if there exists \(\mu_x>0\) such that, for every \(y\in Y\), the map \(x\mapsto L(x,y)-(\mu_x/2)\lVert x\rVert^2\) is convex on \(X\), while, for every \(x\in X\), the map \(y\mapsto L(x,y)\) is concave on \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-sided strong-curvature regimes assume strong curvature in one variable block and ordinary convexity or concavity in the other; they need not exclude additional strong curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\) satisfies either the convex–strongly concave conditions or the strongly convex–concave conditions stated above.

notation.meaning: Positive one-sided curvature moduli, as applicable.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex–Strongly Concave Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth or nonsmooth minimax problems with strong concavity only in the maximizing block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, let \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). The problem \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\) is nonconvex–strongly concave if no convexity is imposed on \(x\mapsto L(x,y)\), while there exists \(\mu_y>0\) such that \(y\mapsto L(x,y)+(\mu_y/2)\lVert y\rVert^2\) is concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). Thus each inner maximization has at most one maximizer whenever it is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The outer minimization may be nonconvex, but every inner maximization is uniformly strongly concave and therefore has at most one solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\) lies in the nonconvex–strongly concave regime.

notation.meaning: Uniform strong-concavity modulus in the maximizing variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex–Concave Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, let \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex–Nonconcave Minimax Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General minimax problems for which global convexity and concavity are not imposed on the respective variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty sets, and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). The problem \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\) belongs to the nonconvex–nonconcave regime when global convexity of \(x\mapsto L(x,y)\) for every \(y\in Y\) and global concavity of \(y\mapsto L(x,y)\) for every \(x\in X\) are not imposed. Consequently, minimax equality and convex saddle-set geometry do not follow from block curvature assumptions alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neither block is required to have the global curvature used by convex–concave saddle theory, so minimax equality and convex saddle geometry are not automatically guaranteed.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\) belongs to the nonconvex–nonconcave regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex–concave saddle existence under compactness and continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty compact convex sets. Suppose \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous, \(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\), and \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). Then there exists \((x^\star,y^\star)\in X\times Y\) satisfying \(L(x^\star,y)\leq L(x^\star,y^\star)\leq L(x,y^\star)\) for all \((x,y)\in X\times Y\), and \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous convex–concave objective on compact convex domains attains a saddle point, and its primal and dual minimax values coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty compact convex sets.
\(L\) is convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Saddle}(L;X,Y)\neq\varnothing\) and the attained minimax values are equal.

notation.meaning: A saddle point of the objective.
Set of saddle points on the stated domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Coercivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional growth conditions used to prevent escape to infinity in saddle-point problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty closed sets, and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). A coercive–anticoercive condition holds if there exist \(\bar y\in Y\) and \(\bar x\in X\) such that \(L(x,\bar y)\to+\infty\) as \(\lVert x\rVert\to\infty\) within \(X\), and \(L(\bar x,y)\to-\infty\) as \(\lVert y\rVert\to\infty\) within \(Y\). Equivalently, for every \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), the sets \(\{x\in X:L(x,\bar y)\leq\alpha\}\) and \(\{y\in Y:L(\bar x,y)\geq\beta\}\) are bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Growth in the minimizing direction and decay in the maximizing direction make every fixed-cross-section lower sublevel set and upper superlevel set bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty closed subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\) satisfies the stated coercive–anticoercive condition relative to \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Reference points defining the two fixed cross-sections.

knowledge_statements.title: Compactness-Based Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment of the outer minimax value from compactness and semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty compact topological spaces, and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). Assume \(L(\cdot,y)\) is lower semicontinuous on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\), and \(L(x,\cdot)\) is upper semicontinuous on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). Define \(\phi(x)=\max_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\). Then every inner maximum is attained, \(\phi\) is lower semicontinuous, and there exists \(x^\star\in X\) such that \(\phi(x^\star)=\min_{x\in X}\phi(x)\). Thus the sequential minimax problem attains both optimization stages, without asserting minimax equality or a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact domains and the appropriate semicontinuity make every inner maximum and the resulting outer minimum attainable.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty compact topological spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\) is attained at some pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\in X\times Y\).

notation.meaning: An attaining outer minimizer and associated inner maximizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of an attained saddle point under two-sided strong curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty convex sets, and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) be \((\mu_x,\mu_y)\)-strongly convex–strongly concave with \(\mu_x,mu_y>0\). If a saddle point of \(L\) on \(X\times Y\) exists, then it is unique. Equivalently, \(\operatorname{Saddle}(L;X,Y)\) is empty or a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whenever a saddle point exists, positive strong curvature in both variable blocks makes it unique.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
For every \(y\in Y\), \(L(\cdot,y)\) is strongly convex on \(X\) with modulus \(\mu_x>0\).
For every \(x\in X\), \(L(x,\cdot)\) is strongly concave on \(Y\) with modulus \(\mu_y>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\operatorname{Saddle}(L;X,Y)\rvert\leq 1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and Uniqueness from Contractivity of the Projected VI Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A contraction condition on the metric-projection fixed-point map guarantees a unique VI solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty, closed, and convex. Suppose there exist \gamma>0, G=G^{\mathsf T}\succ0, and \alpha\in[0,1) such that the projected map R_G:X\to X associated with \operatorname{VI}(X,f) satisfies \|R_G(x)-R_G(y)\|_G\leq\alpha\|x-y\|_G for all x,y\in X. Then \operatorname{VI}(X,f) has a unique solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the projected VI map is a contraction in a symmetric positive-definite metric, its unique fixed point is the unique solution of the variational inequality.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left|\operatorname{Sol}(\operatorname{VI}(X,f))\right|=1.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product structure and convexity of the saddle set for convex–concave objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be convex sets, let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\), and suppose the saddle set \(S\) is nonempty with saddle value \(v\). Define \(X^\star=\{x\in X:\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=v\}\) and \(Y^\star=\{y\in Y:\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=v\}\). Then \(X^\star\) and \(Y^\star\) are convex, \(S=X^\star\times Y^\star\), and every crossed pair formed from the primal component of one saddle point and the dual component of another is again a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex–concave problem with saddle points, the saddle set is a Cartesian product of convex primal and dual solution sets.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\).
The global saddle set \(S\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=X^\star\times Y^\star\) is convex and is closed under crossing saddle-point components.

notation.meaning: Primal and dual optimal component sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of strict curvature permits continua of saddle points even under convexity and concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=[-1,1]\) and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) be given by \(L(x,y)=0\) for every \((x,y)\in X\times Y\). Then \(L\) is convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\), while \(\operatorname{Saddle}(L;X,Y)=X\times Y\). In particular, the saddle set is uncountable, so convexity–concavity alone does not ensure uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant convex–concave objective makes every feasible pair a saddle point, showing that ordinary convexity and concavity do not ensure uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Saddle}(L;X,Y)=X\times Y\), so uniqueness does not follow from convexity–concavity alone.

notation.meaning: Feasible product set and the entire saddle set in this example.

children.title: Error-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structures connecting computable residuals to distance from a solution set.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-to-solution distance control for saddle variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z=X\times Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) be nonempty and closed, let \(F:Z\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) be the saddle optimality operator, and let \(S=\{z\in Z:0\in F(z)+N_Z(z)\}\) be nonempty. Given a residual mapping \(R:Z\to\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) satisfying \(R(z)=0\) exactly on \(S\), a local error-bound regime at \(\bar z\in S\) holds if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(\operatorname{dist}(z,S)\leq\kappa\lVert R(z)\rVert\) whenever \(z\in Z\) and \(\lVert z-\bar z\rVert\leq\varepsilon\). A global regime requires the inequality for every \(z\in Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to the saddle solution set is bounded by a constant multiple of a computable optimality residual, locally or globally.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a set-valued saddle optimality operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(z,S)\leq\kappa\lVert R(z)\rVert\) on the specified neighborhood, or on all of \(Z\) in the global regime.

notation.meaning: Normal-cone mapping of the feasible set.
