children.title: Weak-Sharpness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Solution-set growth structures associated with sharp variational behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Sharpness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-growth weak sharpness for a nonnegative merit function of a variational problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(S\subset H\) be the nonempty solution set, and let \(\psi:H\to[0,+\infty]\) satisfy \(S=\{x:\psi(x)=0\}\). The problem has global weak sharpness with modulus \(\alpha>0\) when
\[\psi(x)\geq \alpha\,\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{dom}\psi.\]
It has local weak sharpness at \(\bar x\in S\) when the same inequality holds for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\psi\cap B(\bar x,r)\) for some \(r>0\). The supremum of admissible \(\alpha\) is the weak-sharpness modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak sharpness means that a nonnegative merit function grows at least linearly with distance from the solution set, either globally or near a selected solution.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(\varnothing\neq S\subset H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\psi(x)\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) globally or locally, according to the regime.

notation.meaning: solution set, equal to the zero set of the merit function

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The merit-function definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no source identifies this particular weak-sharpness formulation or its modulus convention.

children.title: Metric Subregularity
children.top_down_role: Local inverse-stability structure for the governing operator or inclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Subregularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local metric subregularity of a set-valued operator at a solution of a monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space and \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\). For \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}T\), the operator \(T\) is metrically subregular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) if there exist \(\kappa\geq0\) and \(r>0\) such that
\[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,T^{-1}(\bar y)\bigr)\leq \kappa\,\operatorname{dist}\bigl(\bar y,T(x)\bigr)\qquad\text{for all }x\in B(\bar x,r).\]
For the inclusion \(0\in T(x)\), this is precisely a local residual error bound around \(\bar x\in T^{-1}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity bounds distance to the solution set by a constant times the operator residual near a reference solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,T^{-1}(\bar y))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,T(x))\) locally at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: inverse image of the reference value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inequality is the standard local metric-subregularity definition and matches the plain statement, but the record has no inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Regularity-Notion Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Implications, separations, and scope boundaries among the three regularity notions.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-Notion Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local correspondence among metric subregularity, residual error bounds, and weak sharpness for a compatible merit function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\), set \(S=T^{-1}(0)\neq\varnothing\), and define \(r_T(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,T(x))\). Metric subregularity of \(T\) at \(\bar x\in S\) for \(0\) is exactly the existence of \(\kappa>0\) and a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa r_T(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in V.\]
If, on one neighborhood of \(\bar x\), a merit function \(\psi:H\to[0,+\infty]\) satisfies \(S=\psi^{-1}(0)\), \(\psi(x)\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\), and \(\psi(x)\leq Lr_T(x)\) for constants \(\alpha,L>0\), then \(T\) is metrically subregular there with constant \(L/\alpha\). Conversely, if subregularity holds with \(\kappa>0\) and \(r_T(x)\leq M\psi(x)\) locally for \(M>0\), then \(\psi(x)\geq(\kappa M)^{-1}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) locally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity is precisely a local residual error bound. Local two-sided comparisons between the operator residual and a merit function transfer subregularity to weak sharpness, and conversely, with the stated constants.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space, \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\), and \(\bar x\in S=T^{-1}(0)\neq\varnothing\).
All inequalities used in a transfer hold on one common neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
The constants \(\alpha\), \(L\), \(\kappa\), and \(M\) used in reciprocal expressions are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transferred subregularity constant is \(L/\alpha\), while the transferred weak-sharpness constant is \((\kappa M)^{-1}\).

notation.meaning: operator residual defined by distance from zero to the operator value
zero set of the operator and merit function

children.title: Solution Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Variation of solutions or solution sets under changes in problem data.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz-like sensitivity of the solution mapping for additive perturbations of a variational inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\), and define \(S(p)=\{x\in H:p\in T(x)\}=T^{-1}(p)\). The solution mapping has local Lipschitz-like sensitivity at \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\), together with \(L\geq0\), such that
\[S(p)\cap V\subset S(q)+L\lVert p-q\rVert B_H\qquad\text{for all }p,q\in U.\]
Thus every solution in the localization \(S(p)\cap V\) can be matched to a solution for \(q\) within displacement \(L\lVert p-q\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitz-like solution sensitivity means that every nearby localized solution for one perturbation lies within a distance proportional to the perturbation change from a solution for another nearby perturbation.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(p)\cap V\subset S(q)+L\lVert p-q\rVert B_H\) for all \(p,q\) in a neighborhood of \(\bar p\).

notation.meaning: closed unit ball of the Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-convex-set best-approximate solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic residual and norm minimization for a bounded linear equation restricted to a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\in\mathcal L(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y)\) and let \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal X\) be closed and convex. A \(\mathcal C\)-best-approximate solution \(x_{\mathcal C}^{\dagger}\in\mathcal C\) satisfies
\[
\|Tx_{\mathcal C}^{\dagger}-y\|=\inf_{x\in\mathcal C}\|Tx-y\|
\]
and
\[
\|x_{\mathcal C}^{\dagger}\|=\min\{\|x\|:x\in\mathcal C,\ \|Tx-y\|=\|Tx_{\mathcal C}^{\dagger}-y\|\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained best-approximate solution minimizes the residual over the closed convex feasible set and, among all residual minimizers, has minimum norm.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal X\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{\mathcal C}^{\dagger}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal C}\|Tx-y\|\quad\text{and}\quad x_{\mathcal C}^{\dagger}\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{\|x\|:x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathcal C}\|Tz-y\|\}

children.title: Perturbation Stability
children.top_down_role: Persistence of solution behavior under operator, constraint, or oracle perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local stability furnished by strong metric regularity of the defining operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) and suppose \((\bar x,\bar p)\in\operatorname{gph}T\). Assume that \(T\) is strongly metrically regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar p\): there exist neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar x\) and \(U\) of \(\bar p\) such that the localization \(s(p)=T^{-1}(p)\cap V\) is single-valued on \(U\) and satisfies \(\lVert s(p)-s(q)\rVert\leq\kappa\lVert p-q\rVert\). Then the perturbed inclusion \(p\in T(x)\) has a unique solution in \(V\) for every \(p\in U\), and this local solution is Lipschitz stable with modulus \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity guarantees a unique nearby solution to every small perturbation and Lipschitz dependence of that solution on the perturbation.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is strongly metrically regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar p\) with modulus \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The localized solution \(s(p)\) exists uniquely and obeys \(\lVert s(p)-s(q)\rVert\leq\kappa\lVert p-q\rVert\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conclusion correctly restates the local existence, uniqueness, and Lipschitz consequences encoded by strong metric regularity, and theorem is suitable for this leaf. An authoritative theorem or definition locator is missing.

children.title: Stability-Modulus Regimes
children.top_down_role: Qualitative and quantitative classes of response to perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Stability-Modulus Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative Lipschitz and Hölder regimes, together with qualitative upper-semicontinuous stability, for localized solution mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) and \(X\) be normed spaces, let \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\), and let \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\). A local Hölder stability regime of order \(\theta\in(0,1]\) and constant \(L\geq0\) holds when there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[S(p)\cap V\subset S(q)+L\lVert p-q\rVert^\theta B_X\qquad\text{for all }p,q\in U.\]
The case \(\theta=1\) is the Lipschitz regime, while \(0<\theta<1\) is a Hölder regime. For fixed \(\theta\), the infimum of admissible constants \(L\) is the corresponding local stability modulus. A qualitative upper-semicontinuity regime at \(\bar p\) requires that, for every open set \(W\subset X\) containing \(S(\bar p)\cap V\), there exists a neighborhood \(U_W\) of \(\bar p\) such that \(S(p)\cap V\subset W\) for every \(p\in U_W\); it prescribes no numerical modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Localized solution mappings may obey Lipschitz or Hölder displacement bounds with a quantitative modulus, or only upper-semicontinuous stability without a rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quantitative regimes use the bound \(L\lVert p-q\rVert^\theta\); the qualitative regime requires localized upper semicontinuity without a rate.

notation.meaning: closed unit ball of the normed solution space

children.title: Oracle Information Models
children.top_down_role: Exact, stochastic, and approximate information interfaces separated from update mechanisms.

children.title: Exact Operator Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information interfaces providing exact evaluations of the governing operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Operator Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic exact evaluation interface for a single-valued variational operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset H\) and let \(F:C\to H\) be a single-valued operator. An exact operator oracle is a deterministic map \(\mathcal O_F:C\to H\) satisfying
\[\mathcal O_F(x)=F(x)\qquad\text{for every query }x\in C.\]
An oracle call returns the full operator value without stochastic error, deterministic approximation error, or hidden dependence on previous calls. In a first-order saddle formulation with differentiable coupling \(\Phi(x,y)\), the canonical operator is \(F(x,y)=(\nabla_x\Phi(x,y),-\nabla_y\Phi(x,y))\), and the exact oracle returns this pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact operator oracle deterministically returns the true operator value at every admissible query, with neither bias nor sampling noise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_F(x)=F(x)\) for every \(x\in C\).

children.title: Composite Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information interfaces separating smooth operator access from structured nonsmooth components.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle access for a sum of an explicit operator and a proximable set-valued component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the monotone inclusion \(0\in F(z)+A(z)\) on a Hilbert space \(H\), where \(F:H\to H\) is single-valued and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone. A composite oracle supplies, for each admissible query, the exact value \(F(z)\) and access to the resolvent
\[J_{\gamma A}(u)=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}(u),\qquad \gamma>0.\]
It need not return an arbitrary element of \(A(z)\). This interface supports forward evaluation of \(F\) and implicit treatment of \(A\), including normal cones and subdifferentials whose resolvents are projections or proximal maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite oracle evaluates the explicit operator and computes the resolvent of the implicit monotone component, enabling forward–backward or primal–dual splitting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface returns \(F(z)\) and \(J_{\gamma A}(u)=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}(u)\).

children.title: Oracle-Composition Interface
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of operator evaluations with proximal or structured component access.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Composition Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typed composition of exact forward evaluations, linear maps, and resolvent calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an inclusion \(0\in F(z)+\sum_{i=1}^m L_i^*A_i(L_i z-b_i)\), an oracle-composition interface represents one admissible call as the tuple
\[\mathfrak O(z,(u_i)_{i=1}^m,(\gamma_i)_{i=1}^m)=\bigl(F(z),(L_i z,L_i^*u_i,J_{\gamma_iA_i}(u_i))_{i=1}^m\bigr).\]
Here \(F\) and the bounded linear maps \(L_i,L_i^*\) are evaluated exactly, while each set-valued component is accessed only through its resolvent. An algorithm using this interface may compose returned values algebraically but may not query undeclared derivatives, inverse operators, or elements of \(A_i(z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface exposes exact forward and linear-map evaluations plus declared resolvent calls, thereby fixing which composite operations an algorithm may use.
assumptions_latex: Each \(A_i\) is maximally monotone and each \(L_i\) is bounded linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Available information is exactly \(F(z)\), \(L_i z\), \(L_i^*u_i\), and \(J_{\gamma_iA_i}(u_i)\).

children.title: Unbiased Stochastic Oracles
children.top_down_role: Stochastic operator information with expectation aligned to the target operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbiased Stochastic Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditionally unbiased stochastic evaluation of a variational operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\geq0}\) be the history filtration and let the query \(x_k\) be \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable. A stochastic operator oracle returns \(G(x_k,\xi_k)\in H\). It is conditionally unbiased for \(F:C\to H\) when
\[\mathbb E\!\left[G(x_k,\xi_k)\mid\mathcal F_k\right]=F(x_k)\quad\text{almost surely for every }k.\]
A standard finite-variance regime additionally requires \(\mathbb E[\lVert G(x_k,\xi_k)-F(x_k)\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\leq\sigma^2\). Unbiasedness alone imposes no almost-sure bound on an individual oracle response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbiased stochastic oracle returns a random operator estimate whose conditional expectation, given the entire query history, equals the true operator value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[G(x_k,\xi_k)\mid\mathcal F_k]=F(x_k)\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: information available before oracle call k

children.title: Biased Stochastic Oracles
children.top_down_role: Stochastic operator information containing systematic approximation bias.

knowledge_statements.title: Biased Stochastic Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic operator evaluation with a nonzero conditional mean error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under a history filtration \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\geq0}\), let \(x_k\) be \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable and let the oracle return \(G_k=G(x_k,\xi_k)\). Define its conditional bias by
\[b_k=\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]-F(x_k).\]
The oracle is biased at iteration \(k\) when \(b_k\neq0\) on an event of positive probability. A bounded-bias regime requires \(\lVert b_k\rVert\leq\delta_k\) almost surely for a specified deterministic or predictable sequence \((\delta_k)\). Bias and centered stochastic noise are separated by \(G_k-F(x_k)=b_k+\varepsilon_k\), where \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biased stochastic oracle has conditional mean error. Its total error decomposes into predictable bias and conditionally mean-zero noise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_k-F(x_k)=b_k+\varepsilon_k\) with \(b_k=\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]-F(x_k)\) and \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional bias and centered-noise decomposition is correct for conditionally integrable Hilbert-valued responses, but no source supports the selected biased-oracle model or bounded-bias convention.

children.title: Bias-Control Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes governing persistent, diminishing, or state-dependent oracle bias.

knowledge_statements.title: Bias-Control Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinct quantitative bias conditions for stochastic approximation with step-size-weighted oracle updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b_k=\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]-F(x_k)\) be the conditional oracle bias and let \(\gamma_k>0\) be the step size. Common bias-control regimes include exact unbiasedness,
\[b_k=0\qquad\text{almost surely for every }k,\]
weighted summability,
\[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma_k\lVert b_k\rVert<\infty\qquad\text{almost surely},\]
and vanishing bias,
\[\lVert b_k\rVert\to0\qquad\text{almost surely}.\]
Exact unbiasedness implies both other conditions. Weighted summability and vanishing bias are otherwise not comparable without additional assumptions on \((\gamma_k)\) or \((b_k)\). For updates in which the bias enters as \(-\gamma_k b_k\), weighted summability makes the total norm of the accumulated bias increments finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bias can be absent, summable after step-size weighting, or asymptotically vanishing. Apart from exact unbiasedness, weighted summability and vanishing bias do not imply one another without extra assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(b_k\) is the conditionally integrable oracle bias.
\(\gamma_k>0\) is the step size multiplying the oracle response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact unbiasedness implies weighted summability and vanishing bias, while the latter two regimes are generally incomparable; weighted summability ensures \(\sum_k\gamma_k\lVert b_k\rVert<\infty\).

notation.meaning: step size multiplying the oracle response

children.title: Finite-Sum Oracles
children.top_down_role: Operator information organized through a finite aggregate of component mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-sum operator interface for variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) be positive, and let \(F_i:C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A finite-sum oracle model represents the target operator by \[F(z)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n F_i(z),\qquad z\in C,\] and permits indexed queries \((i,z)\mapsto F_i(z)\). A full evaluation of \(F(z)\) may be obtained by aggregating all component values; its assigned cost depends on the declared oracle model and any available structure or cached information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-sum oracle represents an operator as the average of finitely many component operators and permits indexed component evaluations; the cost of full aggregation is specified separately by the computational model.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) is positive and each \(F_i:C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is evaluable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(z)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nF_i(z)\), with indexed access to \(F_i(z)\).

children.title: Component Oracles

knowledge_statements.title: Component Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indexed first-order oracle for one term of a finite-sum operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) be positive, and suppose \[F(z)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nF_i(z),\qquad F_i:C\to\mathbb{R}^d.\] A component oracle accepts an input \((i,z)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\times C\) and returns the indexed value \(F_i(z)\). The choice of indices and any probability reweighting are specified by a separate component-sampling interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A component oracle returns the value of one indexed component of a finite-sum operator; index selection and reweighting are separate sampling-interface choices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle implements \((i,z)\mapsto F_i(z)\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\times C\).

children.title: Component-Sampling Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Sampling structures governing access to finite operator components.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Sampling Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Filtration-adapted single-component sampling contract for finite-sum operator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) be positive, and let \(F_i:C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) be Borel measurable with \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nF_i\). Let \((\mathcal{F}_k)_{k\geq0}\) be the pre-query filtration and let \(z_k\) be \(\mathcal{F}_k\)-measurable. A component-sampling interface draws \(I_k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \[p_{k,i}=\mathbb{P}(I_k=i\mid\mathcal{F}_k)>0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^np_{k,i}=1,\] and returns \[G_k=\frac{F_{I_k}(z_k)}{n p_{k,I_k}}.\] Whenever \(G_k\) is integrable, the response satisfies \[\mathbb{E}[G_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]=F(z_k).\] A minibatch interface must separately declare its joint sampling law and the corresponding unbiased weighting rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface samples one component using positive history-dependent probabilities and applies inverse-probability weighting so that an integrable response has conditional mean equal to the full operator; minibatch laws require a separate specification.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) is positive, and each \(F_i:C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is Borel measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[G_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]=F(z_k)\).

notation.meaning: conditional probability of sampling component i

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tailed Operator Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased stochastic operator oracle controlled by a fractional moment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(Z(z,\xi)\) be an oracle response, and fix \(p\in(1,2]\). The oracle is \(p\)-moment controlled if, for every \(z\in C\), \[\mathbb{E}[Z(z,\xi)\mid z]=F(z),\qquad \mathbb{E}[\|Z(z,\xi)-F(z)\|_*^p\mid z]\leq \sigma^p.\] It is heavy-tailed in the strict second-moment sense when the displayed bound holds for some \(p<2\) while \(\mathbb{E}[\|Z(z,\xi)-F(z)\|_*^2\mid z]\) need not be finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A heavy-tailed operator oracle is unbiased and has a bounded fractional noise moment, although its noise variance may be infinite.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) lies in a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle noise has uniformly bounded conditional \(p\)-th moment; for \(p<2\), no finite variance is required.

notation.meaning: dual norm used to measure oracle noise

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fractional-moment formulation is plausible, but no source is supplied and heavy-tailed oracle definitions vary regarding unbiasedness, uniformity in z, and whether p=2 is included. An authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Inexact Operator Oracles
children.top_down_role: Approximate information interfaces for evaluations of the governing operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Operator Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic additive-error interface for an operator evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:C\to X^*\) be an operator on a normed space \(X\). An inexact operator oracle with tolerance \(\delta\geq0\) returns \(\widetilde F(z)\in X^*\) at each query \(z\in C\) such that \[\|\widetilde F(z)-F(z)\|_*\leq\delta.\] A query-dependent interface may instead expose a certified tolerance \(\delta_k\) and require the same inequality at \(z_k\). Equivalently, for every \(u\in X\), the response error satisfies \(|\langle\widetilde F(z)-F(z),u\rangle|\leq\delta\|u\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact operator oracle returns an approximate operator value accompanied by a uniform or query-dependent certified dual-norm error bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\delta\geq0\) is known to the calling method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\widetilde F(z)-F(z)\|_*\leq\delta\) at every admissible query.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive dual-norm model is mathematically coherent, but it is only one of several inequivalent inexact-operator oracle conventions. A source is required to establish this exact interface and its exclusion of relative or model-based errors.

children.title: Inexact Prox Oracles
children.top_down_role: Approximate information interfaces for proximal or resolvent computations.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Prox Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate proximal minimization certified by objective suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Hilbert space, let \(h:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). Given \(v\in X\) and \(\varepsilon\geq0\), an inexact prox oracle returns \(x^+\in\operatorname{dom}h\) satisfying \[h(x^+)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x^+-v\|^2\leq\inf_{x\in X}\left\{h(x)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x-v\|^2\right\}+\varepsilon.\] Thus \(x^+\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal solution of the proximal subproblem; \(\varepsilon=0\) recovers the exact proximal mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact prox oracle returns a point whose proximal-subproblem objective is within a certified additive tolerance of the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, closed, and convex on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned \(x^+\) has proximal-objective suboptimality at most \(\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Objective-suboptimality is a valid inexact proximal criterion, but residual, epsilon-subdifferential, and enlargement criteria are not equivalent without additional hypotheses. The exact convention needs an authoritative source.

children.title: Oracle-Error Control Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Absolute, relative, deterministic, or stochastic controls on oracle inexactness.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Error Control Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic and conditional-moment contracts for iteration-dependent oracle errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e_k=\widetilde F_k-F(z_k)\), with \(z_k\) measurable relative to the pre-query history \(\mathcal F_k\). An oracle-error control interface must expose bounds sufficient for the calling method, such as \[\|e_k\|_*\leq\delta_k\quad\text{or}\quad \|\mathbb E[e_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_*\leq b_k,\qquad \mathbb E[\|e_k-\mathbb E[e_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_*^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\leq v_k.\] A convergence specification then declares the required schedule, for example \(\sum_k\alpha_k\delta_k<\infty\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k b_k<\infty\), and \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2v_k<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface reports deterministic error or conditional bias and variance bounds together with the summability schedule required by the consuming algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oracle errors are controlled by declared pointwise or conditional-moment bounds and an explicit weighted summability regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed pointwise and conditional-moment controls are plausible examples, but the summability schedules are algorithm-dependent and do not define a universal oracle-error interface. A source and a precisely delimited consuming-method regime are required.

children.title: Stochastic Linearized-Model Interface
children.top_down_role: A cross-chapter interface for model-based stochastic updates, not a saddle-specific method family.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Linearized-Model Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic model-based stochastic update shared across first-order method families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a closed convex set \(C\), a proper convex regularizer \(h\), a differentiable loss \(f\), a stepsize \(\alpha_k>0\), and \(x_0\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\), sample \(\xi_k\) at iteration \(k\) and obtain \(g_k\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[g_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\). Compute \[x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\left\{h(x)+\langle g_k,x-x_k\rangle+\frac{1}{2\alpha_k}\|x-x_k\|^2\right\}.\] Stop according to a declared iteration or residual criterion and output either the last iterate or a specified weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iteration samples an unbiased first-order model, minimizes its regularized local linearization, and returns a declared last or averaged iterate.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex; \(h\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\alpha_k>0\) and the proximal subproblem has a solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\) minimizes the sampled linearized model plus the proximal regularizer over \(C\).

notation.meaning: information available before sampling at iteration k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric-Projection Fixed-Point Characterization of VI Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of classical VI solutions as fixed points of a metric-scaled projected forward step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty, closed, and convex, let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n, let \gamma>0, and let G=G^{\mathsf T}\succ0. If [z]^+_G denotes projection onto X in the norm \|u\|_G=(u^{\mathsf T}Gu)^{1/2}, then x^* solves \operatorname{VI}(X,f) if and only if [x^*-\gamma G^{-1}f(x^*)]^+_G=x^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive stepsize and symmetric positive-definite metric, a point solves the variational inequality exactly when it is a fixed point of the corresponding metric-projected forward step.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
[z]^+_G\text{ is the projection of }z\text{ onto }X\text{ in }\|\cdot\|_G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in\operatorname{Sol}(\operatorname{VI}(X,f))\iff [x^*-\gamma G^{-1}f(x^*)]^+_G=x^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric Convergence of VI Projection under Strong Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small-step contractivity and geometric convergence of the projection algorithm for a Lipschitz, strongly monotone VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty, closed, and convex. Suppose there exist K and \alpha>0 such that \|f(x)-f(y)\|_2\leq K\|x-y\|_2 and (x-y)^{\mathsf T}(f(x)-f(y))\geq\alpha\|x-y\|_2^2 for all x,y\in X. For every G=G^{\mathsf T}\succ0, there exists \gamma_0>0 such that, for every \gamma\in(0,\gamma_0], T_G is a contraction in \|\cdot\|_G. Consequently, \operatorname{VI}(X,f) has a unique solution, and the sequence generated by the projection algorithm with such a \gamma converges to it geometrically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Lipschitz and strongly monotone mapping, each symmetric positive-definite projection metric admits sufficiently small positive stepsizes for which the projection map is contractive, the VI solution is unique, and the projection algorithm converges geometrically.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\gamma_0>0\ \forall\gamma\in(0,\gamma_0]:\ T_G\text{ is contractive in }\|\cdot\|_G,\quad\operatorname{VI}(X,f)\text{ has a unique solution, and the projection iterates converge geometrically to it}.

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Projected-Operator Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean forward-projection iteration for a constrained variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:C\to\mathbb R^d\), choose \(z_0\in C\), and choose stepsizes \(\gamma_k>0\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), compute \[z_{k+1}=P_C\bigl(z_k-\gamma_kF(z_k)\bigr),\qquad P_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}\frac12\|z-y\|_2^2.\] Stop when a prescribed iteration budget or variational-inequality residual tolerance is reached, and output the last iterate or a declared weighted average. Fixed points satisfy \(z=P_C(z-\gamma F(z))\), equivalently \(0\in F(z)+N_C(z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method takes a forward step along the negative operator value and projects the result onto the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{k+1}=P_C(z_k-\gamma_kF(z_k))\), and every fixed point solves \(0\in F(z)+N_C(z)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected-operator iteration in a fixed positive-definite metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) be symmetric positive definite. Define \[P_C^M(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}\frac12\|z-y\|_M^2,\qquad \|u\|_M^2=\langle Mu,u\rangle.\] Given \(z_0\in C\) and \(\gamma_k>0\), perform \[z_{k+1}=P_C^M\bigl(z_k-\gamma_kM^{-1}F(z_k)\bigr).\] Stop under a declared budget or residual rule. A fixed point satisfies \(0\in F(z)+N_C(z)\); the metric changes the step geometry but not the target inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled projection uses a fixed positive-definite metric for both the preconditioned operator step and the projection geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{k+1}=P_C^M(z_k-\gamma_kM^{-1}F(z_k))\), with fixed points solving \(0\in F(z)+N_C(z)\).

notation.meaning: projection onto C in the M-metric

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity of Scaled Gradient-Projection Limit Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subsequential convergence of scaled gradient projection with uniformly positive-definite, uniformly bounded metrics and feasible-direction line searches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{x^k\}\subseteq X\) be generated by the scaled gradient projection method, with \(\alpha^k\) selected by limited minimization or by the Armijo rule along the feasible direction. Suppose there are constants \(c_1,c_2>0\) such that \(c_1\|z\|^2\le z'H^kz\le c_2\|z\|^2\) for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and every \(k\ge0\). Then every limit point of \(\{x^k\}\) is stationary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled gradient projection has only stationary limit points when its scaling matrices are uniformly positive definite and uniformly bounded and its relaxation parameters are selected by limited minimization or an Armijo search along the feasible direction.
assumptions_latex: \(\{x^k\}\) is generated by the scaled gradient projection method.
Each \(\alpha^k\) is chosen by limited minimization or by the Armijo rule along the feasible direction.
There exist \(c_1,c_2>0\) such that \(c_1\|z\|^2\le z'H^kz\le c_2\|z\|^2\) for all \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and all \(k\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Every limit point of }\{x^k\}\text{ is stationary.}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric Convergence of Scaled Projection for Positive-Definite Affine VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine specialization of fixed-metric projection convergence allowing a nonsymmetric positive-definite operator matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let f(x)=Ax+b, where b\in\mathbb{R}^n and A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is positive definite but need not be symmetric. For every fixed symmetric positive-definite projection metric, sufficiently small positive stepsizes give geometric convergence of scaled projection to that solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Properties and convergence of variable-metric gradient projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects the projection, Lipschitz, fixed-point, descent, and limit-point conclusions of the scaled projection theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{M(t)\}_{t\ge0}\) be a bounded sequence of symmetric \(n\times n\) matrices such that, for some \(\alpha>0\), \[(u-v)^{\mathsf T}M(t)(u-v)\ge\alpha\|u-v\|_2^2\quad\forall u,v\in X,\ \forall t,\] and let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) satisfy Assumption 3.1. Then: (a) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), the \(M(t)\)-projection \([x]^+_t\) onto \(X\) exists uniquely; (b) \(z=[x]^+_t\) iff \((y-z)^{\mathsf T}M(t)(x-z)\le0\) for every \(y\in X\); (c) there is \(A_1\) independent of \(t\) with \(\|[x]^+_t-[y]^+_t\|_2\le A_1\|x-y\|_2\); (d) if \(M(t)\succ0\), then \(\|[x]^+_t-[y]^+_t\|_{M(t)}\le\|x-y\|_{M(t)}\). For the quadratic-update map \(T_t:X\to X\) with \(\gamma>0\): (e) \(T_t(x)=x\) iff \((y-x)^{\mathsf T}\nabla F(x)\ge0\) for every \(y\in X\), and under convexity this is equivalent to minimizing \(F\) over \(X\); (f) there is \(A_2\) independent of \(t\) with \(\|T_t(x)-T_t(y)\|_2\le A_2\|x-y\|_2\); (g) for sufficiently small \(\gamma\), there is \(A_3>0\) such that \(F(T_t(x))\le F(x)-A_3\|T_t(x)-x\|_2^2\) for all \(x\in X\) and all \(t\); and (h) for sufficiently small \(\gamma\), every limit point \(x^*\) of the iterates satisfies \((y-x^*)^{\mathsf T}\nabla F(x^*)\ge0\) for every \(y\in X\), and is a minimizer when \(F\) is convex on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly positive, bounded variable metrics give unique metric projections with a variational characterization, uniform Lipschitz continuity, and metric nonexpansiveness when the metric is positive definite. The resulting quadratic projected-gradient map has fixed points exactly at variationally stationary points, is uniformly Lipschitz, yields sufficient descent for small stepsizes, and has only stationary limit points; under convexity, its fixed points and limit points are constrained minimizers.
assumptions_latex: M(t)\succ0\text{ is additionally required for conclusion (d).}
F\text{ convex on }X\text{ is additionally required for the minimizer equivalences in (e) and (h).}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conclusions (a)--(h) above hold for the metric projections }[\cdot]^+_t\text{ and update maps }T_t.

children.title: Variable-Metric Projection
children.top_down_role: Projection methods whose metric changes across iterations or states.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected-operator iteration with an iteration-dependent positive-definite metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Given \(z_0\in C\), positive stepsizes \(\gamma_k\), and symmetric positive-definite matrices \(M_k\), define \[z_{k+1}=P_C^{M_k}\bigl(z_k-\gamma_kM_k^{-1}F(z_k)\bigr),\qquad P_C^{M_k}(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}\frac12\langle M_k(z-y),z-y\rangle.\] The metric may depend on information available before the update. Stop under a declared budget or residual rule and output the last iterate or a specified average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable-metric projection changes the positive-definite preconditioner and projection geometry from one iteration to the next.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Each \(M_k\) is symmetric positive definite and selected before computing \(z_{k+1}\).

notation.meaning: projection onto C in the current metric

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-metric projection iteration on the nonnegative orthant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The stated formulation is for nonnegativity constraints. Analogous constructions are indicated for box constraints and Cartesian products of simplices, but no general result for those sets is asserted here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the problem \(\min\{f(x):x\ge 0\}\), a two-metric projection iteration is
\[
x^{k+1}=\bigl[x^k-\alpha^kD^k\nabla f(x^k)\bigr]^+,
\]
where \(D^k\) is positive definite and need not be diagonal, while \([\cdot]^+\) denotes Euclidean projection onto \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\). Thus \(D^k\) scales the gradient step, whereas the identity matrix defines the projection metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization over the nonnegative orthant, a two-metric projection step scales the gradient by a positive-definite, possibly nondiagonal matrix and then applies ordinary Euclidean orthant projection. The gradient scaling and projection therefore use different metrics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^{k+1}=\bigl[x^k-\alpha^kD^k\nabla f(x^k)\bigr]^+

children.title: Metric-Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural choices governing admissible fixed or changing projection metrics.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform conditioning and controlled variation for variable projection metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence of symmetric metric matrices \((M_k)_{k\geq0}\) satisfies the uniformly controlled variable-metric regime if there exist \(0<m\leq M<\infty\) and nonnegative \((\eta_k)\) such that \[mI\preceq M_k\preceq MI,\qquad M_{k+1}\preceq(1+\eta_k)M_k,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_k<\infty.\] The first inequalities give uniform norm equivalence and bounded inverse metrics; the final two conditions limit cumulative metric expansion. A fixed-metric regime is recovered by taking \(M_k=M_0\) and \(\eta_k=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Admissible metrics remain uniformly positive definite and bounded, while their cumulative multiplicative variation is summable; a constant metric is the special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(mI\preceq M_k\preceq MI\) and the multiplicative metric variation is summably controlled.

notation.meaning: uniform spectral lower and upper bounds

children.title: Relaxed Projection
children.top_down_role: Projection variants governed by under-relaxation or over-relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation of the metric projection onto a closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(P_C\) denote its metric projection. Given \(z^0\in H\) and relaxation parameters \(\lambda_k>0\), the relaxed projection iteration is
\[z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_k(P_Cz^k-z^k)=(1-\lambda_k)z^k+\lambda_kP_Cz^k.\]
Stop when a prescribed residual tolerance \(\lVert z^k-P_Cz^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) is met, and return \(z^k\). For every fixed \(\lambda\neq0\), the fixed-point set of \((1-\lambda)I+\lambda P_C\) is exactly \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move a chosen fraction of the way from the current point toward its metric projection; feasible points are precisely the fixed points.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}=(1-\lambda_k)z^k+\lambda_kP_Cz^k\), with \(\operatorname{Fix}((1-\lambda)I+\lambda P_C)=C\) for \(\lambda\neq0\).

children.title: Hyperplane Projection
children.top_down_role: Projection variants using separating or supporting hyperplanes.

knowledge_statements.title: Hyperplane Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form orthogonal projection onto an affine hyperplane or its associated halfspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a\in H\setminus\{0\}\), \(b\in\mathbb R\), and define the affine hyperplane \(M=\{z\in H:\langle a,z\rangle=b\}\). Its metric projection has the representation
\[P_Mz=z-\frac{\langle a,z\rangle-b}{\lVert a\rVert^2}a.\]
For the closed halfspace \(Q=\{z\in H:\langle a,z\rangle\leq b\}\),
\[P_Qz=z-\frac{(\langle a,z\rangle-b)_+}{\lVert a\rVert^2}a.\]
Thus each projection requires only one affine residual, one scalar scaling, and a displacement parallel to the normal \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection subtracts the constraint violation in the normal direction, scaled by the squared norm of the hyperplane normal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_Mz=z-(\langle a,z\rangle-b)a/\lVert a\rVert^2\) and \(P_Qz=z-(\langle a,z\rangle-b)_+a/\lVert a\rVert^2\).

notation.meaning: Affine hyperplane with normal a and offset b.

children.title: Relaxation-Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Parameter regimes separating stable relaxation from unstable projection behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp relaxation interval for a metric projection, illustrated by a singleton feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\) in a real Hilbert space, define \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda)I+\lambda P_C\). If \(0<\lambda<2\), then for every \(c\in C\),
\[\lVert T_\lambda z-c\rVert^2\leq\lVert z-c\rVert^2-\lambda(2-\lambda)\lVert z-P_Cz\rVert^2.\]
The coefficient vanishes at \(\lambda=2\), so strict residual decrease is no longer guaranteed. The interval is sharp: for \(H=\mathbb R\) and \(C=\{0\}\), \(T_\lambda z=(1-\lambda)z\); hence \(\lambda=2\) preserves \(|z|\), while \(\lambda<0\) or \(\lambda>2\) expands every nonzero iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxed projection is Fejér-decreasing for relaxation strictly between zero and two; the endpoints lose decay, and parameters outside expand a singleton example.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space.
\(P_C\) is the metric projection and \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda)I+\lambda P_C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual decrease coefficient is \(\lambda(2-\lambda)>0\) exactly when \(0<\lambda<2\), and the singleton example shows sharpness.

children.title: Gradient Descent–Ascent Family
children.top_down_role: Simultaneous, alternating, and unequal-timescale dynamics for saddle and game models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected-payoff gradient and mixed-policy gradient-play update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and last-observed-action gradient updates for independent mixed policies in a finite multiagent game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
U^i(\boldsymbol\pi_t)=\sum_{\mathbf a}R^i(\mathbf a)\prod_j\pi_t^j(a^j).
\]
For each action \(a^i\), the ambient coordinate derivative is
\[
\frac{\partial U^i(\boldsymbol\pi_t)}{\partial\pi_t^i(a^i)}=\sum_{\mathbf a^{-i}}R^i(a^i,\mathbf a^{-i})\prod_{j\ne i}\pi_t^j(a^j).
\]
Gradient play applies
\[
\pi_{t+1}^i(a^i)=\pi_t^i(a^i)+\alpha_t^i\frac{\partial U^i(\boldsymbol\pi_t)}{\partial\pi_t^i(a^i)},
\]
followed by projection onto the probability simplex when the update is not a valid distribution. If the other agents' unknown policies are approximated as replaying their most recently observed actions \(\mathbf a_t^{-i}\), then
\[
\widehat{\frac{\partial U^i}{\partial\pi_t^i(a^i)}}=R^i(a^i,\mathbf a_t^{-i}).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under independent mixed policies, the payoff derivative for one of agent i's actions is that action's expected payoff under the other agents' policies. The agent takes a gradient-ascent step and restores simplex feasibility when necessary. If the other policies are unknown, assuming that the other agents replay their latest observed actions yields the payoff against those actions as a surrogate gradient; it is not the exact gradient without that assumption.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A^j\text{ is finite for every agent }j.
\boldsymbol\pi_t\text{ is a product of independent mixed policies }\pi_t^j.
\text{The surrogate formula assumes that every }j\ne i\text{ replays its most recently observed action.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\partial U^i}{\partial\pi_t^i(a^i)}=\sum_{\mathbf a^{-i}}R^i(a^i,\mathbf a^{-i})\prod_{j\ne i}\pi_t^j(a^j),\qquad \boldsymbol\pi_{t+1}^i\text{ is projected onto }\Delta(\mathcal A^i)\text{ when needed},\qquad \widehat{\frac{\partial U^i}{\partial\pi_t^i(a^i)}}=R^i(a^i,\mathbf a_t^{-i})\text{ under the replay assumption}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient-ascent iteration and geometric step decay
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the basic differentiable maximization update and records its optional geometric step-factor schedule and lack of a global-optimality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a differentiable function \(f\), gradient ascent generates iterates by \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)\), where \(\alpha_k>0\). A constant \(\alpha_k\) is often called a learning rate. An optional geometrically decaying schedule is \(\alpha_{k+1}=\gamma\alpha_k\) with \(0<\gamma<1\). The method does not guarantee attainment of a global maximizer; very small steps may require many iterations, while excessively large steps may oscillate near a local maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable objective, gradient ascent repeatedly moves in the gradient direction using a positive step factor. The step factor may remain constant or decay geometrically by a factor strictly between zero and one. The method has no guarantee of finding a global maximum, and step sizes that are too small or too large can respectively cause slow progress or oscillation near a local maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k),\qquad \alpha_{k+1}=\gamma\alpha_k\ \text{ optionally},\qquad \text{with no general guarantee of a global maximizer}

children.title: Simultaneous Gradient Descent–Ascent
children.top_down_role: Gradient descent–ascent dynamics using concurrent block updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Gradient Descent–Ascent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jacobi-style gradient descent–ascent for a differentiable unconstrained minimax problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\max_{y\in\mathbb R^m}L(x,y)\) with differentiable \(L\), choose \((x^0,y^0)\), step sizes \(\alpha_k, eta_k>0\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\). At iteration \(k\), evaluate both partial gradients at the same old pair and update
\[x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha_k
abla_xL(x^k,y^k),\qquad y^{k+1}=y^k+ eta_k
abla_yL(x^k,y^k).\]
Stop when \(\lVert
abla_xL(x^k,y^k)Vert^2+\lVert
abla_yL(x^k,y^k)Vert^2\leq\varepsilon^2\), or at a prescribed iteration limit, and return the latest pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Update the minimizing and maximizing variables in parallel using gradients evaluated at the same current iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both component updates use derivatives evaluated at \((x^k,y^k)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simultaneous GDA update is standard and algorithm is the correct kind, but no inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: Alternating Gradient Descent–Ascent
children.top_down_role: Gradient descent–ascent dynamics using sequential block updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Gradient Descent–Ascent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauss–Seidel-style descent-first gradient descent–ascent for a differentiable minimax problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\max_{y\in\mathbb R^m}L(x,y)\), initialize \((x^0,y^0)\) and choose \(\alpha_k,\beta_k>0\). The descent-first alternating update is
\[x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha_k\nabla_xL(x^k,y^k),\qquad y^{k+1}=y^k+\beta_k\nabla_yL(x^{k+1},y^k).\]
The ascent-first convention instead computes \(y^{k+1}\) from \((x^k,y^k)\) and then computes \(x^{k+1}\) using \((x^k,y^{k+1})\). Stop at a prescribed stationarity tolerance or iteration limit and return \((x^k,y^k)\). The selected ordering is part of the algorithm specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Update one player first, then evaluate the other player’s gradient using the newly updated first variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The second block uses the newly computed first-block iterate, unlike simultaneous gradient descent–ascent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two alternating conventions are mathematically coherent and algorithm fits the leaf, but the ordering conventions have no inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Update-Ordering Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences of concurrent versus sequential block timing.

knowledge_statements.title: Update-Ordering Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal distinction between simultaneous and sequential two-block gradient update maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G_x(x,y)=x-\alpha\nabla_xL(x,y)\) and \(G_y(x,y)=y+\beta\nabla_yL(x,y)\). The simultaneous, descent-first, and ascent-first update maps are respectively
\[T_{\mathrm{sim}}(x,y)=(G_x(x,y),G_y(x,y)),\]
\[T_{x\to y}(x,y)=\bigl(x^+,G_y(x^+,y)\bigr),\quad x^+=G_x(x,y),\]
\[T_{y\to x}(x,y)=\bigl(G_x(x,y^+),y^+\bigr),\quad y^+=G_y(x,y).\]
All three maps have the same fixed points satisfying \(\nabla_xL(x,y)=0\) and \(\nabla_yL(x,y)=0\), provided \(\alpha,\beta>0\), although their transient dynamics and stability may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous ordering uses only old variables; each alternating ordering lets the second update use the first block’s new value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}(T_{\mathrm{sim}})=\operatorname{Fix}(T_{x\to y})=\operatorname{Fix}(T_{y\to x})=\{(x,y):\nabla_xL(x,y)=0,\ \nabla_yL(x,y)=0\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The update-map representation and common fixed-point characterization are correct for positive step sizes, but neither claim has a cited source.

children.title: Two-Time-Scale Ascent Methods
children.top_down_role: Descent–ascent methods using distinct adaptation scales for the variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Time-Scale Ascent Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient descent–ascent with distinct diminishing step-size scales and a faster ascent variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a differentiable objective \(L(x,y)\), initialize \((x^0,y^0)\) and choose positive sequences \((\alpha_k)\) and \((\beta_k)\). The ascent-fast two-time-scale iteration is
\[x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha_k\nabla_xL(x^k,y^k),\qquad y^{k+1}=y^k+\beta_k\nabla_yL(x^k,y^k),\]
with \(\alpha_k/\beta_k\to0\). A standard stochastic-approximation schedule additionally requires \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\sum_k\beta_k=\infty\) and \(\sum_k(\alpha_k^2+\beta_k^2)<\infty\). Stop at a prescribed residual tolerance or iteration budget and return the latest pair. These scheduling conditions define the method and do not alone assert convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use a diminishing ascent step that remains asymptotically larger than the descent step, so the maximizing variable evolves on the faster scale.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is differentiable on the iterates' domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ascent variable is updated on the asymptotically faster step-size scale.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ascent-fast ratio is coherent, but no source supports the selected two-time-scale convention. Moreover, the scope and plain statement call the steps diminishing while the core assumptions only impose positivity and a ratio limit.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stochastic primal–dual descent–ascent on one or two time scales
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous stochastic gradient descent–ascent and its two-time-scale variant for a smooth strictly convex–concave saddle problem, including the additional envelope-identity requirement for the reduced slow dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f:A\times B\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable, strictly convex in \(x\) and strictly concave in \(y\), and has a unique saddle point \((x^*,y^*)\). The simultaneous stochastic recursion is
\[
x_{n+1}=x_n+a_n[-\nabla_x f(x_n,y_n)+M_{n+1}],\qquad y_{n+1}=y_n+a_n[\nabla_y f(x_n,y_n)+M'_{n+1}].
\]
Its limiting ODE is \(\dot x=-\nabla_xf(x,y)\), \(\dot y=\nabla_yf(x,y)\), for which \(V(x,y)=\tfrac12(\|x-x^*\|^2+\|y-y^*\|^2)\) satisfies \(\dot V<0\) whenever \((x,y)\ne(x^*,y^*)\). Thus convergence follows under the additional standard stochastic-approximation noise, well-posedness, stepsize, and stability hypotheses.

For the two-time-scale variant, replace the dual stepsize by \(b_n\), where
\[
\sum_n b_n=\infty,\qquad \sum_n b_n^2<\infty,\qquad b_n=o(a_n).
\]
Under the corresponding two-time-scale hypotheses, with \(g(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_x f(x,y)\),
\[
x_n-g(y_n)\to0\quad\text{a.s.},
\]
and \(y_n\) tracks \(\dot y=\nabla_yf(g(y),y)\). Identifying this ODE with gradient ascent on \(\min_x f(x,y)\) additionally requires
\[
\nabla_y\min_x f(x,y)=\nabla_yf(g(y),y).
\]
Only when this envelope identity is valid and the reduced dynamics satisfy the required convergence and stability conditions does the stated argument yield almost-sure convergence to the saddle point; without those conditions, that reduced-gradient argument need not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous noisy gradient descent in the primal variable and ascent in the dual variable has a strictly decreasing squared-distance Lyapunov function for a differentiable strictly convex–concave saddle problem. Convergence of the stochastic iterates still requires the usual noise, stepsize, well-posedness, and stability conditions. In the two-time-scale variant, the dual steps are asymptotically slower than the primal steps. The fast primal iterates then track the minimizer associated with the current dual variable, while the dual iterates track a reduced ODE. Interpreting that ODE as gradient ascent on the minimized value function requires an additional envelope identity; without suitable conditions for that identity and for convergence of the reduced dynamics, the convergence argument does not apply.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ and }B\text{ are convex domains on which the recursions and limiting ODEs are well defined}
f\text{ is differentiable, strictly convex in }x\text{ for fixed }y,\text{ and strictly concave in }y\text{ for fixed }x
\text{The applicable stochastic-approximation noise, stepsize, well-posedness, and stability hypotheses hold}
g(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_x f(x,y)\text{ is well defined and the fast recursion tracks it}
\nabla_y\min_x f(x,y)=\nabla_yf(g(y),y)\text{ and the reduced dynamics converge, for the final two-time-scale conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dot V<0\text{ off }(x^*,y^*)\text{ for the simultaneous limiting ODE};\qquad x_n-g(y_n)\to0\ \text{a.s. in the two-time-scale regime, with convergence to }(x^*,y^*)\text{ only under the envelope, reduced-dynamics, and standard stochastic-approximation hypotheses.}

children.title: Multi-Step Ascent Methods
children.top_down_role: Descent–ascent methods using repeated maximizing-block updates per outer cycle.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Step Ascent Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One descent update followed by several inner ascent updates against a frozen primal variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For differentiable \(L(x,y)\), choose outer descent steps \(\alpha_k>0\), inner ascent steps \(\beta_{k,j}>0\), and integers \(q_k\geq1\). Initialize \((x^0,y^0)\). At outer iteration \(k\), set \(y^{k,0}=y^k\), compute
\[x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha_k\nabla_xL(x^k,y^k),\]
and, with \(x^{k+1}\) held fixed, perform
\[y^{k,j+1}=y^{k,j}+\beta_{k,j}\nabla_yL(x^{k+1},y^{k,j}),\quad j=0,\ldots,q_k-1.\]
Set \(y^{k+1}=y^{k,q_k}\). Stop at a prescribed outer residual tolerance or iteration limit and return \((x^k,y^k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After each descent step, hold the new minimizing variable fixed and perform one or more ascent steps on the maximizing variable.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is differentiable on the iterates' domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^{k+1}\) is obtained after \(q_k\) ascent steps with \(x^{k+1}\) frozen.

notation.meaning: Number of inner ascent steps at outer iteration k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The descent-first multi-step ascent algorithm is coherent, but no authoritative source or explicit domains for x and y are supplied.

children.title: Time-Scale Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relative-speed regimes governing tracking between minimizing and maximizing variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Scale Separation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Step-size and inner-loop predicates distinguishing comparable, ascent-fast, and idealized equilibrated-ascent regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha_k>0\) and \(\beta_k>0\) be descent and ascent step sizes, and define \(r_k=\beta_k/\alpha_k\). The scales are comparable when
\[0<\liminf_{k\to\infty}r_k\leq\limsup_{k\to\infty}r_k<\infty,\]
and ascent-fast when \(r_k\to\infty\). For an outer method using \(q_k\) inner ascent steps and producing \(y^{k+1}\), the idealized equilibrated-ascent regime is expressed by
\[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(y^{k+1},Y^*(x^{k+1})\bigr)\to0,\qquad Y^*(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y}L(x,y).\]
These predicates classify scheduling; they do not by themselves imply convergence of the coupled iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Step-size ratios distinguish comparable and ascent-fast dynamics; vanishing distance to the current best-response set defines idealized equilibrated inner ascent.
assumptions_latex: The best-response set \(Y^*(x^{k+1})\) is nonempty whenever the equilibrated regime is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Comparable scales have bounded positive \(r_k\); ascent-fast scales have \(r_k\to\infty\); equilibrated ascent has distance to \(Y^*(x^{k+1})\) tending to zero.

notation.meaning: Maximizer or best-response set at fixed x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ratio predicates are coherent and condition fits the leaf, but the classification lacks a citation and the space and metric underlying the distance to the best-response set are unspecified.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Gradient Descent–Ascent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous gradient descent–ascent applied to a quadratically regularized saddle objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and choose \(\mu_x,\mu_y\geq0\). Define
\[L_{\mu}(x,y)=L(x,y)+\frac{\mu_x}{2}\lVert x\rVert^2-\frac{\mu_y}{2}\lVert y\rVert^2.\]
Given \((x^0,y^0)\) and \(\alpha_k,\beta_k>0\), regularized gradient descent–ascent performs
\[x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha_k\bigl(\nabla_xL(x^k,y^k)+\mu_xx^k\bigr),\]
\[y^{k+1}=y^k+\beta_k\bigl(\nabla_yL(x^k,y^k)-\mu_yy^k\bigr).\]
Stop when the regularized gradient residual meets a prescribed tolerance, and return the latest pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply descent–ascent after adding quadratic convexity in the minimizing variable and quadratic concavity in the maximizing variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration is gradient descent–ascent on \(L_\mu=L+(\mu_x/2)\lVert x\rVert^2-(\mu_y/2)\lVert y\rVert^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed iteration is correctly obtained from the quadratically regularized saddle objective, and algorithm fits the topic, but no authoritative citation supports this selected regularization variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Arrow–Hurwicz Dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected continuous-time primal–dual dynamics for differentiable inequality-constrained convex optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_{x\in X} f(x)\) subject to \(g(x)\leq0\), with Lagrangian \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\langle\lambda,g(x)\rangle\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\). The Arrow–Hurwicz projected dynamics are
\[\dot x\in-\nabla_x\mathcal L(x,\lambda)-N_X(x),\qquad \dot\lambda=\Pi_{T_{\mathbb R_+^m}(\lambda)}g(x).\]
Equivalently, componentwise, \(\dot\lambda_i=g_i(x)\) when \(\lambda_i>0\), and \(\dot\lambda_i=\max\{g_i(x),0\}\) when \(\lambda_i=0\). An equilibrium satisfies primal stationarity together with dual feasibility, complementary slackness, and primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal variable follows projected Lagrangian descent while nonnegative multipliers follow projected constraint-violation ascent.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f\) and every component of \(g\) are differentiable.
Solutions are interpreted as projected differential-inclusion trajectories.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every equilibrium satisfies \(0\in\nabla f(x)+Dg(x)^\mathsf T\lambda+N_X(x)\), \(g(x)\leq0\), \(\lambda\geq0\), and \(\lambda_i g_i(x)=0\).

notation.meaning: Normal cone to X at x.
Tangent cone to the nonnegative orthant at lambda.
Euclidean projection onto tangent cone T.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equilibrium conditions are consistent with the displayed dynamics, but the continuous-time projected Arrow–Hurwicz variant and its differential-inclusion formulation require an authoritative source.

children.title: Uzawa Methods
children.top_down_role: Classical primal–dual schemes organized around primal subproblem resolution and multiplier evolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Uzawa Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-primal-solve Uzawa iteration for convex programs with affine equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_{x\in X} f(x)\) subject to \(Ax=b\), with Lagrangian \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\langle\lambda,Ax-b\rangle\). Given \(\lambda^0\in\mathbb R^m\) and step sizes \(\rho_k>0\), the exact Uzawa iteration computes
\[x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\mathcal L(x,\lambda^k),\qquad \lambda^{k+1}=\lambda^k+\rho_k(Ax^{k+1}-b).\]
Stop when both the feasibility residual \(\lVert Ax^{k+1}-b\rVert\) and an appropriate primal optimality residual meet prescribed tolerances, and return \((x^{k+1},\lambda^{k+1})\). The multiplier update is gradient ascent on the differentiable dual function whenever the primal minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly minimize the Lagrangian over the primal variable, then ascend in the multiplier using the resulting equality-constraint residual.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex.
Each displayed primal argmin is nonempty.
Dual differentiability is asserted only when the primal minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}\) solves the current Lagrangian subproblem and \(\lambda^{k+1}=\lambda^k+\rho_k(Ax^{k+1}-b)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-primal equality-constrained Uzawa iteration is coherent and algorithm is the correct kind, but it lacks a citation; the stated sufficient conditions for dual differentiability also require authoritative support.

children.title: Dual-Ascent Methods
children.top_down_role: Multiplier-space ascent methods beyond the classical Uzawa setting.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and each primal subproblem attains its minimum.
\(f\) and every component of \(g\) are proper convex functions on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda^{k+1}=\Pi_{\mathbb{R}_+^m}(\lambda^k+\alpha_k g(x^k))\) is projected supergradient ascent on \(d\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set \(C\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected dual ascent with an exact primal minimization oracle for convex inequality constraints.

source_refs.locator: Section 8.5, The Dual Projected Subgradient Method, p. 232

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(g_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, and define \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\langle\lambda,g(x)\rangle\) for \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\). Given \(\lambda^0\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and stepsizes \(\alpha_k>0\), compute
\[
x^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda^k),\qquad \lambda^{k+1}=\Pi_{\mathbb{R}_+^m}\bigl(\lambda^k+\alpha_k g(x^k)\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, \(g(x^k)\in\partial^+ d(\lambda^k)\) for the concave dual function \(d(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda)\), where \(\partial^+d\) denotes the concave superdifferential. Stop when a prescribed dual-gap, feasibility, or iteration criterion is met, and output the selected primal-dual iterate or an ergodic primal average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly minimize the Lagrangian in the primal variable, then take a projected supergradient-ascent step on the nonnegative dual multipliers.

children.title: Primal-Solve Accuracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exact and approximate primal-resolution regimes within dual-oriented dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Solve Accuracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact, summably inexact, and vanishing-error primal-oracle regimes for dual ascent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At iteration \(k\), an inexact primal oracle returns \(x^k\in X\) satisfying
\[
L(x^k,\lambda^k)\le d(\lambda^k)+\varepsilon_k,
\qquad d(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda),
\]
where \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\). The exact regime is \(\varepsilon_k=0\). A summably weighted inexact regime satisfies \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k\varepsilon_k<\infty\). A vanishing-error regime satisfies \(\varepsilon_k\to0\), while a fixed-accuracy regime satisfies \(\varepsilon_k\le\bar\varepsilon\) and ordinarily supports convergence only to an error neighborhood. The applicable regime must be paired with the stepsize and convergence theorem used for the dual update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal solves may be exact, summably inexact, asymptotically exact, or uniformly approximate; the error regime determines whether exact convergence or only neighborhood convergence is supportable.
assumptions_latex: \(x^k\) is feasible for the primal domain \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal-oracle regime is classified by \(\varepsilon_k=0\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k\varepsilon_k<\infty\), \(\varepsilon_k\to0\), or \(\sup_k\varepsilon_k\le\bar\varepsilon\).

source_refs.locator: Section 8.5, The Dual Projected Subgradient Method, p. 232

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition container fits, but the cited exact dual projected-subgradient section does not inspectably support all four inexact primal-solve regimes. In particular, the role of \(\sum_k\alpha_k\varepsilon_k<\infty\), vanishing error, and fixed-error neighborhoods depends on the accompanying stepsize and convergence theorem. A dedicated inexact dual-ascent source is required.

children.title: Non-Euclidean Learning Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Single-call non-Euclidean dynamics and their online-learning interpretations.

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Mirror Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jacobi-style mirror descent for a differentiable convex-concave saddle problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be closed convex sets, and let \(\Phi:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\). Let \(h_X\) and \(h_Y\) be differentiable strongly convex distance generators. From \((x^0,y^0)\in X\times Y\), simultaneously compute
\[
x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{\alpha_k\langle\nabla_x\Phi(x^k,y^k),x\rangle+D_{h_X}(x,x^k)\right\},
\]
\[
y^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y}\left\{-\alpha_k\langle\nabla_y\Phi(x^k,y^k),y\rangle+D_{h_Y}(y,y^k)\right\}.
\]
Both gradients are evaluated at the same old iterate. Stop by a prescribed saddle-gap or iteration criterion and output a selected iterate or weighted ergodic average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimizing player takes a mirror step along its gradient, while the maximizing player simultaneously takes a mirror step against its negative gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of finite-dimensional normed spaces.
\(\Phi\) is differentiable, convex-concave, and finite on \(X\times Y\).
\(h_X\) and \(h_Y\) are differentiable and strongly convex on their domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed updates define simultaneous mirror descent-ascent for \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}\Phi(x,y)\).

children.title: Dual Averaging
children.top_down_role: Mirror-based dynamics driven by accumulated dual-space information.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularized dual averaging for a convex-concave saddle operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z=X\times Y\), let \(F(x,y)=(\nabla_x\Phi(x,y),-\nabla_y\Phi(x,y))\), and let \(h:Z\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be strongly convex. Initialize \(z^0\in Z\), \(s^0=0\), and choose weights \(\alpha_k>0\) and regularization scales \(\beta_k>0\). For \(k\ge0\), set
\[
s^{k+1}=s^k+\alpha_kF(z^k),\qquad
z^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in Z}\left\{\langle s^{k+1},z\rangle+\beta_{k+1}h(z)\right\}.
\]
Stop using a prescribed variational-inequality gap or iteration budget; a standard reported point is \(\bar z^N=(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_k)^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_k z^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accumulate all past saddle gradients in dual space, then recover each primal-dual iterate through a strongly convex regularized minimization.
assumptions_latex: \(Z=X\times Y\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The regularized minimization has a solution for every accumulated vector \(s^{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}\) is the regularized dual-averaging response to \(\sum_{i=0}^{k}\alpha_iF(z^i)\).

A dedicated dual-averaging locator is required.

children.title: Multiplicative Weights
children.top_down_role: No-regret dynamics using multiplicative reweighting over simplex-like domains.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates remain in \(\Delta_n\times\Delta_m\) and coincide with simultaneous mirror steps generated by negative entropy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entropic simultaneous descent-ascent on probability simplices.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 9, Mirror Descent, p. 247

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\Delta_n\), \(Y=\Delta_m\), and let \(\Phi:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\). Initialize strictly positive \(x^0\in\Delta_n\) and \(y^0\in\Delta_m\). For \(\eta_k>0\), compute simultaneously
\[
x_i^{k+1}=\frac{x_i^k\exp(-\eta_k[\nabla_x\Phi(x^k,y^k)]_i)}{\sum_{r=1}^n x_r^k\exp(-\eta_k[\nabla_x\Phi(x^k,y^k)]_r)},
\]
\[
y_j^{k+1}=\frac{y_j^k\exp(\eta_k[\nabla_y\Phi(x^k,y^k)]_j)}{\sum_{s=1}^m y_s^k\exp(\eta_k[\nabla_y\Phi(x^k,y^k)]_s)}.
\]
Stop by a prescribed saddle-gap or iteration budget and output the chosen iterate or a weighted ergodic average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each player exponentially reweights its simplex coordinates, decreasing the minimizer's costly coordinates and increasing the maximizer's rewarding coordinates, then normalizes.

children.title: Entropic Geometry Interface
children.top_down_role: Geometric correspondence linking multiplicative weighting to entropy-based mirror structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Entropic Geometry Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between simplex mirror steps and normalized exponential reweighting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On the probability simplex \(\Delta_n\), let \(h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i\), with \(0\log0=0\). For \(x^k\in\operatorname{ri}(\Delta_n)\), \(g^k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\eta_k>0\), the entropic mirror step
\[
x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\Delta_n}\left\{\eta_k\langle g^k,x\rangle+D_h(x,x^k)\right\}
\]
has the coordinate representation
\[
x_i^{k+1}=\frac{x_i^k\exp(-\eta_k g_i^k)}{\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^k\exp(-\eta_k g_j^k)},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
Thus the negative-entropy mirror map provides the exact interface between Bregman-proximal geometry and multiplicative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-entropy mirror step on the simplex is exactly a normalized exponential, or multiplicative-weights, update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Mirror}_{h}(x^k,\eta_kg^k)_i=x_i^k e^{-\eta_kg_i^k}/\sum_jx_j^k e^{-\eta_kg_j^k}\).

children.title: Korpelevich Extragradient Family
children.top_down_role: The canonical two-evaluation correction family and projection-saving variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Extragradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Korpelevich's two-projection method for a monotone Lipschitz variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and seek \(z^\star\in C\) such that \(\langle F(z^\star),z-z^\star\rangle\ge0\) for every \(z\in C\). Given \(z^0\in C\) and \(0<\gamma<1/L\), iterate
\[
y^k=\Pi_C\bigl(z^k-\gamma F(z^k)\bigr),\qquad
z^{k+1}=\Pi_C\bigl(z^k-\gamma F(y^k)\bigr).
\]
Stop when a prescribed residual, gap, or iteration criterion is met, and output the selected last iterate or an ergodic average. The predictor \(y^k\) supplies the corrected operator evaluation used in the second projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extragradient first predicts by a projected forward step, then corrects from the old point using the operator evaluated at the predictor.
assumptions_latex: The solution set of the variational inequality is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^k=\Pi_C(z^k-\gamma F(z^k))\) and \(z^{k+1}=\Pi_C(z^k-\gamma F(y^k))\) define Euclidean extragradient.
