children.title: Projection-Method Ergodic Convergence
children.top_down_role: Ergodic convergence guarantees for projected first-order VI methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Method Ergodic Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projected-gradient ergodic bound for bounded monotone variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be a nonempty compact convex subset of a Euclidean space with diameter at most \(D\), and let \(F:Z\to Z^*\) be monotone with \(\|F(z)\|\leq M\). Starting from \(z_1\in Z\), set \(z_{t+1}=\Pi_Z(z_t-\gamma_tF(z_t))\), where \(\gamma_t>0\), and define \(\bar z_T=(\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_tz_t)/(\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_t)\). For the dual variational-inequality gap \(G_D(z)=\sup_{u\in Z}\langle F(u),z-u\rangle\), \[G_D(\bar z_T)\leq\frac{D^2+M^2\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_t^2}{2\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_t}.\] Taking \(\gamma_t=D/(M\sqrt T)\) gives \(G_D(\bar z_T)\leq DM/\sqrt T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaged projected-gradient iterates solve a bounded monotone variational inequality at rate one over the square root of the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and has Euclidean diameter at most \(D\).
\(F\) is monotone on \(Z\) and satisfies \(\|F(z)\|\leq M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_D(\bar z_T)\leq DM/\sqrt T\) for the stated constant stepsize.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the feasible set.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: projected-gradient regret inequality for bounded monotone operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected-gradient ergodic bound is a standard complexity bound under the stated bounded-operator and diameter assumptions, with consistent gap notation. Its exact inequality and constant are unsupported because source_refs is empty.

children.title: Extragradient Ergodic Convergence
children.top_down_role: Ergodic convergence guarantees for prediction-correction extragradient methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Extragradient Ergodic Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean extragradient gap bound for monotone Lipschitz variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be a nonempty compact convex Euclidean set of diameter at most \(D\), and let \(F:Z\to Z^*\) be monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz. For \(0<\gamma\leq 1/L\), generate \(y_t=\Pi_Z(z_t-\gamma F(z_t))\) and \(z_{t+1}=\Pi_Z(z_t-\gamma F(y_t))\). With \(\bar y_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T y_t\) and \(G_D(z)=\sup_{u\in Z}\langle F(u),z-u\rangle\), the ergodic iterate satisfies \[G_D(\bar y_T)\leq\frac{D^2}{2\gamma T}.\] Hence choosing \(\gamma=1/L\) yields \(G_D(\bar y_T)\leq LD^2/(2T)\), requiring two operator evaluations per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extragradient averaging attains an order-one-over-iterations gap for monotone Lipschitz variational inequalities using two operator calls per iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and has diameter at most \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_D(\bar y_T)\leq D^2/(2\gamma T)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Korpelevich extragradient ergodic estimate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record has the correct complexity-bound role and states the deterministic monotone-Lipschitz regime separately. The precise admissible endpoint gamma = 1/L and factor 1/2 depend on the extragradient estimate being used and require an inspectable theorem locator.

children.title: Projection–Extragradient Complexity Separation
children.top_down_role: Operator-geometry regimes distinguishing their ergodic performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection–Extragradient Complexity Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case oracle-complexity separation under boundedness versus Lipschitz regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider monotone variational inequalities on a compact convex Euclidean set of diameter \(D\). If only \(\|F(z)\|\leq M\) is assumed, projected gradient with ergodic averaging guarantees gap at most \(\varepsilon\) after \(T=O(D^2M^2/\varepsilon^2)\) operator calls. If, additionally, \(F\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, extragradient guarantees the same gap after \(T=O(LD^2/\varepsilon)\) iterations and therefore \(O(LD^2/\varepsilon)\) operator calls up to its factor of two. Thus Lipschitz prediction-correction changes the certified ergodic dependence on accuracy from \(\varepsilon^{-2}\) to \(\varepsilon^{-1}\); the comparison is between these stated guarantee regimes, not a universal lower bound for every projection scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded projected gradient needs order epsilon inverse squared calls, while Lipschitz extragradient needs order epsilon inverse calls for ergodic gap accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) is compact and convex with diameter \(D\), and \(F\) is monotone.
Projected gradient uses the boundedness condition \(\|F\|\leq M\); extragradient additionally uses \(L\)-Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{proj}}(\varepsilon)=O(D^2M^2\varepsilon^{-2})\) and \(N_{\mathrm{EG}}(\varepsilon)=O(LD^2\varepsilon^{-1})\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: comparison of standard projected-gradient and extragradient upper bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison is appropriately framed as a separation between two upper-bound regimes rather than a universal lower bound, and complexity_bound fits the leaf. The paired oracle-complexity claims have no cited source, so their exact assumptions and call accounting remain unsupported.

knowledge_statements.title: Mirror-Prox Ergodic Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bregman Mirror-Prox complexity for monotone Lipschitz variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be compact and convex, let \(F:Z\to Z^*\) be monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz with respect to a norm, and let \(\omega\) be differentiable and \(1\)-strongly convex. Write \(V_z(u)=\omega(u)-\omega(z)-\langle\nabla\omega(z),u-z\rangle\) and \(\Omega=\sup_{z,u\in Z}V_z(u)<\infty\). Mirror-Prox performs two Bregman prox steps per iteration, first using \(F(z_t)\) to obtain \(y_t\), then using \(F(y_t)\) to obtain \(z_{t+1}\). For a valid constant stepsize \(\gamma\leq 1/L\), its average \(\bar y_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T y_t\) satisfies \[G_D(\bar y_T)\leq\frac{\Omega}{\gamma T}.\] Consequently, \(T=O(L\Omega/\varepsilon)\) iterations suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mirror-Prox achieves an order-one-over-iterations ergodic gap in a geometry determined by a strongly convex distance-generating function.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz in the chosen primal-dual norms.
\(\omega\) is differentiable and \(1\)-strongly convex on compact convex \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_D(\bar y_T)\leq\Omega/(\gamma T)\), hence \(T=O(L\Omega/\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: Bregman divergence generated by the distance function.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected content kind matches the Mirror-Prox complexity leaf, and the claimed order is standard. The prox updates are only described verbally, while the exact stepsize threshold and coefficient depend on the prox convention; source_refs contains no theorem-level citation resolving these details.

children.title: Stochastic Ergodic Complexity
children.top_down_role: Ergodic oracle complexity under sampled or noisy operator access.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Ergodic Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected stochastic Mirror-Prox complexity with unbiased bounded-variance oracle noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be compact and convex with diameter \(D\), and let \(F\) be monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz. Suppose an oracle returns \(F(z)+\xi\), where \(\mathbb E[\xi\mid z]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[\|\xi\|_*^2\mid z]\leq\sigma^2\), with conditionally independent samples used in the two stochastic Mirror-Prox calls. For a suitable stepsize schedule and the weighted average \(\bar z_T\), the expected dual gap obeys \[\mathbb E[G_D(\bar z_T)]\leq C\left(\frac{LD^2}{T}+\frac{\sigma D}{\sqrt T}\right)\] for a universal constant \(C\). Therefore accuracy \(\mathbb E[G_D]\leq\varepsilon\) requires \(O(LD^2/\varepsilon+\sigma^2D^2/\varepsilon^2)\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic Mirror-Prox combines a deterministic inverse-iteration term with a variance-driven inverse-square-root term in expected ergodic gap.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz on compact convex \(Z\) of diameter \(D\).
Oracle errors are conditionally unbiased with conditional second moment at most \(\sigma^2\).
The two oracle samples within each iteration satisfy the required conditional independence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[G_D(\bar z_T)]\leq C(LD^2/T+\sigma D/\sqrt T)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic-plus-variance rate has the correct complexity-bound role and keeps the stochastic regime explicit. The universal-constant formulation, geometry dependence, averaging rule, and oracle-call complexity require a precise stochastic Mirror-Prox source, but no citation is supplied.

children.title: Inexact Ergodic Complexity
children.top_down_role: Ergodic complexity under controlled deterministic or biased evaluation error.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Ergodic Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ergodic Mirror-Prox bound with deterministic per-iteration prox-oracle errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the deterministic Mirror-Prox assumptions, suppose the two prox computations at iteration \(t\) satisfy their exact three-point inequalities only up to a combined nonnegative error \(\delta_t\). For constant admissible stepsize \(\gamma\), let \(\bar y_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T y_t\). Then the accumulated inexactness enters the certificate additively: \[G_D(\bar y_T)\leq\frac{\Omega+\sum_{t=1}^T\delta_t}{\gamma T}.\] Hence exact-order \(O(1/T)\) convergence is retained when \(\sum_{t=1}^T\delta_t=O(1)\). If instead \(\delta_t\leq\bar\delta\), the method reaches an error neighborhood of order \(\bar\delta/\gamma\), so arbitrarily small certified gaps require vanishing average inexactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mirror-Prox prox errors accumulate in the numerator; summable errors preserve the inverse-iteration rate, while persistent errors create a gap floor.
assumptions_latex: The exact deterministic Mirror-Prox hypotheses and an admissible constant stepsize \(\gamma\) hold.
Each iteration satisfies the specified inexact three-point inequality with combined error \(\delta_t\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_D(\bar y_T)\leq(\Omega+\sum_{t=1}^T\delta_t)/(\gamma T)\).

notation.meaning: Combined additive prox-subproblem error at iteration t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record belongs in an inexact ergodic complexity leaf, but the phrase 'combined nonnegative error' does not fully define the inexact three-point inequalities. The placement and scaling of the accumulated errors are convention-dependent and cannot be validated without an exact source and locator.

children.title: Noise–Inexactness Interactions
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes where stochastic variation coexists with systematic evaluation error.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise–Inexactness Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive decomposition of stochastic variance and deterministic inexactness in an ergodic gap bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider stochastic Mirror-Prox on a compact convex domain of diameter \(D\), with a monotone \(L\)-Lipschitz operator, conditionally unbiased oracle noise of variance at most \(\sigma^2\), and nonnegative inexact-prox errors \(\delta_t\). For an admissible stepsize policy, the standard ergodic analysis has the form \[\mathbb E[G_D(\bar z_T)]\leq C_1\frac{LD^2}{T}+C_2\frac{\sigma D}{\sqrt T}+C_3\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T\frac{\delta_t}{\gamma_t},\] where \(C_1,C_2,C_3\) are universal constants fixed by the prox convention. Thus stochastic noise and deterministic inexactness contribute separate terms; preserving statistical accuracy requires the weighted average inexactness not to dominate \(\sigma D/\sqrt T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variance and prox inexactness add distinct ergodic-error terms; the inexactness schedule must decay fast enough not to overwhelm the stochastic rate.
assumptions_latex: The stochastic oracle is conditionally unbiased with conditional variance at most \(\sigma^2\).
The prox computations incur additive errors \(\delta_t\geq0\) under a fixed inexactness convention.
The stepsizes \(\gamma_t\) satisfy the stability condition of stochastic Mirror-Prox.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T\delta_t/\gamma_t=O(\sigma D/\sqrt T)\) prevents inexactness from dominating the stochastic term.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hilbert-Space Projected Stochastic Primal-Dual Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space specialization for regularity parameter \(r\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the Hilbert case with \(r\ge2\), initialize \(x_1=0\) and \(l_1=0\), and iterate
\[x_{i+1}=\pi_G\bigl(x_i-\rho_i\psi_x(x_i,l_i;F,\omega_i)\bigr),\qquad l_{i+1}=\pi_{G_I}\bigl(l_i+\rho_i\psi_l(x_i,l_i;F,\omega_i)\bigr).\]
Form the ergodic output
\[(x^i,l^i)=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j(x_j,l_j)}{\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j}.\]
Its expected performance satisfies
\[\mathbf M_{\mathbf F_{\omega^{i-1}}}v(x^i,l^i;F)\le v_0+\frac{1+\tfrac14L^2\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j^2}{L\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the underlying spaces are Hilbert and r is at least two, stochastic mirror descent reduces to projected stochastic descent in the primal variable and projected stochastic ascent in the dual variable. The displacement-weighted average obeys the displayed expected-gap bound.
assumptions_latex: \text{The primal and dual geometries are Hilbertian}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf M_{\mathbf F_{\omega^{i-1}}}v(x^i,l^i;F)\le v_0+\frac{1+\frac14L^2\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j^2}{L\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mean Convergence Bound for Averaged Stochastic Mirror Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of process (3.1)–(3.2) under diminishing, nonsummable displacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\rho_i>0\), \(\rho_i\to0\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\rho_i=\infty\), then for every \(\bar F\in D_{r,L^\infty}^{\epsilon,v_0}\), the averaged stochastic mirror-descent process satisfies
\[\limsup_{i\to\infty}\mathbf M_{\mathbf F_{\omega^{i-1}}}v(x^i,l^i;F)\le v_0.\]
Moreover, for every \(i\),
\[\mathbf M_{\mathbf F_{\omega^{i-1}}}v(x^i,l^i;F)\le v_0+\frac{2+3L\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j\bigl(\omega_{V,r}(2L\rho_j)+\omega_{V_I,r}(2L\rho_j)\bigr)}{2L\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For positive displacements that vanish but have divergent sum, the expected performance value of the averaged stochastic mirror-descent iterates has asymptotic upper limit at most v0. A finite-iteration upper bound is given by the accumulated continuity moduli divided by the accumulated displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \limsup_{i\to\infty}\mathbf M_{\mathbf F_{\omega^{i-1}}}v(x^i,l^i;F)\le v_0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Saddle points and the minimax characterization of convex–concave games
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the saddle-point definition with its primal–dual minimax characterization and compactness-based existence statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G\subset E$ and $G_\ell\subset E_\ell$ be nonempty, bounded, closed, convex sets in reflexive normed spaces, and let $F:G\times G_\ell\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, convex in $x$ for every $\ell$, and concave in $\ell$ for every $x$. Define $\overline F(x)=\sup_{\ell\in G_\ell}F(x,\ell)$ and $\underline F(\ell)=\inf_{x\in G}F(x,\ell)$. A pair $(x^*,\ell^*)$ is a saddle point iff $F(x,\ell^*)\ge F(x^*,\ell^*)\ge F(x^*,\ell)$ for all $(x,\ell)\in G\times G_\ell$. Equivalently, $x^*\in\arg\min_G\overline F$, $\ell^*\in\arg\max_{G_\ell}\underline F$, and $\min_G\overline F=\max_{G_\ell}\underline F$. The saddle-point set is $X^*(F)\times L^*(F)$, and under the stated assumptions it is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous convex–concave payoff on nonempty bounded closed convex subsets of reflexive spaces, a saddle point is a pair at which the first variable minimizes and the second maximizes. Saddle points are exactly pairs of optimal strategies whose primal and dual game values agree; all such pairs form the product of the two optimal-strategy sets, and at least one exists.
assumptions_latex: E\text{ and }E_\ell\text{ are reflexive normed spaces}
\varnothing\ne G\subset E,\ \varnothing\ne G_\ell\subset E_\ell\text{ are bounded, closed, and convex}
F:G\times G_\ell\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous, convex in }x\text{, and concave in }\ell
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Saddle}(F)=X^*(F)\times L^*(F)\ne\varnothing,\qquad \min_{x\in G}\sup_{\ell\in G_\ell}F(x,\ell)=\max_{\ell\in G_\ell}\inf_{x\in G}F(x,\ell).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Repeated finite-game model with uncoupled randomized play
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the repeated-play process, conditional action distributions, observation model, and uncoupled information restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each round $t\geq1$ of a repeated finite $K$-player game, player $k$ chooses a history-dependent mixed strategy $p_t^{(k)}\in\Delta(A_k)$ and independently samples $I_t^{(k)}\sim p_t^{(k)}$, independently of the other players' current randomizations conditional on past play. Thus $\Pr(I_t^{(k)}=i\mid I_1,\ldots,I_{t-1})=p_{i,t}^{(k)}$. Under full action monitoring, $p_t^{(k)}$ may depend on $(I_1,\ldots,I_{t-1})$; an uncoupled procedure additionally uses player $k$'s own loss function and observed loss history but not the other players' loss functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a repeated finite game, each player selects a history-dependent mixed strategy each round and independently samples an action from it. With full action monitoring, strategies may use past joint plays; an uncoupled learner knows and uses its own losses but not the other players' loss functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(I_t^{(k)}=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=p_{i,t}^{(k)},\qquad p_t^{(k)}\text{ may be history-dependent and uncoupled.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite-Step Stochastic Primal-Dual Mirror Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithm statement for positive deterministic displacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(\varphi _0=0\) and \(\lambda _0=0\). For deterministic \(\rho_i>0\), set \(x_i=V'(\varphi_{i-1})\), \(\bar x_i=\pi_G(x_i)\), \(l_i=V_I'(\lambda_{i-1})\), and \(\bar l_i=\pi_{G_I}(l_i)\). Given the stochastic oracle realization \(\omega_i\), update
\[\varphi_i=\varphi_{i-1}-\rho_i\bigl(\psi_x(\bar x_i,\bar l_i;F,\omega_i)+\|\psi_x(\bar x_i,\bar l_i;F,\omega_i)\|_*\mu_G(x_i)\bigr),\]
\[\lambda_i=\lambda_{i-1}+\rho_i\bigl(\psi_l(\bar x_i,\bar l_i;F,\omega_i)-\|\psi_l(\bar x_i,\bar l_i;F,\omega_i)\|_{I*}\mu_{G_I}(l_i)\bigr),\]
and output the weighted averages
\[(x^i,l^i)=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j(\bar x_j,\bar l_j)}{\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from zero dual accumulators, each iteration maps the accumulators through the two mirror maps, projects the resulting primal and dual points, applies stochastic primal descent and dual ascent with projection-correction terms, and returns the displacement-weighted average of the projected iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^i,l^i)=\left(\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j\right)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^i\rho_j(\bar x_j,\bar l_j)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymmetric-Game Coercivity, Decoupling, and Bounded-Control Assumptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additional hypotheses supplementing the individual-player assumptions in the asymmetric case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every $i=1,\ldots,N$: (A) $\Xi_{ii}\succ0$ with $\lambda_{\min}(\Xi_{ii})=\sigma_i^\Xi>0$, while $W_{ii}=W_{ii}^\top\succeq0$; (W) $W_{ii'}=0$ for every $i'\ne i$; and (D) $$D_i u_i\ge0\ \Longrightarrow\ u_i=0.$$ Consequently, for every state $x_i$, the feasible-control set $$U_i(x_i):=\{u\in\mathbb R^{m_i}:f_i+C_i x_i+D_i u\ge0\}$$ is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the asymmetric case, each player's diagonal Xi block is positive definite, its diagonal W block is symmetric positive semidefinite, cross-player W blocks vanish, and the only direction satisfying D_i u_i at least zero is the zero direction. The last condition makes every state-dependent feasible-control set bounded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fictitious play and its convergence boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines fictitious play and records its principal finite-game convergence cases and failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a finite repeated game, player \(k\) uses fictitious play if, for every \(t\ge 2\), it selects
\[
I_t^{(k)}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{i_k\in\{1,\ldots,N_k\}}\frac{1}{t-1}\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\ell^{(k)}(\mathbf I_s^{-},i_k).
\]
This rule is not Hannan consistent. If both players use it in a two-player zero-sum game, the product of their empirical action distributions converges to the set of Nash equilibria; the same conclusion holds for arbitrary two-player games when both players have two actions. It does not extend to all two-player non-zero-sum games: empirical play frequencies can fail even to converge to the set of correlated equilibria.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each round, a fictitious-play player chooses a best response to the opponents' empirical play through the preceding round. The rule is not Hannan consistent. When both players use it, empirical product distributions converge to the Nash-equilibrium set in two-player zero-sum games and in arbitrary two-player games with two actions per player. For some two-player non-zero-sum games, however, empirical frequencies fail even to approach the correlated-equilibrium set.
assumptions_latex: K=2\text{ and both players use fictitious play for the stated convergence guarantees}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{cases}\text{the empirical product distributions converge to the Nash-equilibrium set},&\text{for two-player zero-sum games or two-player games with }N_1=N_2=2,\\\text{convergence can fail even for the correlated-equilibrium set},&\text{for general two-player non-zero-sum games.}\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex–Concave Minimax Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax equality for a bounded convex–concave function with compactness and continuity on the minimizing side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Y\) be convex sets, with \(\mathcal X\) compact, and let \(f:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\) be bounded. If, for every \(y\in\mathcal Y\), \(f(\cdot,y)\) is convex and continuous, and, for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), \(f(x,\cdot)\) is concave, then
\[
\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\sup_{y\in\mathcal Y}f(x,y)=\sup_{y\in\mathcal Y}\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x,y).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If X and Y are convex, X is compact, and a bounded real-valued function on X × Y is convex and continuous in its first argument and concave in its second argument, then its infimum–supremum equals its supremum–infimum.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\text{ is bounded}
\forall y\in\mathcal Y,\ f(\cdot,y)\text{ is convex and continuous}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\sup_{y\in\mathcal Y}f(x,y)=\sup_{y\in\mathcal Y}\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x,y)

knowledge_statements.title: Extragradient Last-Iterate Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional last-iterate convergence of extragradient for monotone Lipschitz variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(F:Z\to Z\) be monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz, and suppose the solution set \(Z^*=\{z^*\in Z:\langle F(z^*),z-z^*\rangle\geq0\ \text{for all }z\in Z\}\) is nonempty. Generate \(y_t=\Pi_Z(z_t-\gamma F(z_t))\) and \(z_{t+1}=\Pi_Z(z_t-\gamma F(y_t))\) with a fixed \(0<\gamma<1/L\). Then the corrected iterates \((z_t)\) converge to some \(z^\infty\in Z^*\); moreover, \(\|z_t-y_t\|\to0\). This is last-iterate convergence and does not require ergodic averaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a strictly stable constant stepsize, finite-dimensional extragradient iterates converge directly to a solution of a monotone Lipschitz variational inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) is nonempty, closed, and convex in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_t\to z^\infty\in Z^*\) and \(\|z_t-y_t\|\to0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Theorem is the correct content kind, and the statement clearly distinguishes finite-dimensional last-iterate convergence from ergodic convergence. The exact convergence theorem, strict stepsize range, and Euclidean identification implicit in F: Z to Z require a theorem-level citation; source_refs is empty.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimistic-Gradient Last-Iterate Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Last-iterate convergence of optimistic gradient in unconstrained bilinear zero-sum games.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and define the bilinear game operator \(M(x,y)=(Ay,-A^\top x)\). Assume the saddle set \(\ker M\) is nonempty, and initialize \(z_{-1},z_0\in\mathbb R^{m+n}\). Optimistic gradient uses \[z_{t+1}=z_t-2\eta Mz_t+\eta Mz_{t-1}.\] If \(0<\eta<1/(2\|M\|_2)\), then \((z_t)\) converges to a point \(z^\infty\in\ker M\), and \(Mz_t\to0\). Thus the current play, rather than merely its running average, converges to the bilinear saddle set under the stated stability restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an unconstrained bilinear zero-sum game and a sufficiently small fixed stepsize, optimistic-gradient iterates converge directly to the saddle set.
assumptions_latex: \(M(x,y)=(Ay,-A^\top x)\) is the linear skew-symmetric bilinear game operator.
\(\ker M\neq\varnothing\), with arbitrary finite initial iterates \(z_{-1},z_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_t\to z^\infty\in\ker M\) and \(Mz_t\to0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role and unconstrained bilinear scope fit the leaf. The precise threshold 1/(2||M||_2), convergence for arbitrary two-point initialization, and nullspace limit are sensitive to the OGDA recurrence convention and need a primary theorem citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Estimated-regret tail bound from small conditional expected regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concentration guarantee for a player's estimated regret over a period in an unknown game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that, during a period of length \(T\), player \(k\) has conditional expected regret \(\mathbb{E}[r_{m,i_k}^{(k)}\mid \mathbf I_1,\ldots,\mathbf I_{mT}]\le \varepsilon\). For sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), with the parameter choices of Theorem 7.8, \[\mathbb{P}\!\left[\widehat r_{m,i_k}^{(k)}\ge \rho\right]\le cT^{-1/3}+\exp\!\left(-T^{1/3}(\rho-\varepsilon)^2\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If player k's conditional expected regret during a period of length T is at most epsilon, then, for sufficiently small epsilon and the prescribed parameter choices, the probability that its estimated regret is at least rho is at most c times T^(-1/3) plus exp(-T^(1/3)(rho-epsilon)^2).
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is the length of the period}
\text{The parameters are chosen as in Theorem 7.8}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb{P}[\widehat r_{m,i_k}^{(k)}\ge \rho]\le cT^{-1/3}+\exp(-T^{1/3}(\rho-\varepsilon)^2)

children.title: Stochastic Last-Iterate Convergence
children.top_down_role: Last-iterate convergence under sampled or noisy operator information.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Last-Iterate Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-square last-iterate convergence under strong monotonicity and Robbins–Monro stepsizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be closed and convex, and let \(F:Z\to Z^*\) be \(\mu\)-strongly monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz, so its variational inequality has a unique solution \(z^*\). Suppose \(g_t=F(z_t)+\xi_t\), where \(\mathbb E[\xi_t\mid z_t]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[\|\xi_t\|^2\mid z_t]\leq\sigma^2\), and set \(z_{t+1}=\Pi_Z(z_t-\alpha_tg_t)\). If \(\sum_t\alpha_t=\infty\), \(\sum_t\alpha_t^2<\infty\), and eventually \(\alpha_t<2\mu/L^2\), then \(z_t\to z^*\) almost surely and in mean square. For \(\alpha_t=a/(t+b)\) with \(2\mu a>1\), \(\mathbb E\|z_t-z^*\|^2=O(1/t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity, unbiased bounded-variance noise, and square-summable but nonsummable stepsizes yield direct stochastic convergence to the unique solution.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz on closed convex \(Z\).
Oracle noise is conditionally unbiased with conditional second moment at most \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_t\to z^*\) almost surely and in mean square; for the stated harmonic stepsize, \(\mathbb E\|z_t-z^*\|^2=O(t^{-1})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Theorem fits the stochastic last-iterate leaf, but conditioning only on z_t does not explicitly impose the martingale-difference condition relative to the full past normally used for almost-sure convergence. The mean-square conclusion and O(1/t) harmonic-stepsize rate also require an exact stochastic-approximation theorem locator, which is absent.

children.title: Learning-Dynamic Last-Iterate Convergence
children.top_down_role: Last-iterate behavior of adaptive game-learning dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Learning-Dynamic Last-Iterate Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Almost-sure last-iterate convergence for projected stochastic approximation in a strongly monotone game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\mu\)-strongly monotone with \(\mu>0\). Consider the learning dynamic \(x_{t+1}=P_C(x_t-\eta_t(F(x_t)+\xi_{t+1}))\). If \(\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\), \(\mathbb{E}[\|\xi_{t+1}\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\leq \sigma^2\), \(\eta_t>0\), \(\sum_t\eta_t=\infty\), and \(\sum_t\eta_t^2<\infty\), then the variational inequality has a unique solution \(x^\star\), and \(x_t\to x^\star\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected learning dynamic with unbiased bounded-variance noise and Robbins–Monro step sizes converges almost surely in its last iterate when the game operator is strongly monotone and Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex; \(F\) is Lipschitz and strongly monotone.
\((\xi_{t+1})\) is a martingale-difference noise sequence with uniformly bounded conditional second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t\to x^\star\) almost surely, where \(x^\star\) is the unique solution of \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the feasible set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Robbins–Monro convergence under strong monotonicity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem and content kind fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the almost-sure last-iterate result with these exact hypotheses.

children.title: Stochastic Learning-Dynamic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Last-iterate regimes combining learning dynamics with stochastic feedback.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Learning-Dynamic Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible noise and step-size regime for stochastic projected learning dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an adapted recursion \(x_{t+1}=P_C(x_t-\eta_t(F(x_t)+\xi_{t+1}))\), the classical diminishing-step stochastic regime is defined by \(\eta_t>0\), \(\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\eta_t=\infty\), \(\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\eta_t^2<\infty\), \(\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\), and \(\mathbb{E}[\|\xi_{t+1}\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\leq \sigma^2\) almost surely for some finite \(\sigma\). A constant-step regime instead takes \(\eta_t\equiv\eta>0\) and generally supports convergence only to a noise-controlled neighborhood unless the noise variance vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The diminishing-step regime combines persistent but square-summable learning rates with unbiased bounded-variance noise; constant steps generally leave a nonzero stochastic error floor.
assumptions_latex: The projection and noisy operator evaluations are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed predicates distinguish the almost-sure stochastic-approximation regime from the constant-step error-floor regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diminishing-step conditions are standard, but the constant-step error-floor assertion depends on stability, geometry, and noise assumptions that require a precise source.

children.title: Strong-Geometry Convergence
children.top_down_role: Sharper convergence enabled by strong monotonicity, strong saddle curvature, error bounds, or weak sharpness.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Monotone VI Linear Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projected-gradient contraction for a Lipschitz strongly monotone variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Suppose \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\mu\)-strongly monotone, with \(0<\mu\leq L\). For \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\gamma F(x_k))\) and \(0<\gamma<2\mu/L^2\), the unique solution \(x^\star\) satisfies \[\|x_{k+1}-x^\star\|\leq q\|x_k-x^\star\|,\qquad q=\sqrt{1-2\gamma\mu+\gamma^2L^2}<1.\] Hence \(k\geq \log(\|x_0-x^\star\|/\varepsilon)/(-\log q)\) iterations ensure \(\|x_k-x^\star\|\leq\varepsilon\). With \(\gamma=\mu/L^2\), this is \(O((L/\mu)^2\log(1/\varepsilon))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected gradient contracts geometrically for a Lipschitz strongly monotone VI; its basic worst-case condition-number dependence is quadratic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x_k-x^\star\|\leq q^k\|x_0-x^\star\|\) with \(q<1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex–Strongly Concave Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear convergence of simultaneous projected descent–ascent under strong convexity–concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\times Y\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f\) be differentiable, \(\mu\)-strongly convex in \(x\), and \(\mu\)-strongly concave in \(y\). Assume the saddle operator \(F(x,y)=(\nabla_x f(x,y),-\nabla_y f(x,y))\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz. For \(z_{k+1}=P_{X\times Y}(z_k-\gamma F(z_k))\), where \(0<\gamma<2\mu/L^2\), the saddle point \(z^\star\) is unique and \[\|z_k-z^\star\|\leq(1-2\gamma\mu+\gamma^2L^2)^{k/2}\|z_0-z^\star\|.\] Thus simultaneous projected descent–ascent converges linearly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity–concavity makes the saddle operator strongly monotone, so projected simultaneous descent–ascent converges geometrically for a sufficiently small step.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and strongly convex–strongly concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_k\to z^\star\) linearly with factor \(\sqrt{1-2\gamma\mu+\gamma^2L^2}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reduction of strong convexity–concavity to strong monotonicity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction to a strongly monotone saddle operator is plausible and theorem fits, but the exact projected descent–ascent rate and existence claim lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Error-Bound Convergence
children.top_down_role: Convergence regimes controlled by error-bound geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear distance convergence obtained from residual error bounds and sufficient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the nonempty solution set of a variational inequality, and let \(R:C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) be a residual satisfying the local error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\|R(x)\|\) on a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\). Suppose an iteration remains in \(U\) and satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)^2\leq\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^2-c\|R(x_k)\|^2\] for some \(c>0\). Then \[\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)^2\leq(1-c/\kappa^2)\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^2.\] When \(0<c\leq\kappa^2\), the iterates converge locally linearly in distance to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual error bound converts sufficient residual descent into local geometric convergence of the distance to the VI solution set.
assumptions_latex: A local residual error bound holds with constant \(\kappa>0\).
The iteration satisfies sufficient descent with constant \(c>0\).
All relevant iterates remain in the error-bound neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\leq(1-c/\kappa^2)^{k/2}\operatorname{dist}(x_0,S)\).

notation.meaning: computable residual vanishing on the solution set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract contraction implication is mathematically coherent and theorem fits, but no source identifies an admissible VI residual and supports this local convergence formulation.

children.title: Weak-Sharpness Convergence
children.top_down_role: Convergence regimes controlled by weak-sharpness geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Sharpness Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of merit decay into distance convergence under weak sharpness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\neq\varnothing\) be the solution set and let \(G:C\to[0,\infty]\) be a merit function with \(G(x)=0\) exactly on \(S\). If weak sharpness holds, meaning that \(G(x)\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) for every \(x\) in a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\), then every sequence \((x_k)\subset U\) satisfying \(G(x_k)\leq\varepsilon_k\) obeys \[\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\leq\varepsilon_k/\alpha.\] Consequently, sublinear, linear, or finite termination of the merit values transfers with the same qualitative regime to distance from the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak sharpness turns any bound on a valid VI merit function into a proportional bound on distance to the solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is nonnegative and vanishes exactly on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x_k)\leq\varepsilon_k\) implies \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\leq\varepsilon_k/\alpha\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elementary merit-to-distance implication is valid, but C is not introduced and calling the assumed inequality VI weak sharpness requires a specific source and definition.

children.title: Error-Bound–Weak-Sharpness Relations
children.top_down_role: Implication and separation regimes between the two geometric conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound–Weak-Sharpness Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between linear merit error bounds and merit-based weak sharpness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\neq\varnothing\), let \(U\) be a neighborhood of \(S\), and let \(G:U\to[0,\infty]\) vanish exactly on \(S\). The linear merit error bound \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa G(x)\qquad(x\in U)\] is equivalent to the weak-sharpness inequality \[G(x)\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\qquad(x\in U)\] under the reciprocal identification \(\alpha=1/\kappa\). This equivalence concerns the same merit function and neighborhood; it does not by itself identify a norm-residual error bound with weak sharpness without additional comparison inequalities between the residual and \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For one merit function, a linear distance error bound and weak sharpness are reciprocal inequalities; residual-based bounds require an additional merit–residual comparison.
assumptions_latex: Both predicates use the same set, neighborhood, and merit function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa G(x)\) if and only if \(G(x)\geq\kappa^{-1}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic equivalence for a common merit function

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reciprocal inequalities are algebraically equivalent, but the ambient metric space is unspecified, the VI terminology is unsupported, and property may fit this relation better than duality.

children.title: Oracle Complexity Boundary System
children.top_down_role: Complexity classes and information-theoretic boundaries separated by geometry and oracle access.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Monotone-VI Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ergodic first-order complexity of Euclidean extragradient for deterministic monotone VIs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be compact and convex with diameter at most \(D\), and let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) be monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz. Euclidean extragradient with \(\gamma=1/L\) computes \(y_t=P_C(x_t-\gamma F(x_t))\) and \(x_{t+1}=P_C(x_t-\gamma F(y_t))\). For \(\bar y_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}y_t\), its dual gap satisfies \[\sup_{z\in C}\langle F(z),\bar y_T-z\rangle\leq\frac{LD^2}{2T}.\] Therefore at most \(2\lceil LD^2/(2\varepsilon)\rceil\) deterministic operator evaluations suffice for gap at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deterministic extragradient solves a compact Lipschitz monotone VI to ergodic gap accuracy ε using order LD²/ε operator evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is compact, convex, and has diameter at most \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic oracle complexity is \(O(LD^2/\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: diameter bound for the feasible set

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Stochastic VI Complexity
children.top_down_role: VI complexity under unbiased, noisy, or distributional oracle access.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic VI Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-gap complexity for stochastic first-order solution of compact monotone VIs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be compact and convex with diameter at most \(D\), and let \(F\) be monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz. Suppose a stochastic oracle returns \(F(x)+\xi\) with conditional mean \(F(x)\) and conditional second moment \(\mathbb{E}[\|\xi\|^2\mid x]\leq\sigma^2\). A suitably stepped stochastic mirror-prox method admits an averaged point \(\bar x_T\) satisfying \[\mathbb{E}[G(\bar x_T)]\leq c_1\frac{LD^2}{T}+c_2\frac{\sigma D}{\sqrt{T}},\] where \(c_1,c_2>0\) are universal constants. Thus \(O(LD^2/\varepsilon+\sigma^2D^2/\varepsilon^2)\) oracle calls suffice for expected gap at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic mirror-prox combines a deterministic 1/T term with a noise-limited 1/√T term, yielding deterministic-plus-statistical oracle complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is compact and convex with diameter at most \(D\).
Oracle noise is conditionally unbiased with variance at most \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon)=O(LD^2/\varepsilon+\sigma^2D^2/\varepsilon^2)\) stochastic oracle calls.

notation.meaning: oracle calls required for expected gap ε

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated stochastic Mirror-Prox rate is plausible, but G and the precise method are not defined, and no source supports the oracle model, constants, or resulting complexity.

children.title: Finite-Sum VI Complexity
children.top_down_role: VI complexity under explicit finite-component operator structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum VI Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance-reduced component-oracle complexity in strongly monotone finite-sum VIs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nF_i(x)\) on a closed convex set \(C\), where each component is \(L\)-Lipschitz and the average operator is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone. In the component-oracle model, variance-reduced extragradient methods exist whose expected squared-distance guarantee \(\mathbb{E}\|x-x^\star\|^2\leq\varepsilon\|x_0-x^\star\|^2\) uses \[O\!\left(\left(n+\sqrt n\,\frac{L}{\mu}\right)\log\frac1\varepsilon\right)\] component evaluations, under the standard sampling and component-regularity conditions of the selected method. The bound exploits repeated access to the fixed components and is not an online stochastic-oracle guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variance reduction can solve strongly monotone finite-sum VIs with logarithmic accuracy dependence and a complexity reflecting both dataset size and conditioning.
assumptions_latex: Accuracy is relative expected squared distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The component complexity is \(O((n+\sqrt n L/\mu)\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for an appropriate variance-reduced extragradient method.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact finite-sum rate cannot be assessed from the phrase 'standard conditions of the selected method'; the algorithm, component assumptions, sampling model, and authoritative source are required.

children.title: Stochastic-to-Finite-Sum Separations
children.top_down_role: Oracle-access distinctions governing achievable complexity across the two models.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic-to-Finite-Sum Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy-dependence separation between online noisy and reusable finite-sum operator oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a strongly monotone problem with condition parameter \(\mu>0\), an online unbiased oracle with irreducible variance \(\sigma^2>0\) generally requires \(\Omega(\sigma^2/(\mu^2\varepsilon))\) samples to guarantee \(\mathbb{E}\|x-x^\star\|^2\leq\varepsilon\). By contrast, when \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nF_i\) and the same components can be revisited, variance reduction may attain complexity logarithmic in \(1/\varepsilon\), after paying a dataset-dependent term. Hence a finite-sum oracle cannot be modeled merely as an online stochastic oracle without losing the reusable-component structure responsible for linear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Irreducible online noise forces inverse-accuracy sample growth, while reusable finite-sum components permit variance reduction and logarithmic accuracy dependence.
assumptions_latex: The online oracle has nonvanishing variance \(\sigma^2\).
The finite-sum oracle permits repeated indexed access to fixed components.
Accuracy is expected squared distance to the strongly monotone solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Online stochastic and finite-sum component models have different attainable dependence on \(\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure_boundary fits the leaf, but the lower bound lacks a defined oracle and problem class, while the finite-sum comparison depends on an unspecified variance-reduced theorem.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Saddle Conditioning Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition-number comparison of basic descent–ascent and extragradient in strongly monotone saddle systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the saddle operator \(F\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\mu\)-strongly monotone, and write \(\kappa=L/\mu\). Optimally stepped projected simultaneous descent–ascent has worst-case contraction factor \(\sqrt{1-1/\kappa^2}\), hence requires \(O(\kappa^2\log(1/\varepsilon))\) operator evaluations to reduce distance by a factor \(\varepsilon\). Under the same deterministic first-order oracle model, an appropriate extragradient or proximal-point approximation achieves a contraction yielding \(O(\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon))\) operator evaluations. Thus strong saddle geometry permits linear convergence, while the method determines whether conditioning enters linearly or quadratically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity gives linear convergence, but basic simultaneous descent–ascent may scale quadratically in condition number whereas extragradient can scale linearly.
assumptions_latex: The oracle is deterministic and first order.
Accuracy is measured by relative distance contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Basic descent–ascent has \(O(\kappa^2\log(1/\varepsilon))\) complexity, while suitable extragradient schemes attain \(O(\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected-gradient quadratic conditioning follows the earlier contraction, but the claimed linear-conditioning extragradient or inexact proximal result requires a particular algorithm, constraints, step rule, and oracle-counting source.

children.title: VI Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Information-based lower bounds for variational inequality problem classes.

knowledge_statements.title: VI Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic first-order oracle lower bound for Lipschitz monotone variational inequalities on Euclidean balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z\) be a Euclidean ball of radius \(R\), and let an oracle return \(F(z)\) for an unknown monotone, \(L\)-Lipschitz operator \(F:Z\to Z\)'s ambient space. For every deterministic method making at most \(T\) adaptive oracle calls, in sufficiently large dimension there exists such an operator for which its output \(z_T\) satisfies
\[
G_D(z_T):=\sup_{u\in Z}\langle F(u),z_T-u\rangle\ge \frac{cLR^2}{T+1},
\]
where \(c>0\) is a universal constant. Consequently, guaranteeing \(G_D(z_T)\le\varepsilon\) requires \(\Omega(LR^2/\varepsilon)\) oracle calls in this model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic first-order method needs order LR²/ε oracle calls, in the worst case, to reduce the dual gap of a Lipschitz monotone VI below ε.
assumptions_latex: \(F:Z\to E\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz on a Euclidean ball \(Z\) of radius \(R\).\)
The method is deterministic and accesses the instance only through evaluations of \(F\).
The ambient dimension may grow with the query budget \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_D(z_T)\ge cLR^2/(T+1)\) for some admissible instance, hence \(T=\Omega(LR^2/\varepsilon)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical deterministic black-box lower-bound form for Lipschitz monotone variational inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role and mathematical form are plausible, but the exact deterministic oracle model, dimension requirement, gap convention, and unrestricted-method lower bound require an authoritative lower-bound source.

children.title: Saddle Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Information-based lower bounds for convex–concave and structured saddle problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case lower bound for affine-bilinear convex-concave saddle problems under a first-order oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Euclidean balls with radii bounded by \(R\). Consider affine-bilinear payoffs
\[
\Phi(x,y)=\langle Ax,y\rangle+\langle a,x\rangle+\langle b,y\rangle
\]
whose saddle operator \(F(x,y)=(Ay+a,-A^{\mathsf T}x-b)\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz. For every deterministic method using at most \(T\) evaluations of this first-order oracle, sufficiently large-dimensional instances exist whose output \((x_T,y_T)\) obeys
\[
\max_{y\in Y}\Phi(x_T,y)-\min_{x\in X}\Phi(x,y_T)\ge \frac{cLR^2}{T+1}.
\]
Thus worst-case saddle-gap accuracy \(\varepsilon\) requires \(\Omega(LR^2/\varepsilon)\) oracle evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine-bilinear saddle problems can force any deterministic first-order method to use order LR²/ε oracle evaluations for saddle-gap accuracy ε.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are bounded Euclidean balls with radii at most \(R\).\)
The deterministic method receives only first-order oracle values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Gap}(x_T,y_T)\ge cLR^2/(T+1)\) on some sufficiently high-dimensional instance.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: affine-bilinear saddle instances are the standard transfer class for monotone-VI lower bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed lower bound needs an authoritative source. In addition, for the displayed payoff <Ax,y>, the stated operator has transposes reversed: the associated operator should be (A^T y+a,-Ax-b) under the usual dimensions.

children.title: VI-to-Saddle Lower-Bound Transfers
children.top_down_role: Reductions and representation conditions transferring hardness between VI and saddle formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: VI-to-Saddle Lower-Bound Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact gap-preserving reduction for affine-bilinear saddle problems and their monotone variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty compact convex \(X,Y\), define \(Z=X\times Y\),
\[
\Phi(x,y)=\langle Ax,y\rangle+\langle a,x\rangle+\langle b,y\rangle,
\qquad F(x,y)=(A^{\mathsf T}y+a,-Ax-b).
\]
For every \(z=(x,y)\in Z\), cancellation of the skew bilinear terms gives
\[
\sup_{u\in Z}\langle F(u),z-u\rangle
=
\max_{v\in Y}\Phi(x,v)-\min_{u_x\in X}\Phi(u_x,y).
\]
Moreover, evaluating \(F(x,y)\) uses exactly the saddle first-order information \((\nabla_x\Phi(x,y),-\nabla_y\Phi(x,y))=(A^{\mathsf T}y+a,-Ax-b)\). Hence any oracle lower bound for this VI class transfers without loss to the corresponding saddle-gap problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For affine-bilinear games, the VI dual gap equals the saddle gap and both oracles return the same information, so VI lower bounds transfer directly.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty compact convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(\Phi\) is affine-bilinear with the displayed coefficients.
The VI is measured by its dual gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_D(x,y)=\max_{v\in Y}\Phi(x,v)-\min_{u_x\in X}\Phi(u_x,y)\), with oracle-preserving lower-bound transfer.

children.title: First-Order Stationarity
children.top_down_role: First-order targets for nonconvex minimax formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained first-order stationarity for a differentiable zero-sum minimax problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be closed convex sets, and let \(f\) be continuously differentiable near \((x,y)\in X\times Y\). The pair \((x,y)\) is first-order stationary for \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)\) when
\[
0\in \nabla_x f(x,y)+N_X(x),
\qquad
0\in-\nabla_y f(x,y)+N_Y(y).
\]
Equivalently, \(\langle\nabla_x f(x,y),u-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(u\in X\), and \(\langle\nabla_y f(x,y),v-y\rangle\le0\) for every \(v\in Y\). For interior points, both partial gradients vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimax pair is first-order stationary when neither player has a feasible first-order improving direction; at an interior point, both partial gradients are zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable near the candidate pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\nabla_x f(x,y)+N_X(x)\) and \(0\in-\nabla_y f(x,y)+N_Y(y)\).

children.title: Value-Function Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Stationarity targets induced by outer value functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Function Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity of the outer value function under a unique differentiable inner maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y\) be compact, let \(f:\mathbb R^n\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and suppose \(f(\cdot,y)\) is continuously differentiable for every \(y\). Define
\[
\varphi(x)=\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y).
\]
If the maximizer \(y^*(x)\) is unique and the hypotheses of the differentiable Danskin formula hold at \(x\), then
\[
\nabla\varphi(x)=\nabla_x f(x,y^*(x)).
\]
Thus unconstrained value-function stationarity is the condition \(\nabla_x f(x,y^*(x))=0\). If instead \(x\in X\) for a closed convex set \(X\), stationarity is \(0\in\nabla_x f(x,y^*(x))+N_X(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a unique regular inner maximizer, the value-function gradient is the payoff’s x-gradient at that maximizer, yielding an explicit outer stationarity condition.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is compact and the inner maximum is attained uniquely at \(y^*(x)\).
\(f\) satisfies the continuity and differentiability hypotheses of the differentiable Danskin formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla\varphi(x)=\nabla_x f(x,y^*(x))\), so value-function stationarity reduces to the corresponding outer first-order condition.

notation.meaning: normal cone to the outer feasible set

children.title: Stationarity Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Regimes linking the two stationarity notions.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between value-function and joint first-order stationarity under exact inner maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume the setting of the differentiable value-function formula, and let \(y^*(x)\) be the unique inner maximizer. If \(y^*(x)\) lies in the interior of \(Y\), then \(\nabla_y f(x,y^*(x))=0\). Therefore
\[
\nabla\varphi(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\nabla_x f(x,y^*(x))=0,
\]
and either side, together with exact inner optimality, implies
\[
\nabla_x f(x,y^*(x))=0,
\qquad
\nabla_y f(x,y^*(x))=0.
\]
Conversely, joint first-order stationarity alone does not imply value-function stationarity unless the selected \(y\) is an actual inner maximizer for that \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an exact unique interior inner maximizer, outer value stationarity and joint stationarity correspond; an arbitrary jointly stationary pair need not satisfy this relation.
assumptions_latex: The inner maximizer \(y^*(x)\) is unique, exact, and interior to \(Y\).
The differentiable Danskin formula holds at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla\varphi(x)=0\) is equivalent to joint first-order stationarity at \((x,y^*(x))\); the converse fails without inner optimality.

children.title: Inner-Solution Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of value-function targets on inner-solution behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Solution Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz sensitivity of a unique maximizer under uniform strong concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be closed and convex, and suppose \(f(x,\cdot)\) is differentiable and \(\mu\)-strongly concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). Assume
\[
\|\nabla_y f(x_1,y)-\nabla_y f(x_2,y)\|\le L_{yx}\|x_1-x_2\|
\]
for all admissible \(x_1,x_2,y\). If \(y^*(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in Y}f(x,y)\) exists, then it is unique and
\[
\|y^*(x_1)-y^*(x_2)\|\le \frac{L_{yx}}{\mu}\|x_1-x_2\|.
\]
Thus the inner solution map has condition number at most \(L_{yx}/\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform strong concavity makes the inner maximizer unique and Lipschitz in the outer variable, with sensitivity bounded by the cross-gradient Lipschitz constant divided by curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x,\cdot)\) is differentiable and uniformly \(\mu\)-strongly concave on closed convex \(Y\).
\(\nabla_y f\) is \(L_{yx}\)-Lipschitz with respect to \(x\), uniformly in \(y\).
An inner maximizer exists for every considered \(x\).

children.title: Local Minimax Points
children.top_down_role: Local leader–follower solution targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Minimax Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential local minimax notion for smooth unconstrained zero-sum games.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\), a pair \((x^*,y^*)\) is a local minimax point if there exist \(\delta_0>0\) and a function \(h:(0,\delta_0]\to(0,\infty)\) with \(h(\delta)\to0\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\), such that for every \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\), every \(x\) with \(\|x-x^*\|\le\delta\), and every \(y\) with \(\|y-y^*\|\le\delta\),
\[
f(x^*,y)\le f(x^*,y^*)
\le \max_{\|y'-y^*\|\le h(\delta)}f(x,y').
\]
The maximizer may respond locally to each nearby outer decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimax point is locally maximal in y, while each nearby x is assessed after allowing a shrinking local y-response.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is real-valued on a neighborhood of \((x^*,y^*)\).
The local response radius \(h(\delta)\) is positive and converges to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed two-sided local minimax inequalities hold for all sufficiently small \(\delta\).

notation.meaning: shrinking radius allowed for the maximizing player's response

children.title: Differential Nash Points
children.top_down_role: Local simultaneous-game equilibrium targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Differential Nash Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict second-order differential Nash equilibrium for a smooth unconstrained zero-sum game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. A pair \((x^*,y^*)\) is a strict differential Nash point of the zero-sum game \(\min_x\max_y f(x,y)\) when
\[
\nabla_x f(x^*,y^*)=0,
\qquad
\nabla_y f(x^*,y^*)=0,
\]
and the own-action Hessians satisfy
\[
\nabla_{xx}^2f(x^*,y^*)\succ0,
\qquad
\nabla_{yy}^2f(x^*,y^*)\prec0.
\]
These conditions make \(x^*\) a strict local minimizer against fixed \(y^*\) and \(y^*\) a strict local maximizer against fixed \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict differential Nash point is jointly stationary, locally strictly minimizing in the minimizer’s own variable and locally strictly maximizing in the maximizer’s own variable.
assumptions_latex: The strategy spaces are locally unconstrained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(
abla f(x^*,y^*)=0\), \(
abla_{xx}^2f(x^*,y^*)\succ0\), and \(
abla_{yy}^2f(x^*,y^*)\prec0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential Nash equilibrium for constrained dynamic games
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open-loop finite-horizon dynamic games in which each player chooses an absolutely continuous state trajectory and an integrable control subject to linear dynamics and mixed state-control constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\mathcal T>0\). For each player \(i=1,\ldots,N\), admissible trajectories satisfy \(x^i(0)=\xi^i\) and, for almost every \(t\in[0,\mathcal T]\), \[\dot x^i(t)=r^i+A^i x^i(t)+B^i u^i(t),\qquad f^i+C^i x^i(t)+D^i u^i(t)\ge0,\] with \(x^i\) absolutely continuous and \(u^i\) integrable. A feasible tuple \((x^*,u^*)=((x^{*,i},u^{*,i}))_{i=1}^N\) is a differential Nash equilibrium if, for every player \(i\), \[ (x^{*,i},u^{*,i})\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x^i,u^i)\text{ admissible}}V_i(x^i,x^{*,-i},u^i,u^{*,-i}). \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differential Nash equilibrium is a feasible collection of state-control trajectories such that, for every player, the player's trajectory pair minimizes that player's objective among all pairs satisfying its initial condition, linear dynamics, and mixed state-control constraints when all rival trajectories are held fixed.

f^i+C^i x^i(t)+D^i u^i(t)\ge0\text{ for almost every }t

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Notion Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order relationship between strict differential Nash and strict local minimax points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be twice continuously differentiable and let \((x^*,y^*)\) be jointly stationary with \(H_{yy}:=\nabla_{yy}^2f(x^*,y^*)\prec0\). Define the reduced Hessian
\[
S:=H_{xx}-H_{xy}H_{yy}^{-1}H_{yx}.
\]
If \(S\succ0\), the pair satisfies the strict second-order local-minimax condition. In particular, every strict differential Nash point satisfies \(S\succ0\), because \(H_{xx}\succ0\) and \(-H_{xy}H_{yy}^{-1}H_{yx}\succeq0\); hence it is a strict local minimax point. The converse need not hold, since \(S\succ0\) does not force \(H_{xx}\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict differential Nash points are strict local minimax points under smoothness, but local minimax curvature can arise through coupling even when the x-Hessian is not positive.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable near a jointly stationary pair.
\(H_{yy}\prec0\), so the local maximizing response is nondegenerate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict differential Nash implies \(S\succ0\) and strict local minimax; the reverse implication generally fails.

children.title: Second-Order Separation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Curvature regimes where the local notions diverge.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Separation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic example separating strict local minimax points from strict differential Nash points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the scalar zero-sum payoff
\[
f(x,y)=-\frac12x^2+2xy-\frac12y^2.
\]
At \((0,0)\), both partial gradients vanish and \(H_{yy}=-1<0\). The locally maximizing response is \(y^*(x)=2x\), and the reduced value is
\[
\varphi(x)=f(x,2x)=\frac32x^2,
\]
so \((0,0)\) is a strict local minimax point. Equivalently, its reduced Hessian is
\[
S=H_{xx}-H_{xy}H_{yy}^{-1}H_{yx}=-1-2(-1)^{-1}2=3>0.
\]
However, \(H_{xx}=-1<0\), so the point is not a differential Nash point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-player curvature can make a point strict local minimax even when the minimizer’s own Hessian is negative, excluding differential Nash status.
assumptions_latex: The local-minimax notion permits the maximizing player to respond locally to a nearby \(x\).
Differential Nash requires positive minimizer own-action curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,0)\) is strict local minimax but not differential Nash for the displayed quadratic payoff.

children.title: Two-Time-Scale Methods
children.top_down_role: Minimax dynamics using separated outer and inner time scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Time-Scale Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected simultaneous descent-ascent with a slower outer descent scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given closed convex sets \(X,Y\), a differentiable payoff \(f\), initial \((x_0,y_0)\in X\times Y\), and positive steps \(\alpha_t,\beta_t\), perform
\[
y_{t+1}=\Pi_Y\bigl(y_t+\beta_t\nabla_y f(x_t,y_t)\bigr),
\qquad
x_{t+1}=\Pi_X\bigl(x_t-\alpha_t\nabla_x f(x_t,y_t)\bigr).
\]
A two-time-scale regime requires the maximizing dynamics to be asymptotically faster, typically \(\alpha_t/\beta_t\to0\), with standard stochastic-approximation conditions imposed when gradients are noisy. Stop when a prescribed stationarity residual is below tolerance, or after \(T\) iterations and output the designated last, averaged, or randomly selected iterate specified by the convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-time-scale descent-ascent updates y on a faster scale than x, so the inner maximization can track its moving solution while the outer variable changes slowly.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are closed convex sets with computable Euclidean projections.
\(f\) is differentiable and the partial-gradient estimates satisfy the regularity required by the chosen deterministic or stochastic regime.
The positive steps satisfy a separation condition such as \(\alpha_t/\beta_t\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates are generated by projected descent-ascent with the outer step asymptotically smaller than the inner step.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical projected two-time-scale gradient descent-ascent recursion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but the record blends deterministic and stochastic regimes and leaves the output rule dependent on an unspecified convergence theorem. A source and a clearly delimited method variant are required.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Ascent Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic projected nested descent–ascent for a smooth nonconvex–concave minimax problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be closed convex sets, and let \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and concave in its second argument. Given \((x_0,y_0)\), outer step sizes \(\alpha_k>0\), inner step sizes \(\beta_{k,t}>0\), and inner lengths \(T_k\geq1\), set \(y_{k,0}=y_k\) and compute
\[y_{k,t+1}=\Pi_Y\!\left(y_{k,t}+\beta_{k,t}\nabla_y f(x_k,y_{k,t})\right),\qquad 0\leq t<T_k.\]
Then set \(y_{k+1}=y_{k,T_k}\) and
\[x_{k+1}=\Pi_X\!\left(x_k-\alpha_k\nabla_x f(x_k,y_{k+1})\right).\]
The output is a prescribed last, averaged, or stationarity-selected outer iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each outer descent step uses a maximization variable obtained from several projected ascent steps at the current outer point.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(f\) is differentiable on \(X\times Y\) and \(f(x,\cdot)\) is concave for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_{k+1},y_{k+1})\) is generated by the displayed nested projected descent–ascent recursion.

children.title: Time-Scale Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Operating regimes determined by relative update frequencies.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Scale Separation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic step-size condition making ascent evolve on the faster time scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a two-time-scale recursion with outer descent steps \(\alpha_k>0\) and inner ascent steps \(\beta_k>0\), the ascent-fast separation regime is
\[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\beta_k=\infty,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(\alpha_k^2+\beta_k^2)<\infty,\qquad \frac{\alpha_k}{\beta_k}\longrightarrow0.\]
For nested iterations using \(T_k\) ascent steps, an analogous deterministic requirement is that the terminal inner error \(e_k=\operatorname{dist}(y_{k,T_k},Y^*(x_k))\) satisfy \(e_k\to0\), where \(Y^*(x)=\arg\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)\). Thus the maximizing variable tracks its equilibrium before the outer variable changes appreciably.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both step sequences remain persistent, their squared noise effects are summable, and the outer step becomes negligible relative to the ascent step.
assumptions_latex: \(Y^*(x_k)\neq\varnothing\) when the nested-error formulation is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed limits define an ascent-fast time-scale separation regime.

notation.meaning: Set of maximizers of the inner concave problem at x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the leaf, but the record combines stochastic-approximation step-size conditions with a deterministic terminal-error condition that is not an equivalent time-scale-separation statement. The claimed analogy and tracking interpretation require separate authoritative sources and hypotheses.

children.title: Inexact Inner-Ascent Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Reliability limits caused by incomplete inner maximization.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Inner-Ascent Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-bias boundary induced by terminating a strongly concave inner maximization inexactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\phi(x)=\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)\), and suppose \(f(x,\cdot)\) is \(\mu\)-strongly concave with unique maximizer \(y^*(x)\), while \(\nabla_x f(x,\cdot)\) is \(L_{xy}\)-Lipschitz. If an inner point \(\tilde y_k\) satisfies
\[f(x_k,y^*(x_k))-f(x_k,\tilde y_k)\leq\varepsilon_k,\]
then
\[\|\nabla_x f(x_k,\tilde y_k)-\nabla\phi(x_k)\|\leq L_{xy}\sqrt{2\varepsilon_k/\mu}.\]
Consequently, vanishing outer stationarity generally requires this bias to vanish; for weighted descent analyses, the sufficient boundary is typically \(\sum_k\alpha_k\sqrt{\varepsilon_k}<\infty\). A fixed positive error can leave a nonzero stationarity floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong concavity converts inner value error into outer gradient bias; persistent inner error can prevent convergence to exact stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x,\cdot)\) is \(\mu\)-strongly concave on the convex set \(Y\).
The value function is differentiable with \(\nabla\phi(x)=\nabla_x f(x,y^*(x))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The outer-gradient error is at most \(L_{xy}\sqrt{2\varepsilon_k/\mu}\), and a nonvanishing \(\varepsilon_k\) permits a nonvanishing bias floor.

notation.meaning: Outer value function obtained by exact inner maximization.
Inner objective suboptimality at iteration k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, and the displayed bias bound follows under the stated strong-concavity, Lipschitz, and differentiability assumptions. The additional claim that weighted descent typically requires sum_k alpha_k sqrt(epsilon_k) < infinity depends on the outer descent analysis and is not adequately specified or sourced.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Envelope Minimax Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inexact proximal-point construction for the Moreau envelope of a weakly convex minimax value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\phi(x)=\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex. Choose \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\). At iterate \(x_k\), approximately solve
\[(u_k,y_k)\approx\arg\min_{u\in X}\max_{y\in Y}\left\{f(u,y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|u-x_k\|^2\right\},\]
and set \(x_{k+1}=u_k\), possibly with relaxation. For an exact inner solution \(u_k=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\phi}(x_k)\), the Moreau envelope
\[\phi_\lambda(x)=\min_u\left\{\phi(u)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|u-x\|^2\right\}\]
is differentiable and satisfies \(\nabla\phi_\lambda(x_k)=\lambda^{-1}(x_k-u_k)\), providing the stationarity measure used by the method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal regularizer makes each minimax subproblem strongly convex in the outer variable, while the proximal displacement measures envelope stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
The maximum defining \(\phi\) and the required proximal subproblem solutions exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For an exact proximal step, \(\nabla\phi_\lambda(x_k)=\lambda^{-1}(x_k-x_{k+1})\).

notation.meaning: Moreau envelope of the minimax value function.
Proximal mapping of the value function with parameter lambda.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Nonconvex–Concave Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected stochastic descent–ascent using unbiased first-order samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x,y)=\mathbb E[f(x,y;\xi)]\) on closed convex sets \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\), with \(f(\cdot,y)\) possibly nonconvex and \(f(x,\cdot)\) concave. Given \((x_0,y_0)\), draw samples \(\xi_k\) and obtain stochastic gradients \(g^x_k,g^y_k\) satisfying
\[\mathbb E[g^x_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla_x f(x_k,y_k),\qquad \mathbb E[g^y_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla_y f(x_k,y_k).\]
Update
\[x_{k+1}=\Pi_X(x_k-\alpha_k g^x_k),\qquad y_{k+1}=\Pi_Y(y_k+\beta_k g^y_k).\]
The output is a last iterate or an iterate sampled using predetermined weights; convergence claims require additional smoothness, variance, and step-size conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method replaces exact descent and ascent gradients by conditionally unbiased samples, with projections enforcing feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
The stochastic gradients are conditionally unbiased and have finite conditional second moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed recursion defines projected stochastic gradient descent–ascent for the nonconvex–concave problem.

notation.meaning: Information available before the stochastic oracle call at iteration k.
Stochastic outer and inner gradient estimates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal Gauss–Seidel surrogate best-response iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential player updates using current values for earlier blocks and previous-iterate values for later blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose $x^0=(x^{0,i})_{i=1}^N\in X_C$ and $\lambda>0$. For $\nu=0,1,\ldots$, update successively for $i=1,\ldots,N$ by setting
\[
\widehat x^{\nu+1,-i}:=(x^{\nu+1,<i},x^{\nu,>i})
\]
and solving the strongly convex subproblem
\[
x^{\nu+1,i}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x^i\in X_C^i(\widehat x^{\nu+1,-i})}\left\{\widehat f_i(x^i;\widehat x^{\nu+1,-i})+g_i(x^i)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|x^i-x^{\nu,i}\|^2\right\}.
\]
Continue until the prescribed stopping rule is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible profile and a positive proximal parameter, update players in Gauss–Seidel order. Each player minimizes its surrogate objective plus its nonsmooth term and a quadratic proximal term, using newly updated earlier blocks and old later blocks.
assumptions_latex: X_C^i(\widehat x^{\nu+1,-i})\ne\varnothing\text{ whenever the subproblem is solved}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines common-multiplier and positively scaled common-multiplier refinements of QNE for shared-constrained games.
