knowledge_statements.statement_title: GVI formulation and KKT sufficient conditions for shared-constrained games
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the shared-constraint construction, Clarke-equilibrium GVI formulation, and playerwise KKT sufficient condition for a quasi-Nash equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X_C=X\cap\prod_{i=1}^N C^i and X_C^i(x^{-i})=\{x^i\in C^i:(x^i,x^{-i})\in X\}. A Clarke-NE of the shared-constrained game is a solution of the GVI with \Phi(x)=\prod_{i=1}^N\partial^C_{x^i}\zeta_i(x) and constant feasible set X_C. If X=\{x:g(x)\le0,\ h(x)=0\}, each \zeta_i(\cdot,x^{-i}) is B-differentiable, and suitable playerwise constraint qualifications hold, then a feasible x^* is a QNE whenever, for every i, there are (\pi^i,\mu^i)\in\mathbb R_+^k\times\mathbb R^\ell such that, for all x^i\in C^i,\quad \zeta_i(\cdot,x^{*,-i})'(x^{*,i};x^i-x^{*,i})+\sum_{j=1}^k\pi_j^i\nabla_{x^i}g_j(x^*)^\top(x^i-x^{*,i})+\sum_{j=1}^\ell\mu_j^i\nabla_{x^i}h_j(x^*)^\top(x^i-x^{*,i})\ge0,\quad 0\le\pi^i\perp g(x^*)\le0,\quad h(x^*)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A game has shared constraints when every player's feasible set is obtained by slicing one common set. Its Clarke-Nash equilibria solve a generalized variational inequality over the common feasible set. With continuously differentiable shared constraints, B-differentiable player objectives, and suitable playerwise constraint qualifications, any feasible tuple satisfying each player's directional KKT system with that player's own multipliers is a quasi-Nash equilibrium.
assumptions_latex: g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^k\text{ and }h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^\ell\text{ are continuously differentiable}
\text{Suitable playerwise constraint qualifications, such as MFCQ, hold}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ClarkeNE}\subseteq\operatorname{SOL}(\Phi,X_C),\qquad [\text{playerwise KKT conditions at }x^*]\Longrightarrow x^*\text{ is a QNE}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Convergence and Commuting Limits for Asynchronous MIMO IWFA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence theorem for the asynchronous iterative water-filling algorithm applied to \(\mathcal G_\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\mathcal G_\alpha\) and \(\mathcal G_\infty\). Assume \(r_{\widehat U_q}<r_{H_{qq}}=n_{T_q}=n_{R_q}\) for every \(q\in\Omega\), and condition \((\mathrm C7)\). For every feasible initialization and every asynchronous updating schedule satisfying \((\mathrm A1)-(\mathrm A3)\), the asynchronous MIMO IWFA iterates \(Q_\alpha^{(n)}\) converge as \(n\to\infty\), uniformly in \(\alpha\in\mathbb R_+\), to the unique Nash equilibrium of \(\mathcal G_\alpha\). Furthermore, \[\lim_{n\to+\infty}\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}Q_\alpha^{(n)}=\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}\lim_{n\to+\infty}Q_\alpha^{(n)}=Q_\infty^\star,\] where \(Q_\infty^\star\) is the unique Nash equilibrium of \(\mathcal G_\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated rank and contraction condition, asynchronous iterative water-filling converges uniformly over the nonnegative parameter for every feasible initialization and every schedule satisfying the asynchronous-update assumptions. The iteration limit and the infinite-parameter limit commute and both yield the unique equilibrium of the limiting game.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NE, QNE, local NE, and Clarke-NE solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines four playerwise solution notions for a GNEP with B-differentiable objectives and closed feasible slices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a GNEP \mathcal G(\zeta,\Xi_C), suppose each u\mapsto\zeta_i(u,x^{-i}) is B-differentiable and each \Xi_C^i(x^{-i}) is closed. A tuple x^* is an NE if x^{*,i}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in\Xi_C^i(x^{*,-i})}\zeta_i(u,x^{*,-i}) for every i; it is a QNE if every x^{*,i} is B-stationary for that player problem; and it is an LNE if x^{*,i}\in\operatorname*{arglocmin}_{u\in\Xi_C^i(x^{*,-i})}\zeta_i(u,x^{*,-i}) for every i. If every \Xi_C^i(x^{*,-i}) is convex, x^* is a Clarke-NE if 0\in\partial_{x^i}^{\mathrm C}\zeta_i(x^{*,i},x^{*,-i})+\mathcal N(x^{*,i};\Xi_C^i(x^{*,-i})) for all i.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Nash equilibrium is a simultaneous global minimizer of every player's frozen-rivals problem. A quasi-Nash equilibrium requires only playerwise B-stationarity, while a local Nash equilibrium requires playerwise local minimality. For convex feasible slices, a Clarke-NE satisfies the playerwise Clarke-subdifferential normal-cone inclusions.
assumptions_latex: \Xi_C^i(x^{*,-i})\text{ is convex for every }i\text{ when defining a Clarke-NE}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}x^*\text{ is NE}&\iff \forall i,\ x^{*,i}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in\Xi_C^i(x^{*,-i})}\zeta_i(u,x^{*,-i}),\\x^*\text{ is QNE}&\iff \forall i,\ x^{*,i}\text{ is B-stationary},\\x^*\text{ is LNE}&\iff \forall i,\ x^{*,i}\in\operatorname*{arglocmin}_{u\in\Xi_C^i(x^{*,-i})}\zeta_i(u,x^{*,-i}),\\x^*\text{ is Clarke-NE}&\iff \forall i,\ 0\in\partial_{x^i}^{\mathrm C}\zeta_i(x^*)+\mathcal N(x^{*,i};\Xi_C^i(x^{*,-i})).\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Surrogate-to-original directional stationarity implication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency condition at a candidate limit point for each player and every feasible unilateral direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a given $x^\infty=(x^{\infty,i})_{i=1}^N$, for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$, every $x^i\in X_C^i(x^{\infty,-i})$, and every $a^{\infty,i}\in\partial g_i(x^{\infty,i})$, require
\[
\left[\nabla_{x^i}\widehat f_i(x^\infty)+a^{\infty,i}\right]^\top(x^i-x^{\infty,i})\ge0
\]
to imply
\[
f_i(\bullet,x^{\infty,-i})'(x^{\infty,i};x^i-x^{\infty,i})+(a^{\infty,i})^\top(x^i-x^{\infty,i})\ge0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed convex inverse-image representation of a GQVI feasible map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the inverse-image representation, its sufficient closedness and convexity conditions, and its playerwise and shared-constraint specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb R^\ell be closed and convex and let M:\mathbb R^{2n}\to\mathbb R^\ell be continuous. Define \Xi(x)=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:M(z,x)\in K\}. Suppose that, for every fixed x, whenever M(z^1,x),M(z^2,x)\in K and \tau\in(0,1),\quad M(\tau z^1+(1-\tau)z^2,x)-\tau M(z^1,x)-(1-\tau)M(z^2,x)\in K. Then \Xi(x) is closed and convex. The construction includes M(z,x)=Az+b(x); if M(z,x)=Q(z), it yields the shared constraint X=Q^{-1}(K). It also represents playerwise systems \Xi^i(x^{-i})=\{z^i:g^i(z^i,x^{-i})\le0,\ h^i(z^i,x^{-i})=0\} by taking K=\prod_i(\mathbb R_-^{m_i}\times\mathbb R^{\ell_i}) and M=(M^i)_i with M^i=(g^i,h^i).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state-dependent feasible set may be represented as the inverse image of a closed convex set under a continuous mapping. Under the stated K-convexity condition in the decision argument, every value of the feasible-set map is closed and convex. This representation contains affine-plus-state maps, fixed shared constraints, and Cartesian products of playerwise equality-and-inequality systems as special cases.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^\ell\text{ is closed and convex}
\forall x,z^1,z^2,\tau\in(0,1):\ M(z^1,x),M(z^2,x)\in K\Rightarrow M(\tau z^1+(1-\tau)z^2,x)-\tau M(z^1,x)-(1-\tau)M(z^2,x)\in K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\mathbb R^n,\quad \Xi(x)=\{z:M(z,x)\in K\}\text{ is closed and convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothness, block convexity, and bounded cross-block coupling condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity condition for playerwise surrogate objectives in a Gauss–Seidel best-response method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ and $\bar x\in C$, the map $\widehat f_i(\bullet;\bar x^{-i}):\mathcal O^i\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, convex on $C^i$, and differentiable in $x^i$. Its block gradient $\nabla_{x^i}\widehat f_i(\bullet;\bullet)$ is continuously differentiable on $C^i\times C^{-i}$. Define
\[
\gamma_i:=\inf_{x^i\in C^i}\inf_{\bar x^{-i}\in C^{-i}}\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\nabla^2_{x^i}\widehat f_i(x^i;\bar x^{-i})\right)
\]
and, for every $i'\ne i$,
\[
\bar\gamma_{ii'}:=\sup_{x^i\in C^i}\sup_{\bar x^{-i}\in C^{-i}}\left\|J_{\bar x^{i'}}\nabla_{x^i}\widehat f_i(x^i;\bar x^{-i})\right\|<\infty.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each player’s surrogate is continuous, convex in that player’s variable, and differentiable; its block gradient is continuously differentiable jointly in all blocks. The smallest block-Hessian eigenvalue has the stated global infimum, and every cross-player Jacobian of the block gradient is uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat f_i(\bullet;\bar x^{-i})\text{ is continuous and convex on }C^i,\quad \nabla_{x^i}\widehat f_i\in C^1(C^i\times C^{-i}),\quad \bar\gamma_{ii'}<\infty\ \forall i'\ne i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MOPEC model and solution concept
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the auxiliary equilibrium coupling, the nonsmooth/nonconvex solution pair, and the existence boundary caused by an unbounded auxiliary feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiple-optimization problem with equilibrium constraints couples players' optimization problems, parameterized by p\in K, to the inclusion 0\in\Psi(x,p)+N_K(p), where K\subseteq\mathbb R^r is closed and convex. In the nonconvex or nondifferentiable case, a solution is a pair (x,p) such that x is a QNE or Clarke-NE of \mathcal G(\zeta(\cdot;p),\Xi_C) and p solves \operatorname{VI}(\Psi(x,\cdot),K), equivalently 0\in\Psi(x,p)+N_K(p). If K is unbounded, solvability of the game for each fixed p does not by itself ensure existence or computability of a coupled MOPEC solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A MOPEC is a game whose players' problems depend on an auxiliary variable, commonly a price, which must simultaneously satisfy a variational inequality, complementarity condition, or market-clearing inclusion. For nonconvex or nonsmooth games, a solution pairs a quasi-Nash or Clarke-Nash equilibrium with a solution of the auxiliary variational inequality. When the auxiliary feasible set is unbounded, fixed-parameter game solvability alone is insufficient for the coupled problem.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^r\text{ is closed and convex}
\text{Each player's optimization problem is parameterized by }p\in K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x,p)\text{ solves the MOPEC}\iff x\in\operatorname{QNE/ClarkeNE}(\mathcal G(\zeta(\cdot;p),\Xi_C))\ \text{and}\ 0\in\Psi(x,p)+N_K(p);\quad K\text{ unbounded permits an existence/computation gap despite fixed-}p\text{ solvability}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized Nash and Nash equilibrium problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an N-player game with private and rival-dependent coupled constraints and identifies the uncoupled Nash specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let N\ge 1. For each player i, let C^i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i} be closed and convex, let \mathcal O^i\supseteq C^i be open, let \zeta_i:\prod_{j=1}^N\mathcal O^j\to\mathbb R, and let \Xi^i:\mathcal O^{-i}\rightrightarrows\mathcal O^i. Define \Xi_C^i(x^{-i})=C^i\cap\Xi^i(x^{-i}). The generalized Nash equilibrium problem \mathcal G(\zeta,\Xi_C) consists, for every i=1,\ldots,N and fixed rivals' strategy x^{-i}\in C^{-i}, of \min_{x^i\in\Xi_C^i(x^{-i})}\zeta_i(x^i,x^{-i}). If \Xi^i(x^{-i})=\mathbb R^{n_i} for every i and x^{-i}, this reduces to the Nash equilibrium problem \mathcal G(\zeta,C), in which player i minimizes over C^i.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An N-player generalized Nash problem assigns each player an objective and a feasible set formed from private constraints intersected with constraints depending on the rivals' strategies. When every coupled-constraint map is the whole player space, the model reduces to an ordinary Nash problem with only private feasible sets.
assumptions_latex: C^i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\text{ is closed and convex for }i=1,\ldots,N
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{GNEP}:\ \min_{x^i\in C^i\cap\Xi^i(x^{-i})}\zeta_i(x^i,x^{-i})\quad(i=1,\ldots,N),\qquad \Xi^i\equiv\mathbb R^{n_i}\Longrightarrow\operatorname{NEP}:\ \min_{x^i\in C^i}\zeta_i(x^i,x^{-i}).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A strategic-form game is a triplet \(\mathcal G=\langle\Omega,(\mathcal Q_i)_{i\in\Omega},(u_i)_{i\in\Omega}angle\), where \(\Omega=\{1,\ldots,Q\}\), each \(\mathcal Q_i
eq\varnothing\) is player \(i\)'s pure-strategy set and is independent of the other players' strategies, and \(u_i:\prod_{j=1}^Q\mathcal Q_j	o\mathbb R\). Write \(\mathcal Q=\prod_{j=1}^Q\mathcal Q_j\), \(\mathbf x_{-i}=(\mathbf x_j)_{j
e i}\), and \(\mathcal Q_{-i}=\prod_{j
e i}\mathcal Q_j\). The game is finite if every \(\mathcal Q_i\) is finite, and otherwise it is infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strategic-form game has finitely many players, a nonempty independent pure-strategy set for each player, and a payoff for each player depending on the full strategy profile. It is finite exactly when every strategy set is finite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Soft- and Null-Shaped MIMO Game and Constraint-Redundancy Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model formulation and boundary conditions for removing explicit power or soft-shaping constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each player \(q\), the game \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{soft}}\) maximizes \(R_q(Q_q,Q_{-q})\) over \(Q_q\succeq0\), subject to \(U_q^HQ_q=0\) and the individual soft-shaping constraints, with the transmit-power bound absorbed into the trace soft constraint. Full row rank, \(\operatorname{rank}(G_q)=n_{T_q}\), is necessary to control power in every permitted direction whenever \(\mathcal N(G_q^H)\cap\mathcal R(U_q)^\perp\ne\varnothing\). The explicit transmit-power constraint is redundant if \[P_{\mathrm{SU},q}^{\mathrm{ave}}\le P_q\lambda_{\min}(G_qG_q^H),\] whereas the soft constraint can be removed without loss of optimality if \[P_{\mathrm{SU},q}^{\mathrm{ave}}\ge P_q\lambda_{\max}(G_qG_q^H),\] in which case \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{soft}}\) reduces to \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{null}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The soft-shaped game maximizes each user's rate over positive-semidefinite transmit covariances subject to null and individual soft-shaping constraints. Full row rank of each shaping matrix prevents uncontrolled power along allowed null directions. Eigenvalue thresholds determine when the explicit transmit-power constraint is redundant and when the soft constraint may instead be removed, reducing the model to the null-shaped game.
assumptions_latex: \forall q:\ \operatorname{rank}(G_q)=n_{T_q}\text{ when power must be controlled in all permitted directions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{SU},q}^{\mathrm{ave}}\le P_q\lambda_{\min}(G_qG_q^H)\Rightarrow\text{the explicit power constraint is redundant};\quad P_{\mathrm{SU},q}^{\mathrm{ave}}\ge P_q\lambda_{\max}(G_qG_q^H)\Rightarrow\mathcal G_{\mathrm{soft}}\text{ reduces to }\mathcal G_{\mathrm{null}}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. For \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)\), define the game operator
\[F(x,y)=\bigl(\nabla_x f(x,y),-\nabla_y f(x,y)\bigr).\]
Given \(z_0=(x_0,y_0)\), step sizes \(\eta_k>0\), and the product projection \(\Pi_{X\times Y}\), simultaneous gradient game dynamics are
\[z_{k+1}=\Pi_{X\times Y}\bigl(z_k-\eta_kF(z_k)\bigr).\]
Equivalently,
\[x_{k+1}=\Pi_X\bigl(x_k-\eta_k\nabla_x f(x_k,y_k)\bigr),\qquad y_{k+1}=\Pi_Y\bigl(y_k+\eta_k\nabla_y f(x_k,y_k)\bigr).\]
A stopping rule may use the projected residual \(\eta_k^{-1}\lVert z_k-\Pi_{X\times Y}(z_k-\eta_kF(z_k))\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both players update simultaneously: the minimizing player descends and the maximizing player ascends at the current joint iterate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(\pi_{i,1}\) uniformly on the finite action set \(A_i\). At iteration \(t\ge 1\), with \(a_{-i}\) fixed, define \(r_t(a_i)=u_i(a_i,a_{-i})\) for each \(a_i\in A_i\), and set
\[\pi_{i,t+1}=\operatorname{Proj}_{\Delta(A_i)}\!\left(\pi_{i,t}+\frac{r_t}{\sqrt{t}}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize agent i's policy uniformly. At iteration t, hold the other agents' actions fixed, collect agent i's utility for every available action, add this vector to the current policy with step size 1/sqrt(t), and project the result onto the probability simplex.
assumptions_latex: u_i(a_i,a_{-i})\text{ is defined for every }a_i\in A_i.
a_{-i}\text{ is held fixed during the update}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi_{i,t+1}=\operatorname{Proj}_{\Delta(A_i)}\!\left(\pi_{i,t}+r_t/\sqrt{t}\right)\in\Delta(A_i),\qquad r_t(a_i)=u_i(a_i,a_{-i}).

children.title: Optimistic Game Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Predictive dynamics designed for game interactions.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimistic Game Dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-step optimistic gradient dynamics for a differentiable game operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:Z\to\mathbb R^d\) be the descent–ascent game operator on a closed convex set \(Z\). Given \(z_0\in Z\), set \(z_{-1}=z_0\). With step sizes \(\eta_k>0\), optimistic gradient dynamics use
\[z_{k+1}=\Pi_Z\!\left(z_k-\eta_k\bigl(2F(z_k)-F(z_{k-1})\bigr)\right).\]
For a zero-sum objective \(f\), one takes \(F(x,y)=(\nabla_xf(x,y),-\nabla_yf(x,y))\). The correction \(F(z_k)-F(z_{k-1})\) extrapolates the current field using its most recent change. The output is the prescribed last iterate, with termination based on an operator or projected residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimistic dynamics correct the current game gradient by its change from the preceding iterate, anticipating rotational motion.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(F\) is single-valued at all generated iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates satisfy the displayed projected optimistic-gradient recurrence.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of joint game states.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and recurrence fit optimistic game dynamics, but no citation is supplied. A primary or authoritative source is needed to confirm the exact projected two-step convention, initialization, and naming.

children.title: Rotational Stabilization Regimes
children.top_down_role: Game geometries where optimism controls rotational behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Rotational Stabilization Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact spectral stability test for optimistic dynamics on a bilinear game mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the unconstrained bilinear game \(f(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}Ay\) and its operator
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}0&A\\-A^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}.\]
For constant-step optimistic dynamics \(z_{k+1}=(I-2\eta M)z_k+\eta Mz_{k-1}\), each nonzero singular value \(\sigma\) of \(A\) produces scalar characteristic polynomials
\[p_{\pm,\sigma}(r)=r^2-(1\mp2i\eta\sigma)r\mp i\eta\sigma.\]
The rotational mode is last-iterate stable exactly when every root of both polynomials has modulus strictly below one. Modes in \(\ker M\) remain constant; hence convergence of every state to the origin additionally requires \(M\) to be nonsingular. This root condition is the step-size stability boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimistic dynamics stabilize a bilinear rotational mode precisely when both characteristic roots associated with every singular value lie inside the unit disk.
assumptions_latex: The optimistic recurrence uses a constant step size \(\eta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Last-iterate decay on all nonzero rotational modes is equivalent to \(\max\{|r|:p_{\pm,\sigma}(r)=0\}<1\) for every \(\sigma>0\).

notation.meaning: Skew-symmetric operator of the bilinear game.
A nonzero singular value of A.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role matches the stability-regime leaf, and the characteristic-polynomial formulation is plausible for the stated bilinear recurrence. Its signs, strict-root criterion, kernel qualification, and resulting step-size boundary require an inspectable spectral-analysis source.

children.title: Last-Iterate Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where terminal iterates remain unstable.

knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bilinear counterexample showing last-iterate divergence of simultaneous gradient descent–ascent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}\max_{y\in\mathbb R}f(x,y)\) with \(f(x,y)=xy\). Its unique saddle point is \((0,0)\). Simultaneous gradient descent–ascent with constant \(\eta>0\) gives
\[x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta y_k,\qquad y_{k+1}=y_k+\eta x_k.\]
Therefore
\[x_{k+1}^2+y_{k+1}^2=(1+\eta^2)(x_k^2+y_k^2).\]
Unless \((x_0,y_0)=(0,0)\), the last iterates spiral outward and their norm grows geometrically. Thus smoothness, convexity–concavity, and a unique saddle point do not ensure last-iterate convergence of constant-step simultaneous gradient dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the scalar bilinear game, every positive constant step makes simultaneous descent–ascent spiral outward unless initialized at the saddle.
assumptions_latex: The simultaneous descent–ascent step size is constant and satisfies \(\eta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every nonzero initialization, \(\|(x_k,y_k)\|=(1+\eta^2)^{k/2}\|(x_0,y_0)\|\), so the last iterate diverges.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample role exactly fits the failure-boundary leaf, and the displayed norm identity and divergence conclusion are internally correct. The common contract nevertheless requires source evidence or an explicit standard-field rationale, neither of which is present.

children.title: Consensus Adjustments
children.top_down_role: Corrections targeting local agreement in game dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Consensus Adjustments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jacobian-transpose adjustment penalizing the squared norm of a differentiable game field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) be continuously differentiable, with Jacobian \(J(z)=DF(z)\), and define the consensus potential \(L(z)=\tfrac12\|F(z)\|^2\). Since \(\nabla L(z)=J(z)^{\mathsf T}F(z)\), a consensus-adjusted operator is
\[F_{\mathrm{con}}(z)=F(z)+\gamma J(z)^{\mathsf T}F(z),\qquad \gamma\geq0.\]
Given \(z_0\), the unconstrained iteration is
\[z_{k+1}=z_k-\eta_kF_{\mathrm{con}}(z_k).\]
For constrained games, project this update onto the feasible joint set. A stopping rule tests \(\|F(z_k)\|\) or the corresponding projected residual; the adjustment does not change any zero of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consensus adjustment adds the gradient of half the squared game-field norm, while preserving every equilibrium represented by a field zero.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of the generated iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(z^*\) satisfying \(F(z^*)=0\) also satisfies \(F_{\mathrm{con}}(z^*)=0\).

notation.meaning: Consensus potential equal to half the squared operator norm.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits consensus adjustment, and the formula preserves every zero of the original field. A primary source is required to validate the operator and sign convention. The statement establishes only preservation of original zeros, not equality of the original and adjusted zero sets.

children.title: Symplectic Adjustments
children.top_down_role: Corrections targeting rotational game components.

knowledge_statements.title: Symplectic Adjustments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Antisymmetric-Jacobian correction for rotational components of a differentiable game field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) be continuously differentiable with Jacobian \(J(z)\), and define its antisymmetric component
\[A(z)=\tfrac12\bigl(J(z)-J(z)^{\mathsf T}\bigr).\]
For a coefficient \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), the symplectically adjusted operator is
\[F_{\mathrm{sym}}(z)=F(z)+\lambda A(z)^{\mathsf T}F(z).\]
Starting from \(z_0\), update \(z_{k+1}=z_k-\eta_kF_{\mathrm{sym}}(z_k)\), with projection when the joint feasible set is constrained. The coefficient's sign and magnitude are selected by a stated alignment or local-stability rule. Because the correction is proportional to \(F(z)\), every zero of the original field remains a zero of the adjusted field.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method corrects the game field using the antisymmetric part of its Jacobian to modify rotational motion without moving field zeros.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable near all generated iterates.
\(\eta_k>0\), and \(\lambda\) is chosen by a specified stability convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(F(z^*)=0\), then \(F_{\mathrm{sym}}(z^*)=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, and the displayed correction preserves original field zeros. No source supports the normalization of the antisymmetric Jacobian, the transpose/sign convention, or the unspecified alignment and stability rule for lambda.

children.title: Consensus–Symplectic Hybrid Adjustments
children.top_down_role: Combined correction structures for mixed game geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Consensus–Symplectic Hybrid Adjustments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hybrid game-field correction combining consensus and antisymmetric-Jacobian terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) be continuously differentiable, let \(J(z)=DF(z)\), and set \(A(z)=\tfrac12(J(z)-J(z)^{\mathsf T})\). For coefficients \(\gamma\geq0\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), define
\[F_{\mathrm{hyb}}(z)=F(z)+\gamma J(z)^{\mathsf T}F(z)+\lambda A(z)^{\mathsf T}F(z).\]
Given \(z_0\), use
\[z_{k+1}=\Pi_Z\bigl(z_k-\eta_kF_{\mathrm{hyb}}(z_k)\bigr),\]
where \(Z\) is the joint feasible set. The consensus coefficient controls squared-residual damping, while the symplectic coefficient controls rotational correction. Terminate using \(\|F(z_k)\|\) or a projected residual. Every zero of \(F\) remains a zero of the hybrid operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hybrid adds both squared-residual damping and an antisymmetric rotational correction, with separate coefficients and unchanged field zeros.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(\eta_k>0\), \(\gamma\geq0\), and \(\lambda\) follows a stated stability convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(F(z^*)=0\), then \(F_{\mathrm{hyb}}(z^*)=0\).

notation.meaning: Antisymmetric component of the game Jacobian.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role matches the hybrid-adjustment leaf, but no authoritative source establishes this precise additive hybrid as a recognized method or validates its coefficient and sign conventions. Separate sources for the component methods are not sufficient unless the hybrid construction is explicitly justified.

children.title: Adjustment Stability Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Stability limits introduced by correction strength or interaction.

knowledge_statements.title: Adjustment Stability Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear tradeoff for consensus-type Jacobian adjustments near a game equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) be continuously differentiable, let \(z^\star\) satisfy \(F(z^\star)=0\), and write \(J=DF(z^\star)\). For \(\gamma\ge 0\), define the adjusted field \(F_\gamma(z)=F(z)+\gamma DF(z)^\top F(z)\). Then \(z^\star\) remains an equilibrium and \(DF_\gamma(z^\star)=J+\gamma J^\top J\). Consequently,
\[\operatorname{Sym}(DF_\gamma(z^\star))=\operatorname{Sym}(J)+\gamma J^\top J.\]
Thus the adjustment adds positive-semidefinite local damping, but if \(\|DF(z)\|\le L\), its added term can increase the field's local Lipschitz scale by order \(\gamma L^2\), restricting stable explicit step sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consensus adjustment preserves existing equilibria and adds positive-semidefinite local damping, while increasing stiffness and potentially requiring smaller explicit steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DF_\gamma(z^\star)=J+\gamma J^\top J\), so its symmetric part gains \(\gamma J^\top J\succeq0\) at the cost of increased stiffness.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the field at the equilibrium

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equilibrium-preservation and Jacobian identities are algebraically consistent, and property fits the tradeoff leaf. A primary source is required for identifying this field as the intended consensus-type adjustment and for the stable-step-size interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Local-Equilibrium Dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit proximal regularization of a smooth, possibly nonmonotone game field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a continuously differentiable game field \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\), an initial point \(z_0\), and parameters \(\lambda_k>0\), compute a locally selected solution \(z_{k+1}\) of
\[0=F(z_{k+1})+\lambda_k(z_{k+1}-z_k).\]
Equivalently, when the local inverse exists, \(z_{k+1}=(I+\lambda_k^{-1}F)^{-1}(z_k)\). Stop when \(\|F(z_{k+1})\|\le\varepsilon\), and output \(z_{k+1}\). The regularization makes the local equation better conditioned when \(DF(z)+\lambda_k I\) is nonsingular; in a nonmonotone game, the resolvent may be multivalued, so a local branch-selection rule is part of the algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each step solves a proximal, implicitly regularized game equation; nonsingularity improves local stability, but nonmonotonicity can make the update multivalued.
assumptions_latex: A local solution branch is available at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(z_{k+1}\) satisfies \(\|F(z_{k+1})\|\le\varepsilon\), with updates defined by the regularized local equilibrium equation.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implicit update is coherent as an algorithm, including its local branch qualification, but no evidence identifies it with the terminal topic's intended published dynamics. The record also supplies no guarantee that the stopping condition is reached.

children.title: Nonconvex Minimax Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity families separated by inner curvature and stationarity target.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex–Strongly Concave Stationarity Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-inner-oracle complexity for stationarity of a smooth nonconvex value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Phi(x)=\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)\), where \(Y\) is closed and convex, \(f(\cdot,y)\) may be nonconvex, and \(f(x,\cdot)\) is \(\mu\)-strongly concave. Suppose \(
abla_{xx}^2 f\) has norm at most \(L_{xx}\) and \(\|
abla_{xy}^2 f\|\le L_{xy}\). Then \(\Phi\) is differentiable with gradient Lipschitz constant at most \(L_\Phi=L_{xx}+L_{xy}^2/\mu\). Exact gradient descent using \(y(x)\in\arg\max_y f(x,y)\) and step \(1/L_\Phi\) produces an iterate satisfying \(\|
abla\Phi(x_k)\|\le\varepsilon\) within at most
\[\left\lceil 2L_\Phi(\Phi(x_0)-\inf\Phi)\varepsilon^{-2}ightceil\]
outer iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong inner concavity smooths the value function; exact-inner gradient descent reaches epsilon stationarity in order L-value-gap divided by epsilon squared iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x,\cdot)\) is \(\mu\)-strongly concave on closed convex \(Y\), with \(\mu>0\).
\(\inf_x\Phi(x)>-\infty\), and exact inner maximizers are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point of \(\Phi\) is obtained in \(O((L_{xx}+L_{xy}^2/\mu)(\Phi(x_0)-\inf\Phi)\varepsilon^{-2})\) exact-inner iterations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity_bound is appropriate, but the differentiability and exact Lipschitz constant require authoritative support and careful domain and smoothness hypotheses. The bound concerns outer iterations with exact inner maximization, not total first-order oracle complexity.

children.title: Nonconvex–Concave Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity landmarks under concavity of the inner problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex–Concave Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of smooth-value complexity when inner strong concavity is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi(x)=\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)\), with \(f(\cdot,y)\) smooth but possibly nonconvex and \(f(x,\cdot)\) concave. Without strong concavity, the maximizer set can be non-singleton and \(\Phi\) need not be differentiable. For example, with \(Y=[-1,1]\) and \(f(x,y)=xy\), one has \(\Phi(x)=|x|\). Hence no finite Lipschitz constant for \(\nabla\Phi\) exists near \(x=0\), and smooth nonconvex gradient-descent complexity bounds of order \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) cannot be invoked for \(\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) without regularization or a nonsmooth stationarity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concavity alone can yield a nonsmooth value function, so smooth value-gradient complexity requires strong concavity, regularization, or a different stationarity measure.
assumptions_latex: The inner problem is concave but not strongly concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(x)=|x|\) is nondifferentiable at \(0\), invalidating smooth value-gradient stationarity complexity at that point.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly gives the nonsmooth value function |x| and fits a failure-boundary treatment of the leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Nonconcave Game Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity frontiers without inner concavity.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconcave Game Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity ceases to certify local minimax structure without inner concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the unconstrained min-max objective \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\), with \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}\). The simultaneous game field is \(F(x,y)=(\partial_x f,-\partial_y f)=(2x,-2y)\), so \(F(0,0)=0\). Nevertheless, \((0,0)\) is not a local min-max equilibrium because \(y=0\) locally minimizes, rather than maximizes, \(f(0,y)=y^2\). Thus, in the nonconcave inner regime, finding an \(\varepsilon\)-zero of the game gradient certifies only first-order stationarity; its oracle complexity cannot by itself be interpreted as complexity for finding an approximate local minimax equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without inner concavity, a zero game gradient may have the wrong curvature and therefore does not certify even a local min-max equilibrium.
assumptions_latex: The first player minimizes and the second player maximizes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(F(0,0)=0\), the point \((0,0)\) is not a local min-max equilibrium.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly shows that a stationary game field need not certify maximizing-player curvature. A citation and an explicit adopted definition of local minimax equilibrium are required for this complexity boundary.

children.title: Inner-Curvature Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes across weakening inner curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Curvature Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition-number transition as inner strong concavity vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\Phi_\mu(x)=\max_{y\in Y}f_\mu(x,y)\), assume \(f_\mu(x,\cdot)\) is \(\mu\)-strongly concave, \(\|
abla_{xx}^2f_\mu\|\le L_{xx}\), and \(\|
abla_{xy}^2f_\mu\|\le L_{xy}\). Then
\[\operatorname{Lip}(
abla\Phi_\mu)\le L_{xx}+ rac{L_{xy}^2}{\mu}.\]
Accordingly, the exact-inner gradient complexity for \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity scales at most as \(O((L_{xx}+L_{xy}^2/\mu)\varepsilon^{-2})\), up to the initial value gap. The regime \(\mu\gg L_{xy}^2/L_{xx}\) is outer-curvature dominated, while \(0<\mu\ll L_{xy}^2/L_{xx}\) is coupling dominated; at \(\mu=0\), differentiability of the value function is no longer guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complexity changes from outer-curvature dominated to coupling dominated as inner curvature weakens, and smooth-value analysis can fail when strong concavity reaches zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The curvature contribution changes near \(\mu=L_{xy}^2/L_{xx}\), and the smoothness bound diverges as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated crossover follows formally from the proposed smoothness bound and property is a suitable role, but both that bound and the interpretation of the crossover as a recognized transition regime require sources. The ratio also presumes L_xx>0.

children.title: Oracle Lower-Bound Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Oracle limitations separating attainable complexity regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Lower-Bound Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical transfer conditions for minimax oracle lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{O},\varepsilon)\) denote the worst-case number of calls to oracle \(\mathcal{O}\) required to solve every instance in class \(\mathcal{C}\) to accuracy \(\varepsilon\). If \(\mathcal{C}_1\subseteq\mathcal{C}_2\), then \(N(\mathcal{C}_2,\mathcal{O},\varepsilon)\ge N(\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{O},\varepsilon)\). If oracle \(\mathcal{O}_2\) can simulate \(\mathcal{O}_1\) at unit cost, then \(N(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{O}_2,\varepsilon)\le N(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{O}_1,\varepsilon)\). Therefore a lower bound transfers to a larger instance class under the same oracle, but it does not automatically transfer to a richer oracle, a weaker accuracy criterion, or a structurally narrower class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower bounds extend from subclasses to larger classes under the same oracle, but richer information, weaker accuracy, or added structure changes the boundary.
assumptions_latex: Oracle calls have a fixed unit-cost convention.
\(\mathcal{O}_2\) simulates \(\mathcal{O}_1\) at unit cost when oracle dominance is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\mathcal{C}_2,\mathcal{O},\varepsilon)\ge N(\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{O},\varepsilon)\) and \(N(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{O}_2,\varepsilon)\le N(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{O}_1,\varepsilon)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hannan Consistency Bounds the Row Player's Long-Run Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated two-player zero-sum games under Hannan-consistent play by the row player.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be the value of a two-player zero-sum game, and let \(\ell(I_t,J_t)\) be the row player's loss at round \(t\). If the row player uses a Hannan-consistent strategy, then
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\ell(I_t,J_t)\le V
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a two-player zero-sum game, if the row player follows a Hannan-consistent strategy, then the limsup of the row player's average loss is at most the game value almost surely.

children.title: Matrix Zero-Sum Games
children.top_down_role: Finite-dimensional zero-sum game structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Zero-Sum Games
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite zero-sum game as a bilinear saddle problem and primal-dual linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a payoff matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), let the row player minimize and the column player maximize \(x^\top Ay\) over probability simplices. Then
\[\min_{x\in\Delta_m}\max_{y\in\Delta_n}x^\top Ay=\max_{y\in\Delta_n}\min_{x\in\Delta_m}x^\top Ay=v.\]
The common value is equivalently characterized by the dual linear programs
\[v=\min_{x\in\Delta_m,\,t}\{t:A^\top x\le t\mathbf{1}_n\}=\max_{y\in\Delta_n,\,s}\{s:Ay\ge s\mathbf{1}_m\}.\]
Any optimal primal-dual pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\) is a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite zero-sum game is a bilinear saddle problem; minimax equality is exactly strong duality between two linear programs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Saddle characterization and minimax value of a finite zero-sum game
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Corrects the extract's unsupported final converse: attaining the scalar value alone does not establish the saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $L=(\ell(i,j))\in\mathbb R^{N\times M}$ and $\bar\ell(p,q)=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^M p_iq_j\ell(i,j)$. A product profile $p\times q$ is a Nash equilibrium of the two-player zero-sum game if and only if $$\bar\ell(p,q')\leq\bar\ell(p,q)\leq\bar\ell(p',q)\qquad\forall p'\in\Delta_N,\ q'\in\Delta_M.$$ For finite games, $$\min_{p\in\Delta_N}\max_{q\in\Delta_M}\bar\ell(p,q)=\max_{q\in\Delta_M}\min_{p\in\Delta_N}\bar\ell(p,q)=:V,$$ and every Nash equilibrium satisfies $\bar\ell(p,q)=V$. The converse implication $\bar\ell(p,q)=V\Rightarrow p\times q\text{ is Nash}$ is false without the two saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed profile in a finite two-player zero-sum game is Nash exactly when it is a saddle point of expected loss. The minimax and maximin values coincide, and every Nash profile attains that value. Merely having expected loss equal to the value does not by itself make a profile Nash.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\times q\text{ is Nash}\iff\forall p',q',\ \bar\ell(p,q')\leq\bar\ell(p,q)\leq\bar\ell(p',q),\qquad \min_p\max_q\bar\ell(p,q)=\max_q\min_p\bar\ell(p,q)=V,\qquad \bar\ell(p,q)=V\not\Rightarrow p\times q\text{ is Nash}.

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be compact Hausdorff spaces and let \(g:X	imes Y	o\mathbb{R}\) be continuous. For Borel probability measures \(\mu\in\mathcal{P}(X)\) and \(

knowledge_statements.title: Discretization Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform payoff approximation transfers values and approximate equilibria between continuous and finite games.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be compact metric spaces and suppose \(g:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) has modulus of continuity \(\omega\). Let \(X_\delta\subset X\) and \(Y_\delta\subset Y\) be \(\delta\)-nets, and let \(v\) and \(v_\delta\) be the mixed values of the continuous and discretized games. Then
\[|v-v_\delta|\le\omega(\delta).\]
If \((\mu_\delta,\nu_\delta)\) has saddle gap at most \(\varepsilon\) in the finite game and is embedded as atomic measures on \(X\) and \(Y\), then its continuous-game saddle gap is at most \(\varepsilon+2\omega(\delta)\). Thus mesh resolution converts finite-game accuracy into continuous-game accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A delta-net changes the game value by at most the payoff continuity modulus and adds at most twice that error to equilibrium gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|v-v_\delta|\le\omega(\delta)\), and an \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium of the discretization has continuous gap at most \(\varepsilon+2\omega(\delta)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dimensionality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension dependence of entropy-based no-regret solution of finite matrix games.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider an \(m\)-by-\(n\) zero-sum matrix game with payoffs in \([-1,1]\). If both players use entropy-regularized multiplicative weights for \(T\) rounds with optimally tuned constant learning rates, their external regrets satisfy
\[R_x(T)\le\sqrt{2T\log m},\qquad R_y(T)\le\sqrt{2T\log n}.\]
Therefore the empirical mixed strategies have saddle gap at most
\[\frac{R_x(T)+R_y(T)}{T}\le\sqrt{\frac{2\log m}{T}}+\sqrt{\frac{2\log n}{T}}.\]
It suffices to take \(T=O((\log m+\log n)\varepsilon^{-2})\) rounds for gap at most \(\varepsilon\), exhibiting logarithmic action-dimension dependence under the full-information model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entropy-based no-regret dynamics solve a full-information matrix game in order log-action-dimension divided by epsilon squared rounds.
assumptions_latex: Both players observe full payoff vectors each round.
Both use multiplicative weights with tuned constant learning rates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ergodic saddle gap is \(O(\bigl(\sqrt{\log m}+\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)/\sqrt{T})\), giving \(T=O((\log m+\log n)\varepsilon^{-2})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Regret-to-Ergodic-Equilibrium Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: External-regret reduction for averaged play in convex-concave zero-sum games.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be convex sets and let \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\). For plays \((x_t,y_t)_{t=1}^T\), define
\[R_x(T)=\sum_{t=1}^T f(x_t,y_t)-\min_{x\in X}\sum_{t=1}^T f(x,y_t),\]
\[R_y(T)=\max_{y\in Y}\sum_{t=1}^T f(x_t,y)-\sum_{t=1}^T f(x_t,y_t).\]
With \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_t x_t\) and \(\bar y_T=T^{-1}\sum_t y_t\), the ergodic saddle gap obeys
\[\max_{y\in Y}f(\bar x_T,y)-\min_{x\in X}f(x,\bar y_T)\le\frac{R_x(T)+R_y(T)}{T}.\]
Thus sublinear regret implies convergence of averaged play to equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The saddle gap of averaged play is at most the sum of both players' external regrets divided by the number of rounds.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\).
The displayed regret extrema and averages are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_y f(\bar x_T,y)-\min_x f(x,\bar y_T)\le(R_x(T)+R_y(T))/T\).

knowledge_statements.title: Optimistic Learning Dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected optimistic gradient descent–ascent for a differentiable convex–concave game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets, let \(Z=X\times Y\), and define \(F(x,y)=(\nabla_x L(x,y),-\nabla_y L(x,y))\). Given \(z_{-1}=z_0\in Z\) and \(\eta>0\), compute for \(t\geq 0\)
\[
z_{t+1}=\Pi_Z\bigl(z_t-\eta(2F(z_t)-F(z_{t-1}))\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, each player uses the current gradient plus the prediction \(F(z_t)-F(z_{t-1})\) of its next change. Stop when a prescribed residual or iteration limit is reached and output the last iterate \(z_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimistic gradient descent–ascent corrects the current game gradient using its most recent change and returns the final joint strategy.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(Z\).
Euclidean projections onto \(Z\) are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_T\) is the last iterate generated by the projected optimistic update.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the joint strategy set

knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear last-iterate convergence of optimistic descent–ascent in a nonsingular bilinear game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) be nonsingular and consider \(L(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}Ay\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d\). Initialize \(x_{-1}=x_0\) and \(y_{-1}=y_0\), and apply
\[
x_{t+1}=x_t-2\eta Ay_t+\eta Ay_{t-1},\qquad y_{t+1}=y_t+2\eta A^{\mathsf T}x_t-\eta A^{\mathsf T}x_{t-1}.
\]
If \(0<\eta<1/(2\lVert A\rVert_2)\), then there exist constants \(C<\infty\) and \(\rho\in(0,1)\), depending on \(A\) and \(\eta\), such that \(\lVert x_t\rVert_2+\lVert y_t\rVert_2\leq C\rho^t\) for every \(t\). Hence the last iterate converges to the unique saddle point \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonsingular bilinear game and a sufficiently small step size, optimistic descent–ascent converges geometrically in its actual iterates to the saddle point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_t,y_t)\to(0,0)\) geometrically as \(t\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: spectral norm of the payoff matrix
a contraction factor strictly below one

In addition, the stated constant C cannot depend only on A and eta for arbitrary initialization; it must also scale with the initial state unless an initial-state normalization is imposed.

children.title: Optimism-to-Stability Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Structural links between predictive corrections and stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimism-to-Stability Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prediction accuracy converts optimistic regret control into control of iterate motion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:Z\to\mathbb{R}^d\) be \(L_F\)-Lipschitz and let the optimistic prediction be \(m_t=F(z_{t-1})\). Then
\[
\lVert F(z_t)-m_t\rVert_*\leq L_F\lVert z_t-z_{t-1}\rVert.
\]
Consequently, whenever an optimistic mirror-type analysis yields
\[
R_T(z)\leq B(z)+a\sum_{t=1}^T\lVert F(z_t)-m_t\rVert_*^2-b\sum_{t=1}^T\lVert z_t-z_{t-1}\rVert^2,
\]
with \(b>aL_F^2\), it also yields \(R_T(z)\leq B(z)-(b-aL_F^2)\sum_{t=1}^T\lVert z_t-z_{t-1}\rVert^2\). Thus bounded regret forces square-summable movement, the basic stability mechanism behind last-iterate results.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lipschitz gradients make one-step predictions accurate; if the update’s movement penalty dominates prediction error, total squared movement is finite.

children.title: Last-Iterate Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Game regimes where optimism does not stabilize terminal iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous gradient descent–ascent cycles in the elementary bilinear game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(L(x,y)=xy\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and simultaneous gradient descent–ascent with constant \(\eta>0\):
\[
x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta y_t,\qquad y_{t+1}=y_t+\eta x_t.
\]
For every nonzero initialization,
\[
x_{t+1}^2+y_{t+1}^2=(1+\eta^2)(x_t^2+y_t^2).
\]
Hence \(x_t^2+y_t^2=(1+\eta^2)^t(x_0^2+y_0^2)\), so the last iterate diverges from the unique saddle point \((0,0)\). Thus no-regret or averaged-equilibrium conclusions alone cannot supply last-iterate stability for this uncorrected constant-step update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary simultaneous descent–ascent spirals outward on a bilinear game, showing that averaging guarantees do not imply last-iterate convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert(x_t,y_t)\rVert_2=(1+\eta^2)^{t/2}\lVert(x_0,y_0)\rVert_2\to\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial Training Saddles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-example adversarial training as a finite-sample minimax problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given samples \((a_i,b_i)_{i=1}^N\), a perturbation set \(\Delta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\), model parameters \(\theta\in\Theta\), and loss \(\ell\), adversarial empirical training is represented by
\[
\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\max_{\delta_i\in\Delta}\ell(\theta;a_i+\delta_i,b_i)
=\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_N)\in\Delta^N}\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\ell(\theta;a_i+\delta_i,b_i).
\]
The inner variables select admissible worst-case perturbations, while the outer variable selects model parameters. This is a convex–concave saddle problem only when the corresponding convexity and concavity conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adversarial training minimizes empirical loss against worst-case admissible perturbations of every training example.
assumptions_latex: Each inner maximum is attained, or \(\max\) is replaced by \(\sup\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The separable inner maximizations equal the joint maximization over \(\Delta^N\).

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Empirical-Risk Minimax Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributionally robust empirical risk over an ambiguity set of sample weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For observations \((a_i,b_i)_{i=1}^N\), losses \(\ell_i(\theta)=\ell(\theta;a_i,b_i)\), and a nonempty ambiguity set \(Q\subseteq\{q\in\mathbb{R}_+^N:\sum_iq_i=1\}\), the robust empirical-risk problem is
\[
\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{q\in Q}\sum_{i=1}^N q_i\ell_i(\theta).
\]
The empirical-risk model is recovered when \(Q=\{(1/N,\ldots,1/N)\}\). If \(\Theta\) and \(Q\) are compact convex, each \(\ell_i\) is continuous and convex in \(\theta\), and the objective is linear in \(q\), the formulation is a convex–concave minimax model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robust ERM minimizes the largest weighted empirical loss over a prescribed ambiguity set of data distributions.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a nonempty subset of the probability simplex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=\{(1/N,\ldots,1/N)\}\) reduces the model to ordinary empirical-risk minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Generative Adversarial Games
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Original logistic generative-adversarial objective as a two-player minimax game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_{\mathrm{data}}\) be a data distribution, \(P_Z\) a latent distribution, \(G_\theta\) a generator, and \(D_\phi:\mathcal X\to(0,1)\) a discriminator. The logistic generative-adversarial game is
\[
\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{\phi\in\Phi}\left\{\mathbb E_{X\sim P_{\mathrm{data}}}[\log D_\phi(X)]+\mathbb E_{Z\sim P_Z}[\log(1-D_\phi(G_\theta(Z)))]\right\}.
\]
The discriminator maximizes correct separation of real and generated samples; the generator minimizes the same payoff. For parameterized neural classes this objective is generally nonconvex–nonconcave, so convex saddle-point guarantees do not automatically apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A logistic GAN is a minimax game in which the discriminator separates real from generated samples and the generator tries to defeat it.
assumptions_latex: The displayed expectations exist and are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Training seeks a minimax equilibrium of the displayed generator–discriminator payoff.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role and canonical logistic generator-discriminator objective fit the leaf, and the nonconvex-nonconcave qualification is appropriate. No inspectable source is supplied for the original GAN objective.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: GAN minimax formulation and nonconvergence boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the default zero-sum GAN objective, its ideal equilibrium, the stated convex convergence regime, and the failure of simultaneous gradient play in general games.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a generator $x=g(z;\theta^{(g)})$ and discriminator $d(x;\theta^{(d)})$, the default zero-sum GAN objective is
\[
\min_g\max_d v(g,d),\qquad v=\mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}[\log d(x)]+\mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{model}}}[\log(1-d(x))].
\]
At the ideal converged solution, generator samples are indistinguishable from data and $d(x)=\tfrac12$. In the stated regime where $\max_d v(g,d)$ is convex in $\theta^{(g)}$, the procedure is guaranteed to converge and is asymptotically consistent. Without such convexity, simultaneous gradient updates are not generally guaranteed to reach equilibrium: for $v(a,b)=ab$, infinitesimal opposing gradient updates follow circular orbits around $(0,0)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The default GAN formulation is a zero-sum minimax game. At its ideal converged solution, generated samples match the data distribution and the discriminator outputs one half. The stated convex generator-side regime supports convergence and asymptotic consistency, but simultaneous gradient play need not converge in nonconvex games; the bilinear game cycles around its equilibrium.
assumptions_latex: v(g,d)=\mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}[\log d(x)]+\mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{model}}}[\log(1-d(x))]
\max_d v(g,d)\text{ is convex in }\theta^{(g)}\text{ for the stated convergence guarantee}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d(x)=\tfrac12\text{ at the ideal converged solution};\qquad \max_d v(g,d)\text{ convex in }\theta^{(g)}\Rightarrow\text{convergence and asymptotic consistency},\quad\text{whereas general simultaneous gradient play may cycle}.

children.title: Fairness Saddle Models
children.top_down_role: Saddle formulations arising from fairness criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Fairness Saddle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained empirical learning with group-disparity constraints and nonnegative multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R(\theta)\) be empirical risk and let \(d_j(\theta)\) be signed group-disparity measures with tolerances \(\tau_j\). The constrained fairness problem
\[
\min_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta)\quad\text{subject to}\quad d_j(\theta)\leq\tau_j,\quad j=1,\ldots,m,
\]
has Lagrangian saddle form
\[
\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m}\left\{R(\theta)+\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j(d_j(\theta)-\tau_j)\right\}.
\]
Under convexity, lower semicontinuity, and a Slater condition, the saddle value equals the constrained optimum; each multiplier prices violation of its associated fairness constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fairness-constrained learning becomes a saddle problem by assigning a nonnegative multiplier to every group-disparity constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) and every \(d_j\) are convex and lower semicontinuous on convex \(\Theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constrained optimum equals the displayed Lagrangian minimax value, with an attained dual optimum under standard finite-dimensional regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Saddle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian saddle representation of a convex inequality-constrained problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
p^\star=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x):g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,
\ldots,m\},
\]
where \(X\) is convex and \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) are proper convex functions. Define \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}g(x)\) for \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\). If the primal value is finite and there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}(X)\) with \(g_i(\bar x)<0\) for all \(i\), then
\[
p^\star=\sup_{\lambda\geq0}\inf_{x\in X}\mathcal L(x,\lambda).
\]
Whenever primal and dual optima are attained, \((x^\star,\lambda^\star)\) is a saddle point exactly when primal feasibility, dual feasibility, optimality, and complementary slackness hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex constrained problem equals its Lagrangian max–min dual under Slater regularity, and optimal primal-dual pairs are saddle points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex and \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) are proper convex functions.
The primal value is finite and the stated relative-interior Slater point exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star=\sup_{\lambda\geq0}\inf_{x\in X}\mathcal L(x,\lambda)\), with saddle points characterized by the convex KKT conditions when optima are attained.

children.title: Fairness–Feasibility Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between fairness targets and feasible prediction behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Fairness–Feasibility Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint violation certified by a bounded-multiplier saddle gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g_j(\theta)=d_j(\theta)-\tau_j\), let \(f_{\inf}=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta)>-\infty\), and suppose \(\theta^\star\) is feasible. If \((\widehat\theta,\widehat\lambda)\) has restricted saddle gap at most \(\varepsilon\) over \(\Theta\times[0,\Lambda]^m\), then comparison with \(\theta^\star\) and maximization over the multiplier box give
\[
R(\widehat\theta)-R(\theta^\star)+\Lambda\sum_{j=1}^m[g_j(\widehat\theta)]_+\leq\varepsilon.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m[g_j(\widehat\theta)]_+\leq\frac{R(\theta^\star)-f_{\inf}+\varepsilon}{\Lambda}.
\]
Thus the computed saddle gap and multiplier radius jointly certify the fairness–feasibility tradeoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small saddle gap with multiplier cap Λ bounds total fairness violation by a quantity proportional to one over Λ.
assumptions_latex: The restricted primal-dual saddle gap is at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_j[d_j(\widehat\theta)-\tau_j]_+\leq(R(\theta^\star)-f_{\inf}+\varepsilon)/\Lambda\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits the tradeoff leaf, and the displayed violation bound is plausible under the usual full restricted primal-dual gap. However, that gap is not explicitly defined, so its orientation and comparator quantifiers cannot be checked; an exact source or definition is required.

children.title: Multiplier-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of application behavior to dual weighting.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal multipliers control local value sensitivity; unbounded multipliers preclude uniform bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^m\), define \(p(u)=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g(x)\leq u\}\). Suppose strong duality holds at \(u=0\) and \(\lambda^\star\geq0\) is an optimal multiplier there. Weak duality for the perturbed problem gives
\[
p(u)\geq p(0)-(\lambda^\star)^{\mathsf T}u.
\]
Hence any uniform bound \(\lVert\lambda^\star\rVert_*\leq M\) yields \(p(u)\geq p(0)-M\lVert u\rVert\). The boundary is loss of bounded dual solutions: if optimal multipliers become unbounded or do not exist, this argument supplies no finite uniform sensitivity modulus, and multiplier truncation may introduce uncontrolled bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded optimal multipliers give a Lipschitz-type perturbation bound; without bounded dual solutions, no finite uniform sensitivity certificate follows.
assumptions_latex: Strong duality and dual attainment hold for the unperturbed convex problem.
The perturbed primal value \(p(u)\) is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(u)\geq p(0)-\lVert\lambda^\star\rVert_*\lVert u\rVert\); a uniform modulus requires uniformly bounded optimal multipliers.

notation.meaning: optimal value under right-hand-side perturbation u
uniform dual-norm bound on optimal multipliers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, and the one-sided perturbation inequality has the correct sign under the stated value-function convention. A source is required for the sensitivity result, and the final boundary claim must remain explicitly limited to failure of this multiplier-based certificate rather than asserting that no other sensitivity bound can exist.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Correlated equilibrium
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allows arbitrary correlation among players' recommended actions and deviations depending on a player's own recommendation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A distribution $P$ on $\prod_{k=1}^KA_k$ is a correlated equilibrium if, for every player $k$ and every deviation map $\phi_k:A_k\to A_k$, with $I\sim P$, $\mathbb E[\ell^{(k)}(I)]\leq\mathbb E[\ell^{(k)}(I^{-k},\phi_k(I^{(k)}))]$. children.title: Traffic Equilibria

knowledge_statements.title: Traffic Equilibria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wardrop user equilibrium expressed as a variational inequality on feasible path flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^P\) be the nonempty closed convex set of path flows satisfying fixed origin–destination demands. Let \(C:K\to\mathbb{R}^P\) assign path travel costs. A Wardrop equilibrium is a flow \(h^\star\in K\) satisfying
\[
\langle C(h^\star),h-h^\star\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }h\in K.
\]
Equivalently, for each origin–destination pair, every path carrying positive equilibrium flow has minimum travel cost among that pair's paths. If \(C\) is continuous and \(K\) is compact, an equilibrium exists; if \(C\) is strictly monotone on \(K\), the equilibrium path-flow vector is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A traffic equilibrium is a feasible flow whose travel-cost vector satisfies a variational inequality; used paths have minimum cost.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex feasible-flow set.
\(C\) maps each feasible path flow to its path-cost vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h^\star\) is a Wardrop equilibrium exactly when \(\langle C(h^\star),h-h^\star\rangle\geq0\) for all \(h\in K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the traffic-equilibrium leaf, and the Wardrop variational inequality, existence condition, and strict-monotonicity uniqueness statement are standard and internally consistent. No inspectable traffic-equilibrium source is supplied for the VI equivalence or the existence and uniqueness claims.

children.title: Network Equilibria
children.top_down_role: Equilibrium structures on interacting networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Equilibria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational-inequality formulation of a finite-dimensional capacitated network equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be the nonempty closed convex set of feasible network flows, including conservation and capacity constraints, and let \(c:K\to\mathbb{R}^m\) assign marginal route or arc costs. A network equilibrium is a flow \(x^\star\in K\) satisfying
\[
\langle c(x^\star),x-x^\star\rangle\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }x\in K.
\]
Thus no feasible aggregate reallocation has negative first-order cost at \(x^\star\). When \(K\) is a path-flow polytope and path costs are induced by arc costs, this condition expresses the Wardrop requirement that every used path has minimum cost among feasible paths for the same commodity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible network flow is an equilibrium when no feasible flow reallocation decreases aggregate first-order cost; for path flows, used paths have minimum commodity-specific cost.
assumptions_latex: \(c:K\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is well defined; continuity is imposed when existence is considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in K\) is a network equilibrium exactly when \(\langle c(x^\star),x-x^\star\rangle\ge0\) for all \(x\in K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Conditional Regret Implies Convergence to Correlated Equilibrium
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite repeated games with asymptotically nonpositive average conditional regret for every player and action substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a finite $K$-player game with action sets $\{1,\ldots,N_k\}$ and correlated-equilibrium set $\mathcal C$. If, for every player $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ and every pair $j,j'\in\{1,\ldots,N_k\}$, $$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n \widehat r^{(k)}_{(j,j'),t}\le 0,$$ then the empirical distribution $\widehat P_n$ of joint play satisfies $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{P\in\mathcal C}\sum_{\mathbf i}\left|P(\mathbf i)-\widehat P_n(\mathbf i)\right|=0.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite repeated K-player game, if every player's average conditional regret for every ordered pair of actions has nonpositive limiting upper value, then the empirical distribution of joint plays converges in total L1 distance to the set of correlated equilibria.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{P\in\mathcal C}\sum_{\mathbf i}|P(\mathbf i)-\widehat P_n(\mathbf i)|=0

children.title: Market Equilibria
children.top_down_role: Variational formulations for market clearing or exchange.

knowledge_statements.title: Market Equilibria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Price-based market clearing expressed as a complementarity variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\mathbb{R}_+^m\) be the admissible price cone and let \(z:P\to\mathbb{R}^m\) denote aggregate excess demand, with positive components representing shortages. A market equilibrium price is \(p^\star\in P\) satisfying
\[
\langle -z(p^\star),p-p^\star\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }p\in P.
\]
Equivalently, componentwise, \(p^\star\ge0\), \(z(p^\star)\le0\), and \(p_i^\star z_i(p^\star)=0\) for every good \(i\). Hence a positively priced good clears, while a good in excess supply may have zero price.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equilibrium prices are nonnegative, excess demand is nonpositive, and every positively priced good clears; these complementarity conditions form a variational inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(z(p)\) is the aggregate excess-demand vector at price \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(P,-z)\), equivalently \(p^\star\ge0\), \(z(p^\star)\le0\), and \(p_i^\star z_i(p^\star)=0\).

children.title: Cross-Domain VI Structure
children.top_down_role: Shared operator structure across the three application domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Domain VI Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common variational-inequality template shared by network, market, and physical equilibria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, \(K\subset X\) a nonempty closed convex feasible set, and \(F:K\to X\) an equilibrium residual or marginal-response operator. Across equilibrium domains, the governing condition has the representation
\[
0\in F(x^\star)+N_K(x^\star)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle F(x^\star),x-x^\star\rangle\ge0\quad\text{for every }x\in K,
\]
where \(N_K\) is the convex-analytic normal cone. Domain-specific conservation, capacity, clearing, nonpenetration, or obstacle restrictions enter through \(K\); costs, excess supply, forces, or differential operators enter through \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Many equilibrium models share one structure: feasibility is encoded by a convex set, responses by an operator, and equilibrium by a normal-cone inclusion or equivalent VI.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in F(x^\star)+N_K(x^\star)\) is equivalent to \(\langle F(x^\star),x-x^\star\rangle\ge0\) for every \(x\in K\).

children.title: Nash–Cournot Equilibria
children.top_down_role: Quantity-competition equilibrium structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Nash–Cournot Equilibria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable concave Cournot game with independent convex production constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For firms \(i=1,\ldots,n\), let \(K_i\subset\mathbb{R}\) be a nonempty closed convex production set, let \(K=\prod_{i=1}^n K_i\), let \(q=(q_1,\ldots,q_n)\in K\), and let \(\pi_i(q_i,q_{-i})\) be firm \(i\)'s profit. A Nash–Cournot equilibrium is a vector \(q^\star\in K\) such that, for every firm \(i\),
\[
\pi_i(q_i^\star,q_{-i}^\star)\ge \pi_i(r_i,q_{-i}^\star)\qquad\text{for every }r_i\in K_i.
\]
If each \(\pi_i\) is differentiable and concave in \(q_i\), define \(F_i(q)=-\partial\pi_i(q)/\partial q_i\). Then \(q^\star\) is a Nash–Cournot equilibrium if and only if
\[
\langle F(q^\star),q-q^\star\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }q\in K.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With independent convex production constraints, a Nash–Cournot equilibrium permits no profitable unilateral output change. Under differentiability and own-output concavity, these conditions are equivalent to a variational inequality for the negative profit pseudo-gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(K=\prod_{i=1}^n K_i\), with every \(K_i\subset\mathbb{R}\) nonempty, closed, and convex.
Each \(\pi_i\) is differentiable and concave in \(q_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q^\star\) is a Nash–Cournot equilibrium if and only if it solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\), where \(F_i(q)=-\partial_{q_i}\pi_i(q)\).

children.title: General Economic Equilibria
children.top_down_role: Broader economic equilibrium formulations with variational structure.

knowledge_statements.title: General Economic Equilibria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-commodity competitive equilibrium with consumers, firms, and market clearing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(m\) commodities, consumers with endowments \(e_i\), feasible consumption sets \(X_i\), and preferences represented by utilities \(u_i\), together with firms having production sets \(Y_j\). A competitive economic equilibrium consists of a nonzero price vector \(p^\star\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\), consumptions \(x_i^\star\in X_i\), and productions \(y_j^\star\in Y_j\) such that each \(x_i^\star\) maximizes \(u_i(x_i)\) over the consumer's price-feasible budget set, each \(y_j^\star\) maximizes \(\langle p^\star,y_j\rangle\) over \(Y_j\), and
\[
\sum_i x_i^\star=\sum_i e_i+\sum_j y_j^\star.
\]
A normalization such as \(\sum_k p_k^\star=1\) removes price-scale indeterminacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A competitive equilibrium combines utility-maximizing consumption, profit-maximizing production, and commodity-wise market clearing at a nonzero normalized price vector.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many commodities, consumers, and firms.
Each consumer's budget includes endowment value and any assigned profit income.
Prices are nonnegative and normalized to remove positive rescaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((p^\star,(x_i^\star)_i,(y_j^\star)_j)\) is a competitive equilibrium when individual optimality and aggregate market clearing hold simultaneously.

notation.meaning: equilibrium net production of firm j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The competitive-equilibrium definition depends on a precise consumer budget and firm-profit ownership convention. No source or locator is supplied for those conventions.

children.title: Cournot-to-VI Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Operator representations connecting competition models to variational inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Cournot-to-VI Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudo-gradient interface converting differentiable Cournot optimality conditions into a VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=\prod_{i=1}^n K_i\), where each \(K_i\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and let firm \(i\)'s profit \(\pi_i(q_i,q_{-i})\) be differentiable and concave in \(q_i\). Define the Cournot pseudo-gradient by
\[
F(q)=\bigl(-\nabla_{q_i}\pi_i(q)\bigr)_{i=1}^n.
\]
Then \(q^\star\) is a Nash–Cournot equilibrium if and only if
\[
\langle F(q^\star),q-q^\star\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }q\in K.
\]
Thus separate first-order profit-maximization conditions assemble into one variational inequality; monotonicity of \(F\), when available, supplies the standard monotone-operator interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative own-profit gradients form a pseudo-gradient. With convex independent constraints and own-output concavity, Nash–Cournot equilibria are exactly the solutions of its VI.
assumptions_latex: \(K=\prod_i K_i\) with each \(K_i\) nonempty, closed, and convex.
Each \(\pi_i\) is differentiable and concave in its own variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q^\star\) is Nash–Cournot if and only if \(q^\star\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).

children.title: Contact Variational Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Variational inequality structure arising from contact problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Contact Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small-deformation unilateral contact in an abstract energy-space formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a real Hilbert space of admissible displacements, let \(K\subset V\) be the nonempty closed convex set enforcing unilateral nonpenetration, let \(a:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}\) be the elasticity bilinear form, and let \(\ell\in V^*\) be the applied load. The frictionless contact variational inequality is to find \(u^\star\in K\) such that
\[
a(u^\star,v-u^\star)\ge \ell(v-u^\star)\qquad\text{for every }v\in K.
\]
If \(a\) is continuous, symmetric, and coercive, this is the first-order condition for minimizing \(\tfrac12a(v,v)-\ell(v)\) over \(K\), and the displacement solution is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Frictionless unilateral contact seeks a nonpenetrating displacement whose elastic virtual work dominates the external virtual work for every feasible displacement.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a real Hilbert space and \(K\subset V\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique \(u^\star\in K\) satisfying \(a(u^\star,v-u^\star)\ge\ell(v-u^\star)\) for all \(v\in K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The frictionless-contact VI and coercive energy formulation are plausible and internally consistent, but no contact-mechanics source supports the model or the existence-and-uniqueness conclusion.

children.title: Obstacle Variational Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Variational inequality structure arising from obstacle constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Obstacle Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elliptic obstacle problem with a pointwise lower obstacle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be bounded and Lipschitz, let \(V=H_0^1(\Omega)\), and let
\[
K=\{v\in V:v\ge\psi\ \text{almost everywhere in }\Omega\}
\]
be nonempty for an obstacle \(\psi\). Given \(f\in V^*\), the obstacle variational inequality is to find \(u^\star\in K\) such that
\[
\int_\Omega \nabla u^\star\cdot\nabla(v-u^\star)\,dx\ge \langle f,v-u^\star\rangle_{V^*,V}
\qquad\text{for every }v\in K.
\]
Equivalently, \(u^\star\) minimizes \(\tfrac12\int_\Omega|\nabla v|^2dx-\langle f,v\rangle\) over \(K\); coercivity gives uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The obstacle problem minimizes Dirichlet energy minus loading over functions lying above an obstacle, equivalently satisfying an elliptic variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A unique \(u^\star\in K\) satisfies the obstacle variational inequality and minimizes the associated constrained energy.

notation.meaning: closed convex set of functions above the obstacle
load in the dual Sobolev space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supersolution Comparison Principle for the Obstacle Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper comparison for the solution of Problem 6.1 against an admissibly dominating weak supersolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\) solve Problem 6.1. If \(g\) is an \(L-f\) supersolution, \(g\ge\psi\) in \(\Omega\), and \(g\ge0\) on \(\partial\Omega\) in the \(H^1(\Omega)\) sense, then \(u\le g\) in \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The obstacle-problem solution lies below every L-f supersolution that dominates the obstacle in the domain and is nonnegative on the boundary in the Sobolev sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\le g\quad\text{in }\Omega.
