knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sobolev Positivity, Noncontact Set, and Contact Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines pointwise positivity appropriate to H1 functions and applies it to the obstacle solution's contact geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in H^1(\Omega)\), write \(u(x)>0\) in the \(H^1(\Omega)\) sense if there exist \(\rho>0\) and \(\varphi\in H_0^{1,\infty}(B_\rho(x))\) such that \(\varphi\ge0\), \(\varphi(x)>0\), and \(u-\varphi\ge0\) on \(B_\rho(x)\) in the \(H^1\) sense. The set \(\{x\in\Omega:u(x)>0\}\) is open. If \(u\) solves Problem 6.1 with obstacle \(\psi\), then the noncontact set \(\{x\in\Omega:u(x)>\psi(x)\}\) is open and its complement \(I[u]\) is closed in \(\Omega\); formally, \(I[u]=\{x:u(x)=\psi(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sobolev positivity at a point means that locally the function dominates a nonnegative Sobolev test function that is strictly positive at that point. The positivity set is open. For an obstacle-problem solution, the strict noncontact set is open, while its complement—the contact set—is closed and formally consists of points where the solution equals the obstacle.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x\in\Omega:u(x)>0\}\text{ is open},\qquad \{u>\psi\}\text{ is open},\qquad I[u]=\Omega\setminus\{u>\psi\}\text{ is closed in }\Omega.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacity Control of the Obstacle Reaction Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the reaction measure of an obstacle solution in terms of relative capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_N\in L^2(\Omega)\), \(\psi\in H^1(\Omega)\), and \(f=f_0+\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\partial/\partial x_i)f_i\in H^{-1}(\Omega)\). Let \(u\) be the solution of Problem 6.1 in \(\mathbb K_\psi\), and let \(\mu\) be the measure determined by \(u\). Then there exists \(C>0\) such that \(\mu(E)\leq C(\operatorname{cap}E)^{1/2}\) for every compact \(E\subset\Omega\). In particular, \(\operatorname{cap}E=0\) implies \(\mu(E)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated divergence-form data and H1 obstacle, the reaction measure is bounded on compact sets by a constant times the square root of capacity and therefore vanishes on compact capacity-zero sets.
assumptions_latex: u\in\mathbb K_\psi\text{ is the solution of Problem 6.1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists C>0\ \forall E\subset\Omega\text{ compact}:\ \mu(E)\leq C\bigl(\operatorname{cap}E\bigr)^{1/2};\quad\operatorname{cap}E=0\Rightarrow\mu(E)=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Supersolutions of L-f
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines supersolutions through nonnegative Sobolev test functions and records the obstacle solution as an instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(g\in H^1(\Omega)\) is an \(L-f\) supersolution if \(\langle Lg-f,\zeta\rangle:=a(g,\zeta)-\langle f,\zeta\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(\zeta\in H_0^1(\Omega)\) with \(\zeta\ge0\). If \(u\) solves Problem 6.1 and \(u+\zeta\in\mathbb K\) for every such \(\zeta\), then \(u\) is an \(L-f\) supersolution. Positivity in \(H^1(\Omega)\) is identified with almost-everywhere positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Sobolev function is an L-f supersolution when its weak residual is nonnegative against every nonnegative zero-boundary test function. The solution of Problem 6.1 is such a supersolution because the feasible set permits every nonnegative test perturbation. Positivity in H1 is understood almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is an }(L-f)\text{ supersolution}\iff \forall\,0\le\zeta\in H_0^1(\Omega),\ \langle Lg-f,\zeta\rangle\ge0.

knowledge_statements.title: PDE Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract coercive elliptic PDE constrained by a closed convex admissible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a real Hilbert space, \(K\subset V\) a nonempty closed convex set, \(A:V\to V^*\) an operator, and \(f\in V^*\). A PDE variational inequality is the problem of finding \(u^\star\in K\) such that
\[
\langle Au^\star-f,v-u^\star\rangle_{V^*,V}\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }v\in K.
\]
For a linear bounded coercive operator induced by a bilinear form \(a\), the condition becomes \(a(u^\star,v-u^\star)\ge\langle f,v-u^\star\rangle\). If \(A\) is strongly monotone and hemicontinuous, the solution is unique; standard existence additionally follows under the usual coercivity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained PDE is written as a duality inequality between its residual and every feasible displacement; strong monotonicity yields uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a real Hilbert space and \(K\subset V\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(A:V\to V^*\) is hemicontinuous, strongly monotone, and coercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a unique \(u^\star\in K\) with \(\langle Au^\star-f,v-u^\star\rangle\ge0\) for every \(v\in K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Discretization-to-Operator Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conforming finite-dimensional reduction of a Hilbert-space variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V_h\subset V\) be a finite-dimensional conforming space with basis \((\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_N)\), let \(K_h\subset V_h\) be a nonempty closed convex discrete feasible set, and consider \(a(u_h,v_h-u_h)\ge\ell(v_h-u_h)\) for all \(v_h\in K_h\). Writing \(u_h=\sum_j x_j\phi_j\), define \(M_{ij}=a(\phi_j,\phi_i)\), \(b_i=\ell(\phi_i)\), and let \(C_h\subset\mathbb{R}^N\) contain coefficient vectors representing \(K_h\). The discrete problem is exactly
\[
\langle Mx^\star-b,y-x^\star\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C_h,
\]
so its operator is \(F_h(x)=Mx-b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conforming basis converts a variational PDE inequality into a finite-dimensional VI whose matrix and load vector represent the weak operator and forcing.
assumptions_latex: \(V_h\subset V\) is finite-dimensional with a fixed basis.
\(K_h\subset V_h\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The discrete weak inequality is equivalent to \(\operatorname{VI}(C_h,F_h)\) with \(F_h(x)=Mx-b\).

coefficient representation of the discrete feasible set

children.title: Fixed Parameter Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies retaining constant algorithmic parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Parameter Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant stepsize regime for projected forward iteration under strong monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and suppose \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(\mu>0\). For the projected forward iteration
\[
x^{k+1}=P_K\bigl(x^k-\alpha F(x^k)\bigr),
\]
a fixed-parameter policy chooses one constant \(\alpha\) satisfying
\[
0<\alpha<\frac{2\mu}{L^2}.
\]
Then the iteration map is contractive with factor at most \(\sqrt{1-2\alpha\mu+\alpha^2L^2}<1\), and the iterates converge linearly to the unique solution of \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strongly monotone Lipschitz VI, a constant projected-forward stepsize below twice the monotonicity modulus divided by the squared Lipschitz constant gives linear convergence.
assumptions_latex: The update uses Euclidean projection onto \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(0<\alpha<2\mu/L^2\), then \(x^k\) converges linearly to the unique VI solution with contraction factor at most \(\sqrt{1-2\alpha\mu+\alpha^2L^2}\).

children.title: Diminishing Parameter Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies using parameters that decay over time.

knowledge_statements.title: Diminishing Parameter Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robbins–Monro-type diminishing schedule for projected first-order equilibrium iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a projected first-order iteration
\[
x^{k+1}=P_K\bigl(x^k-\alpha_k g_k\bigr),
\]
a standard diminishing-parameter policy uses positive stepsizes satisfying
\[
\alpha_k>0,\qquad \alpha_k\to0,\qquad
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty,
\qquad
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k^2<\infty.
\]
The divergent first sum prevents the method from exhausting its total movement before reaching equilibrium, while square summability controls accumulated bounded-variance noise or quadratic error terms. A power schedule \(\alpha_k=a(k+b)^{-r}\), with \(a>0\), \(b>0\), and \(1/2<r\le1\), satisfies these conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard diminishing schedule tends to zero, has infinite total mass, and is square summable; power laws with exponent strictly above one-half and at most one qualify.
assumptions_latex: The update is projected onto a nonempty closed convex set \(K\).
The direction sequence \((g_k)\) obeys the boundedness or noise hypotheses required by the chosen convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy requires \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<\infty\); \(\alpha_k=a(k+b)^{-r}\) is admissible for \(1/2<r\le1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diminishing and square-summability conditions and the stated power-law range are standard and correctly formulated, but the record supplies no inspectable source.

children.title: Schedule-Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem settings favoring constant or decaying schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule-Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible fixed and diminishing stepsizes for deterministic or persistently noisy variational-inequality iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a closed convex set and let \((\gamma_k)_{k\geq 0}\) be positive stepsizes. A fixed regime has \(\gamma_k=\gamma\) for every \(k\), with \(\gamma\) restricted by the deterministic stability bound of the chosen update. Under unbiased oracle errors with uniformly bounded, nonvanishing second moments, the classical diminishing regime requires
\[\gamma_k\downarrow0,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma_k=\infty,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma_k^2<\infty.\]
Thus \(\gamma_k=c(k+1)^{-p}\) is admissible for this stochastic regime exactly when \(c>0\) and \(1/2<p\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use stability-limited constant steps in deterministic problems; persistent unbiased noise instead calls for nonsummable steps with square-summable magnitudes.
assumptions_latex: Oracle errors are conditionally unbiased with uniformly bounded second moments in the stochastic regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_k=c(k+1)^{-p}\) satisfies the stochastic summability conditions if and only if \(c>0\) and \(1/2<p\leq1\).
review_flags: Exact saddle-point or VI source for the stochastic schedule conditions is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stochastic summability conditions and polynomial example are standard, but no inspectable VI source supports the stated noise regime. The deterministic stability bound is method-dependent and left unspecified, while the plain statement omits the exact polynomial characterization.

children.title: Parameter-Robustness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity limits for prescribed parameter schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Robustness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp scalar obstructions for oversized fixed steps and excessively rapid diminishing schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the monotone Lipschitz variational inequality on \(\mathbb{R}\) with \(F(z)=Lz\), where \(L>0\), and the forward iteration \(z_{k+1}=z_k-\gamma_kF(z_k)\). For a fixed step \(\gamma_k=\gamma\), convergence from every \(z_0\) occurs exactly when \(0<\gamma L<2\); at \(\gamma L=2\) nonzero iterates oscillate, and for \(\gamma L>2\) they diverge. If \(0<\gamma_kL<1\) eventually but \(\sum_k\gamma_k<\infty\), then
\[z_k=z_0\prod_{i<k}(1-L\gamma_i)\]
can converge to a nonzero limit. Hence both an upper stability restriction and sufficient cumulative step length are indispensable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even a scalar monotone problem exposes both boundaries: oversized fixed steps diverge, while summable diminishing steps may stop short of the solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-step stability requires \(0<\gamma L<2\), while \(\sum_k\gamma_k<\infty\) may prevent convergence to \(0\).

notation.meaning: slope and Lipschitz constant of the scalar operator

review_flags: Elementary claim is directly checkable, but an external source locator was not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar calculation correctly illustrates the two claimed failure boundaries, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Backtracking Policies
children.top_down_role: Adaptive parameter selection through repeated trial reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Backtracking Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean extragradient backtracking for a monotone variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_k\in C\), an initial trial \(\bar\gamma_k>0\), a contraction \(\beta\in(0,1)\), and \(\theta\in(0,1)\), test \(\gamma=\bar\gamma_k\beta^j\) for \(j=0,1,\ldots\). Compute
\[y=P_C(x_k-\gamma F(x_k))\]
and accept the first trial satisfying
\[\gamma\lVert F(y)-F(x_k)\rVert\leq\theta\lVert y-x_k\rVert.\]
After acceptance, set
\[x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\gamma F(y)).\]
Stop when a prescribed residual or gap tolerance is met; otherwise return the last iterate or an analysis-specified weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly shrink a trial stepsize until local operator variation is controlled, then perform the extragradient correction with the accepted step.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
\(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is monotone and locally Lipschitz on the tested region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted \(\gamma\) satisfies \(\gamma\lVert F(y)-F(x_k)\rVert\leq\theta\lVert y-x_k\rVert\) and defines \(x_{k+1}\).
review_flags: The supplied line-search locator does not certify this exact extragradient backtracking rule.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and terminal placement are appropriate, but the exact extragradient backtracking rule and its termination assumptions require an authoritative VI-method source.

children.title: Line-Search Policies
children.top_down_role: Search frameworks for locally acceptable parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Search Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract trial-generation and acceptance interface for first-order saddle-point updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), choose a trial scale \(s_{k,0}>0\). For \(j=0,1,\ldots\), construct a candidate \(z_{k,j}=T(z_k,s_{k,j})\), evaluate a computable predicate \(A(z_k,z_{k,j},s_{k,j})\), and accept the first \(j\) for which \(A\) is true. If rejected, set \(s_{k,j+1}=\beta s_{k,j}\) with \(\beta\in(0,1)\). The policy outputs \(z_{k+1}=z_{k,j}\) and the accepted scale \(s_k=s_{k,j}\). A valid policy additionally specifies a termination rule ensuring that some sufficiently small positive trial is accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line search generates trial updates, tests a computable condition, contracts rejected scales, and returns the first accepted candidate and scale.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) and \(A\) are computable using the permitted first-order and proximal oracles.
Every sufficiently small positive trial satisfies the acceptance predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The search terminates finitely and returns \((z_{k+1},s_k)\) satisfying \(A(z_k,z_{k+1},s_k)\).

children.title: Acceptance-Criterion Families
children.top_down_role: Navigation by the structural test used during adaptive search.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceptance-Criterion Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three checkable acceptance predicates for local smoothness control in VI steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a trial pair \(x,y\in C\), scale \(\gamma>0\), and margin \(\theta\in(0,1)\), common admissibility predicates include the norm test
\[\gamma\lVert F(y)-F(x)\rVert_\ast\leq\theta\lVert y-x\rVert,\]
the paired-variation test
\[\gamma\langle F(y)-F(x),y-z\rangle\leq\frac{\theta}{2}\bigl(\lVert y-x\rVert^2+\lVert y-z\rVert^2\bigr),\]
and an inexact version obtained by adding a declared tolerance \(\delta_k\geq0\) to the right-hand side. The selected predicate must be evaluable from trial-point oracle values and must imply the one-step estimate required by the enclosing VI method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceptance can control operator variation by a norm inequality, a paired inner-product inequality, or an explicitly tolerance-relaxed version.
assumptions_latex: The primal norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) and dual norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_\ast\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A trial is accepted only when its chosen computable variation predicate holds.
review_flags: A source establishing these predicates within the intended saddle-point method family is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: These predicates are method-dependent, particularly the paired-variation and inexact forms. An authoritative source must identify the role of the third point and establish that each predicate supplies the required VI one-step estimate.

children.title: Oracle-Cost Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Extra oracle work associated with adaptive parameter search.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Cost Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case number of acceptance tests under geometric backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a line search starts from \(\bar\gamma>0\), replaces each rejected trial by \(\beta\gamma\) with \(\beta\in(0,1)\), and its predicate is guaranteed to hold whenever \(0<\gamma\leq\gamma_\star\). Then the number \(R\) of rejected trials obeys
\[R\leq\max\left\{0,\left\lceil\frac{\log(\bar\gamma/\gamma_\star)}{\log(1/\beta)}\right\rceil\right\}.\]
Consequently there are at most \(R+1\) acceptance tests. If each test uses at most \(q\) new operator evaluations and rejected trial computations cannot be reused, the iteration uses at most \(q(R+1)\) new evaluations; caching can only reduce this count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometric backtracking adds only logarithmically many trial tests, but each rejection may incur extra operator evaluations unless trial data are reusable.
assumptions_latex: Each acceptance test uses at most \(q\) new operator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration performs at most \(R+1\) tests and at most \(q(R+1)\) new operator evaluations.

notation.meaning: maximum new oracle evaluations per test

children.title: Parameter-Free VI Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies avoiding prescribed problem constants.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free VI Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: History-measurable VI policies requiring no regularity constants as inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a monotone variational inequality on \(C\), let the available history before iteration \(k\) be
\[\mathcal H_k=\{x_i,F(x_i),y_i,F(y_i),a_i:0\leq i<k\},\]
where \(a_i\) records past acceptances or residuals. A policy is parameter-free with respect to a parameter set \(\Theta\) if every trial scale, metric, and stopping statistic at iteration \(k\) is a measurable function of \(\mathcal H_k\) and user tolerances, while no element of \(\Theta\) is supplied to the algorithm. Typical choices are \(\Theta=\{L,\nu,\sigma\}\), comprising smoothness scale, regularity exponent, and noise scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VI policy is parameter-free when its decisions use observed history and tolerances, not supplied smoothness, regularity, or noise constants.
assumptions_latex: The oracle history and user-requested tolerances are observable.
The excluded parameter set \(\Theta\) is declared before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All algorithmic decisions are functions of \(\mathcal H_k\) and tolerances, independently of the numerical values in \(\Theta\).

notation.meaning: oracle and acceptance history before iteration k

review_flags: No supplied locator defines parameter-free VI policies in this precise operational sense.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed history-based definition is coherent but is a specific operational convention rather than an uncontroversial standard definition. It needs a source defining parameter-free VI policies in this sense.

children.title: Unknown-Scale Robustness
children.top_down_role: Performance boundaries under unavailable scale information.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Scale Robustness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivariance of VI iterates under positive rescaling of the operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a VI policy generate \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k,\gamma_kF)\), and suppose its update map depends on the operator and step only through their product. The policy is robust to unknown operator scale if, for every \(a>0\), replacing \(F\) by \(F_a=aF\) causes its scale rule to produce \(\gamma_k^{(a)}=\gamma_k/a\). Then
\[\gamma_k^{(a)}F_a=\gamma_kF\]
and, from the same initialization and deterministic tie-breaking, the entire primal iterate sequence is unchanged. Residual values homogeneous of degree one scale by \(a\), so an absolute stopping tolerance must be rescaled or replaced by a relative criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If steps compensate inversely for operator rescaling, all iterates remain unchanged; only homogeneous residual magnitudes and absolute tolerances change.
assumptions_latex: The update depends on \(F\) and \(\gamma_k\) only through \(\gamma_kF\).
Initialization and tie-breaking are identical under rescaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(a>0\), \(x_k^{(a)}=x_k\) for all \(k\), while degree-one residuals are multiplied by \(a\).
review_flags: The equivariance statement is algebraic, but no source locator for this robustness convention was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional equivariance calculation is algebraically sound, but the stated unknown-scale robustness convention and residual-scaling claim lack a cited source and a defined residual class.

children.title: Diagonal Preconditioning
children.top_down_role: Coordinatewise scaling structures for saddle or VI methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Preconditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise metric representation of a preconditioned proximal VI step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(x_k\in C\). For \(\gamma_k>0\), let \(D_k=\operatorname{diag}(d_{k,1},\ldots,d_{k,n})\) with \(d_{k,i}>0\). The diagonally preconditioned proximal step is
\[x_{k+1}=\mathop{\arg\min}_{x\in C}\left\{\langle F(x_k),x\rangle+\frac{1}{2\gamma_k}\lVert x-x_k\rVert_{D_k}^2\right\},\qquad \lVert u\rVert_{D_k}^2=u^\top D_ku.\]
If \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), this is equivalently
\[x_{k+1,i}=x_{k,i}-\gamma_kd_{k,i}^{-1}F_i(x_k),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\]
Thus each diagonal entry independently rescales its coordinate direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive diagonal metric turns one scalar stepsize into coordinatewise steps inversely proportional to the metric entries; the displayed coordinate formula applies in the unconstrained case.
assumptions_latex: \(D_k\) is diagonal and positive definite, and \(\gamma_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), the effective coordinate stepsizes are \(\gamma_k/d_{k,i}\).

notation.meaning: norm induced by the metric matrix
coordinate i of the operator value

children.title: Block Preconditioning
children.top_down_role: Block-structured scaling for coupled variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Preconditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space proximal step under a symmetric positive-definite block metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E=E_1\times\cdots\times E_m\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert product space, let \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:C\to E\), and let \(z_k\in C\). For \(\gamma_k>0\), let \(M_k:E\to E\) be self-adjoint and positive definite with block representation \((M_{k,ij})_{i,j=1}^m\). A block-preconditioned proximal VI step is
\[z_{k+1}=\mathop{\arg\min}_{z\in C}\left\{\langle F(z_k),z\rangle+\frac{1}{2\gamma_k}\langle M_k(z-z_k),z-z_k\rangle\right\}.\]
If \(C=E\) and \(M_k=\operatorname{blkdiag}(M_{k,1},\ldots,M_{k,m})\), then
\[z_{k+1,i}=z_{k,i}-\gamma_kM_{k,i}^{-1}F_i(z_k),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\]
For product constraints, a block-diagonal metric leaves the proximal subproblem separable by blocks. Nonzero off-diagonal blocks generally couple the block variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive block metric rescales variable groups. Block-diagonal metrics preserve blockwise separability, and in the unconstrained case give inverse-metric block steps; off-diagonal blocks generally couple the subproblem.
assumptions_latex: Each \(E_i\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, and each \(C_i\subseteq E_i\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(M_k\) is self-adjoint and positive definite, and \(\gamma_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A block-diagonal \(M_k\) preserves blockwise separability; when \(C=E\), its effective block steps are \(\gamma_kM_{k,i}^{-1}\), whereas nonzero off-diagonal blocks generally couple the subproblem.

notation.meaning: block mapping component j to component i
component i of the product-space operator value

children.title: Coupling-Aware Metric Design
children.top_down_role: Metric choices reflecting primal, dual, or operator coupling.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupling-Aware Metric Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive block metrics compatible with a bilinear primal–dual coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, let \(K:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(T\succ0\) and \(S\succ0\) be primal and dual metric operators. The pair \((T,S)\) is coupling-aware admissible when
\[\left\|S^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\right\|\leq 1.\]
Equivalently, its coupled block metric satisfies
\[\mathcal M=\begin{pmatrix}T^{-1}&-K^*\\-K&S^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\]
Strict inequality gives \(\mathcal M\succ0\). Thus diagonal or block-diagonal choices may use unequal local scales, but their joint scaling must control every coupled direction of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual metrics are admissible when their scaled coupling has norm at most one, equivalently when the associated coupled block matrix is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|S^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\|\leq1\iff \mathcal M\succeq0\).

children.title: Conditioning Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between metric complexity and effective conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of metric conditioning on preconditioned Lipschitz and monotonicity constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\mu\)-strongly monotone in the Euclidean norm, and let \(P\) satisfy \(mI\preceq P\preceq MI\) with \(0<m\leq M\). In the norm \(\|z\|_P^2=\langle Pz,z\rangle\), the operator \(P^{-1}F\) has a Lipschitz constant no greater than \(L/m\) and a strong-monotonicity constant no smaller than \(\mu/M\). Therefore, defining the guaranteed condition ratio by \(\kappa_P=(L/m)/(\mu/M)\), one has
\[\kappa_P=\frac{M}{m}\frac{L}{\mu}.\]
A metric can improve directional scaling, while a large spectral ratio \(M/m\) weakens this worst-case guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preconditioning may balance directional curvature, but the ratio formed from the guaranteed Lipschitz and strong-monotonicity bounds is inflated by the metric's spectral condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\mu\)-strongly monotone in the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_P=(M/m)(L/\mu)\).

children.title: Variable-Metric Geometry
children.top_down_role: Iteration-dependent metric structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration-dependent quadratic geometry under uniform spectral control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. A variable-metric geometry on \(C\) is a sequence of self-adjoint operators \((H_k)_{k\geq0}\) for which constants \(0<m\leq M<\infty\) satisfy
\[mI\preceq H_k\preceq MI\qquad\text{for every }k.\]
At iteration \(k\), it induces the norm \(\|z\|_{H_k}^2=\langle H_kz,z\rangle\), distance \(D_k(x,y)=\tfrac12\|x-y\|_{H_k}^2\), and metric projection
\[P_C^{H_k}(x)=\mathop{\arg\min}_{y\in C}D_k(y,x).\]
Uniform bounds make all iteration-dependent norms uniformly equivalent to the ambient Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable metric is a uniformly positive-definite sequence of operators defining iteration-dependent norms, quadratic distances, and projections.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m\|z\|^2\leq\|z\|_{H_k}^2\leq M\|z\|^2\) uniformly in \(k\).

notation.meaning: Projection onto C in the H_k metric

children.title: Adaptive Bregman Geometry
children.top_down_role: Iteration-dependent non-Euclidean geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Bregman Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mirror-type variational-inequality step with history-dependent distance generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x^0\in C\), stepsizes \(\alpha_k>0\), and a variational-inequality operator \(F:C\to\mathbb R^n\), choose at iteration \(k\) a differentiable, \(\sigma_k\)-strongly convex generator \(h_k\) using only information available through iteration \(k\). Define
\[D_{h_k}(x,y)=h_k(x)-h_k(y)-\langle\nabla h_k(y),x-y\rangle\]
and update
\[x^{k+1}\in\mathop{\arg\min}_{x\in C}\left\{\alpha_k\langle F(x^k),x\rangle+D_{h_k}(x,x^k)\right\}.\]
Stop when a prescribed VI residual is at most \(\varepsilon\); otherwise return the last iterate or a specified weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, select a strongly convex geometry from past information and take a Bregman-proximal step for the current variational-inequality operator value.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(h_k\) is differentiable and strongly convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}\) minimizes the displayed linearized VI objective plus the adaptive Bregman distance.

children.title: Metric-Variation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation by the stability or scale of metric changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Variation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controlled-change regime commonly used in variable-metric convergence analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sequence of self-adjoint metrics \((H_k)_{k\geq0}\) lies in the summably varying regime when constants \(0<m\leq M<\infty\) and numbers \(\eta_k\geq0\) exist such that
\[mI\preceq H_k\preceq MI,\qquad H_{k+1}\preceq(1+\eta_k)H_k,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_k<\infty.\]
The second inequality implies \(\|z\|_{H_{k+1}}^2\leq(1+\eta_k)\|z\|_{H_k}^2\). Hence the accumulated multiplicative expansion is finite because \(\prod_k(1+\eta_k)<\infty\), while uniform coercivity prevents degeneration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A controlled variable metric remains uniformly positive definite and changes by summable relative expansions, yielding finite accumulated metric distortion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_N\prod_{k=0}^{N}(1+\eta_k)<\infty\), with all \(H_k\)-norms uniformly equivalent.

children.title: Geometry-Mismatch Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits caused by poorly aligned adaptive geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Mismatch Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp instability boundary for a quadratic problem under mismatched diagonal geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^n L_i x_i^2\) with \(L_i>0\), and let \(H=\operatorname{diag}(h_1,\ldots,h_n)\succ0\). The metric gradient iteration
\[x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha H^{-1}\nabla f(x^k)\]
has coordinate factors \(1-\alpha L_i/h_i\). It converges to zero from every initial point if and only if
\[0<\alpha L_i/h_i<2\qquad\text{for every }i.\]
If some direction satisfies \(\alpha L_i/h_i>2\), that coordinate grows geometrically; equality gives an undamped sign oscillation. Thus underweighting curvature in even one metric direction crosses the stability boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a diagonal quadratic, metric gradient descent is stable exactly when every scaled directional stepsize lies between zero and two; mismatch beyond two causes divergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k\to0\) for all \(x^0\) if and only if \(0<\alpha L_i/h_i<2\) for all \(i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Coordinate VI Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized block fixed-point execution for a variational-inequality solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\), let \(T:C\to C\) be an averaged map whose fixed points solve the target variational inequality, and let \(U_i\) retain block \(i\) and zero all others. Initialize \(z^0\in C\). Independently sample \(i_k\) with probabilities \(p_i>0\), and update
\[z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_k U_{i_k}\bigl(Tz^k-z^k\bigr),\]
where \(\lambda_k\) lies in the admissible relaxation interval for \(T\). Stop when an estimated fixed-point residual is at most \(\varepsilon\); otherwise output the last iterate or an ergodic average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized block-coordinate VI method updates one positive-probability block of an averaged solution map and monitors its fixed-point residual.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda_k\) is in the averaged-map relaxation range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_kU_{i_k}(Tz^k-z^k)\), with solutions represented by \(\operatorname{Fix}(T)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian Decomposition Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise representation of a variational inequality on a Cartesian feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\) be a Cartesian product of nonempty closed convex sets, and write \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_m)\). A point \(x^*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_m^*)\in C\) solves
\[\langle F(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }x\in C\]
if and only if, for every block \(i\),
\[\langle F_i(x^*),x_i-x_i^*\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }x_i\in C_i.\]
This equivalence exposes block projections or proximal subproblems while retaining the dependence of each \(F_i\) on the full vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VI over a Cartesian product is equivalent to simultaneous blockwise inequalities, enabling decomposed subproblems even when the operator blocks remain coupled.
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\) is nonempty, closed, and convex for each \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VI}(F,C)\) is equivalent to the family of block inequalities for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).

notation.meaning: Block i of the VI operator
Block i of a product-space point

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous VI Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Delayed block-coordinate fixed-point execution without globally synchronized reads.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:C\to C\) be an averaged map encoding a variational inequality, and let \(U_i\) select block \(i\). At update \(k\), form a stale read \(\hat z^k\) whose components satisfy \(\hat z_j^k=z_j^{k-d_{k,j}}\), with delays \(0\leq d_{k,j}\leq\tau\). Select block \(i_k\) and perform
\[z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_kU_{i_k}\bigl(T\hat z^k-\hat z^k\bigr).\]
Unselected blocks remain unchanged. Use stepsizes permitted by the averagedness, delay bound, and activation model; stop at a prescribed residual tolerance or output the final iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asynchronous VI method updates one block using a boundedly stale vector, with stepsizes restricted by map averagedness, delay, and activation assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is averaged and has a fixed point.
Every block is activated according to the stated sampling or fairness model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_kU_{i_k}(T\hat z^k-\hat z^k)\) with bounded componentwise delays.

notation.meaning: Stale vector read at update k

children.title: Operator-Evaluation Cost

knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Evaluation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-count and work model for evaluations of the VI operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an algorithm accessing an operator \(F:C\to\mathbb R^n\), the operator-evaluation cost through iteration \(K\) is
\[N_F(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}q_k,\]
where \(q_k\) is the number of full evaluations of \(F\) during iteration \(k\). If only blocks are evaluated, define the work-weighted cost
\[W_F(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\sum_{i=1}^m q_{k,i}c_i,\]
where \(q_{k,i}\) counts evaluations of \(F_i\) and \(c_i\) is their declared unit cost. Comparisons must state whether they use full-oracle calls, block calls, or weighted arithmetic work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operator cost counts full or block evaluations needed to reach an iteration or accuracy target, optionally weighting blocks by their declared computational costs.
assumptions_latex: \(c_i\geq0\) is fixed under the declared cost model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_F(K)\) counts full calls, while \(W_F(K)\) measures declared block-weighted operator work.

notation.meaning: Number of block-i evaluations at iteration k
Unit cost of evaluating operator block i

children.title: Projection Cost
children.top_down_role: Cost of enforcing feasibility through projection.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost of solving the metric nearest-point primitive used by constrained methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and a metric \(H\succ0\), one projection call maps \(z\) to
\[P_C^H(z)=\mathop{\arg\min}_{x\in C}\frac12\|x-z\|_H^2.\]
The projection cost through iteration \(K\) is \(N_{\mathrm{proj}}(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}r_k\), where \(r_k\) counts exact projection calls. If projections are computed approximately, the cost report must additionally specify inner work and tolerances \(\delta_{k,j}\) satisfying the chosen projection-residual criterion. Euclidean projection is the special case \(H=I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection cost counts exact metric nearest-point solves; approximate projections additionally require their inner work and residual tolerances to be reported.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{proj}}(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}r_k\) under the exact-projection oracle model.

notation.meaning: Projection onto C in metric H
Number of projection calls at iteration k
Tolerance for an approximate projection subsolve

children.title: Proximal-Mapping Cost

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Mapping Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost of evaluating a scaled metric proximal mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper closed convex function \(g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), a metric \(H\succ0\), and \(\lambda>0\), one proximal call computes
\[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}^{H}(z)=\mathop{\arg\min}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{g(x)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x-z\|_H^2\right\}.\]
The proximal-mapping cost through iteration \(K\) is \(N_{\mathrm{prox}}(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}s_k\), where \(s_k\) counts exact calls. For inexact calls, the report must include inner iterations and the adopted objective-gap, residual, or enlargement tolerance. Projection is recovered by taking \(g\) as the indicator of a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal cost counts exact regularized minimization calls; inexact calls must also report inner work and the precise error criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{prox}}(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}s_k\) under the exact proximal-oracle model.

notation.meaning: Number of proximal calls at iteration k

children.title: Composite Cost Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relative cost regimes across operator, projection, or proximal access.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Cost Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted resource model for comparing saddle-point first-order implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an algorithm producing an output with saddle residual or primal-dual gap at most \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(N_j(\varepsilon)\) count uses of primitive \(j\) and let \(c_j\ge 0\) be its implementation-dependent unit cost. Its composite cost is
\[C_{\mathbf c}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal P}c_jN_j(\varepsilon).\]
For two implementations \(A\) and \(B\), implementation \(A\) is preferable under weights \(\mathbf c\) exactly when
\[\sum_{j\in\mathcal P}c_j\bigl(N_j^A(\varepsilon)-N_j^B(\varepsilon)\bigr)\le 0.\]
Thus no weight-independent ranking follows when the primitive-count difference has both positive and negative components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total cost is a weighted sum of primitive counts; crossed count vectors produce implementation rankings that depend on the chosen resource prices.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a finite set of first-order computational primitives.
Both implementations use the same accuracy criterion \(\varepsilon\).
Primitive costs are additive and represented by nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathbf c}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal P}c_jN_j(\varepsilon)\), with rankings determined by the weighted count difference.

notation.meaning: Number of calls to primitive j needed for accuracy epsilon.
Unit cost assigned to primitive j.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak live-state storage for a first-order saddle-point implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a representation in which each live algorithmic object \(s\) occupies \(m(s)\ge 0\) machine words. If \(\mathcal L_k\) is the set of objects simultaneously live while iteration \(k\) is executed, the peak memory cost through termination index \(K\) is
\[M_K=\max_{0\le k\le K}\sum_{s\in\mathcal L_k}m(s).\]
The live set includes current iterates, retained past iterates, dual or auxiliary states, cached operator values, and workspace that has not been released. Read-only problem data may either be included or excluded, but the convention must be fixed across compared implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memory cost is the maximum number of machine words simultaneously occupied by live iterates, cached values, auxiliary states, and workspace.
assumptions_latex: A fixed machine-word representation and allocation convention are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_K=\max_{0\le k\le K}\sum_{s\in\mathcal L_k}m(s)\).

notation.meaning: Objects simultaneously live during iteration k.
Storage occupied by object s in machine words.

children.title: Iterate-Movement Control
children.top_down_role: Policies limiting displacement between iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterate-Movement Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-step displacement constraint for primal-dual iterates in a chosen metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z\) be a finite-dimensional primal-dual space with norm \(\|\cdot\|_P\), where \(P\) is positive definite. An iteration sequence \((z_k)_{k\ge0}\) satisfies movement control with budgets \((\delta_k)_{k\ge0}\) when
\[\|z_{k+1}-z_k\|_P\le \delta_k\qquad\text{for every }k\ge0.\]
It has finite total movement when additionally
\[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_k<\infty.\]
Under both conditions, \((z_k)\) is Cauchy in \(Z\) and therefore converges to some point of \(Z\); this condition alone does not certify that the limit solves the saddle problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Movement control bounds each primal-dual displacement; a summable displacement budget guarantees convergence of the iterates, but not saddle-point correctness.
assumptions_latex: The nonnegative budgets satisfy \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_k<\infty\) for the convergence conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bounds imply that \((z_k)\) is Cauchy and convergent in \(Z\).

notation.meaning: Metric norm defined by the positive-definite operator P.

children.title: State-Reuse Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Memory–computation tradeoffs from retaining reusable state.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Reuse Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage-versus-evaluation accounting for reusable deterministic state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose iteration \(k\) requires deterministic quantities \(q_{k,1},\ldots,q_{k,r}\). For each \(i\), either retain \(q_{k,i}\) at storage cost \(m_i\) until its next use or discard and recompute it at primitive cost \(e_i\). If \(R\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}\) is the retained set, then the incremental resource pair is
\[(M(R),E(R))=\left(\sum_{i\in R}m_i,\ \sum_{i\notin R}e_i\right).\]
For scalar prices \(\alpha,\beta\ge0\), an optimal reuse choice minimizes \(\alpha M(R)+\beta E(R)\). Every minimizer retains item \(i\) when \(\alpha m_i<\beta e_i\), discards it when \(\alpha m_i>\beta e_i\), and may make either choice when \(\alpha m_i=\beta e_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Caching deterministic state consumes memory but avoids recomputation; under additive prices, an item is retained when its storage charge is smaller, discarded when its recomputation charge is smaller, and either choice is optimal at equality.
assumptions_latex: Cached quantities remain valid and unchanged until their next use.
Storage and recomputation costs are additive across quantities.
Recomputation reproduces the required quantity exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimizing retained set contains every \(i\) with \(\alpha m_i<\beta e_i\), excludes every \(i\) with \(\alpha m_i>\beta e_i\), and may treat ties arbitrarily.

notation.meaning: Storage cost of retained quantity i.

children.title: Movement-Limited Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Movement-Limited Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regime in which data movement dominates arithmetic cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an implementation reaching accuracy \(\varepsilon\), let \(B(\varepsilon)\) be transferred machine words, \(F(\varepsilon)\) arithmetic operations, and let \(\tau_B,\tau_F>0\) be their effective unit times. The implementation is movement-limited at accuracy \(\varepsilon\) when
\[\tau_B B(\varepsilon)\ge \tau_F F(\varepsilon),\]
and asymptotically movement-limited as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) when
\[\frac{\tau_B B(\varepsilon)}{\tau_F F(\varepsilon)}\longrightarrow\infty.\]
Within the additive runtime model \(T(\varepsilon)=\tau_BB(\varepsilon)+\tau_FF(\varepsilon)\), reducing arithmetic alone cannot change the leading asymptotic runtime in the latter regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A method is movement-limited when weighted data-transfer work dominates weighted arithmetic; asymptotically, reducing only arithmetic cannot improve the leading runtime.
assumptions_latex: Runtime is modeled additively by transfer and arithmetic terms.
The effective unit times \(\tau_B\) and \(\tau_F\) are positive.
Both implementations use the same accuracy convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the weighted transfer-to-arithmetic ratio diverges, then \(T(\varepsilon)\sim\tau_BB(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: Machine words transferred before reaching accuracy epsilon.
Arithmetic operations before reaching accuracy epsilon.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Message and payload accounting for distributed saddle-point methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(p\) workers executing a distributed method until an output satisfies an accuracy criterion \(\varepsilon\). If communication event \(r\) sends messages with payloads \(b_{r,1},\ldots,b_{r,m_r}\) machine words, define the message and word complexities by
\[N_{\mathrm{msg}}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{r=1}^{R(\varepsilon)}m_r,\qquad N_{\mathrm{word}}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{r=1}^{R(\varepsilon)}\sum_{j=1}^{m_r}b_{r,j}.\]
Under the latency-bandwidth model with nonnegative parameters \(\lambda\) and \(\beta\), communication cost is
\[C_{\mathrm{comm}}(\varepsilon)=\lambda N_{\mathrm{msg}}(\varepsilon)+\beta N_{\mathrm{word}}(\varepsilon).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication cost counts both messages and transmitted words, optionally combining them through latency and per-word prices until the requested accuracy is reached.
assumptions_latex: All compared methods use the same accuracy criterion \(\varepsilon\).
Each communication event has finitely many messages with finite payloads.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{comm}}(\varepsilon)=\lambda N_{\mathrm{msg}}(\varepsilon)+\beta N_{\mathrm{word}}(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: Total number of transmitted machine words.

children.title: Synchronization Cost
children.top_down_role: Coordination overhead imposed by synchronized progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier-round accounting distinct from transmitted payload.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a distributed saddle-point method reach accuracy \(\varepsilon\) after \(R(\varepsilon)\) global synchronization rounds. If round \(r\) blocks progress for effective duration \(s_r\ge0\), including barrier latency and idle time caused by load imbalance, define
\[C_{\mathrm{sync}}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{r=1}^{R(\varepsilon)}s_r.\]
When only round complexity is modeled, take \(s_r=1\), so \(C_{\mathrm{sync}}(\varepsilon)=R(\varepsilon)\). Synchronization cost is separate from payload communication cost: a zero-payload barrier can have positive synchronization cost, while asynchronous messages need not create a global barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronization cost totals blocking barrier rounds or their elapsed durations; it is distinct from the amount of data communicated.
assumptions_latex: A synchronization round has an identifiable blocking interval.
The same termination accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is used across comparisons.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{sync}}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{r=1}^{R(\varepsilon)}s_r\), or \(R(\varepsilon)\) under unit round cost.

notation.meaning: Effective blocking duration of round r.

children.title: Local-Computation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between local work and inter-node exchange.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Computation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal batching balance in a stylized synchronized distributed model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose each worker performs \(q\ge1\) local first-order updates between synchronizations, each local update costs \(c_{\mathrm{loc}}>0\), each synchronization costs \(c_{\mathrm{sync}}>0\), and accuracy \(\varepsilon\) requires \(R(q,\varepsilon)\) synchronization rounds. The modeled total cost is
\[C(q,\varepsilon)=R(q,\varepsilon)\bigl(c_{\mathrm{sync}}+q c_{\mathrm{loc}}\bigr).\]
Increasing \(q\) is beneficial exactly when the decrease in round count offsets the extra local work. If \(q\) is relaxed to a positive real and \(R\) is differentiable, every interior minimizer \(q_*\) satisfies
\[-\frac{\partial_qR(q_*,\varepsilon)}{R(q_*,\varepsilon)}=\frac{c_{\mathrm{loc}}}{c_{\mathrm{sync}}+q_*c_{\mathrm{loc}}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: More local updates can reduce synchronization rounds but increase computation; an interior optimum balances their relative marginal rates.
assumptions_latex: The cost model is additive across rounds.
\(R(q,\varepsilon)>0\) is differentiable in the relaxed batching variable.
The local and synchronization unit costs are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An interior cost-minimizing batch size satisfies the displayed relative-marginal balance equation.

notation.meaning: Local updates performed per synchronization round.

children.title: Delay-Sensitivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cost behavior under latency or synchronization delay.

knowledge_statements.title: Delay-Sensitivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Staleness scale relative to the admissible forward-step stability margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz, and consider an asynchronous forward update
\[z_{k+1}=z_k-\gamma F(z_{k-d_k}),\qquad 0\le d_k\le\tau.\]
Define the dimensionless delay load \(\rho=\gamma L(\tau+1)\). A family of implementations is delay-insensitive when \(\rho\to0\), delay-sensitive when \(\rho=\Theta(1)\), and beyond the usual bounded-delay stability scale when \(\rho\to\infty\). These labels classify the interaction of step size, operator scale, and worst-case staleness; without stronger assumptions they do not themselves assert convergence or divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delay sensitivity is classified by step size times operator scale times maximum staleness; the classification alone is not a convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regimes are determined by the asymptotic size of \(\rho=\gamma L(\tau+1)\).

notation.meaning: Staleness of the operator value used at iteration k.

children.title: Cycling Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Persistent orbiting behavior in saddle dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycling Dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-preserving discrete cycle on the scalar bilinear saddle problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the unconstrained saddle function \(\Phi(x,y)=xy\) and the saddle operator \(F(x,y)=(y,-x)\). For \(\gamma>0\), the implicit-midpoint iteration
\[z_{k+1}=z_k-\gamma F\!\left(\frac{z_k+z_{k+1}}{2}\right)\]
has update matrix
\[Q_\gamma=\left(I+\frac{\gamma}{2}J\right)^{-1}\left(I-\frac{\gamma}{2}J\right),\qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.\]
Since \(Q_\gamma\) is orthogonal, \(\|z_{k+1}\|_2=\|z_k\|_2\). Hence every nonzero initialization remains on a circle about the unique saddle \(z_*=0\) and cannot converge to it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Implicit midpoint applied to a bilinear saddle preserves distance from the saddle, producing persistent circular motion from every nonzero initialization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|z_k\|_2=\|z_0\|_2>0\) for all \(k\), so the iterates do not converge to the saddle.

children.title: Rotational Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Skew-driven motion around equilibrium regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Rotational Dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Skew-symmetric component induces tangential saddle-point motion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) satisfy \(A^{\mathsf T}=-A\), and consider the continuous saddle dynamics
\[\dot z(t)=-Az(t).\]
Along every solution,
\[\frac{d}{dt}\frac12\|z(t)\|_2^2=-z(t)^{\mathsf T}Az(t)=0,\]
so \(\|z(t)\|_2=\|z(0)\|_2\). Moreover, all nonzero eigenvalues of \(A\) are purely imaginary, and on each invariant two-dimensional block with frequency \(\omega>0\), the flow is a rotation through angle \(\omega t\). Thus a purely skew saddle operator supplies no radial contraction toward its zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A purely skew-symmetric saddle operator generates norm-preserving rotations, so its continuous flow has no radial contraction toward equilibrium.
assumptions_latex: The dynamics are \(\dot z=-Az\) on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The flow preserves \(\|z(t)\|_2\) and rotates on every nonzero spectral block.

notation.meaning: Rotation frequency of an invariant spectral block.

children.title: Descent–Ascent Divergence
children.top_down_role: Unbounded or escaping descent–ascent trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Descent–Ascent Divergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous gradient descent-ascent on a scalar bilinear game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the unconstrained saddle problem
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb R}\max_{y\in\mathbb R}\Phi(x,y),\qquad \Phi(x,y)=xy,\]
simultaneous gradient descent-ascent with step size \(\gamma>0\) gives
\[x_{k+1}=x_k-\gamma y_k,\qquad y_{k+1}=y_k+\gamma x_k.\]
Consequently,
\[x_{k+1}^2+y_{k+1}^2=(1+\gamma^2)(x_k^2+y_k^2),\]
and hence
\[\|(x_k,y_k)\|_2=(1+\gamma^2)^{k/2}\|(x_0,y_0)\|_2.\]
Every nonzero initialization therefore diverges geometrically from the unique saddle point \((0,0)\), regardless of how small the fixed positive step size is.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the scalar bilinear game, simultaneous gradient descent-ascent expands distance from the saddle by a fixed factor at every positive step size.
assumptions_latex: The step size \(\gamma\) is fixed and positive.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local spectral diagnostic for a differentiable fixed-point iteration near a fixed point.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Fixed-point iteration p. 33

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\), let \(T_\theta:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) be continuously differentiable near a fixed point \(z^\star=T_\theta(z^\star)\), and set \(J_\theta=DT_\theta(z^\star)\). If \(\rho(J_\theta)<1\), then \(z^\star\) is locally asymptotically stable with a linear rate; if \(\rho(J_\theta)>1\), then it is unstable. The neutral spectral set \(\{\theta\in\Theta:\rho(J_\theta)=1\}\) is the linearized stability-boundary diagnostic, but it need not equal the topological boundary of the stable parameter set without additional regularity assumptions. At points in this set, linearization alone is inconclusive, so Jordan structure, nonlinear terms, or parameter perturbations may need examination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The update Jacobian gives a local diagnostic: spectral radius below one yields local linear convergence, spectral radius above one yields instability, and equality identifies the neutral spectral set requiring further analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Ergodic–Last-Iterate Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex–concave saddle example where averaging gives a perfect certificate while last iterates remain bad.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=[-1,1]\) and \(L(x,y)=xy\). Consider the sequence \((x_k,y_k)=((-1)^k,(-1)^k)\). Its Cesàro averages satisfy \((\bar x_N,\bar y_N)=(0,0)\) for every even \(N\), so the primal–dual gap at the average is zero. Nevertheless, every last iterate has global gap \(\sup_{y\in Y}L(x_k,y)-\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y_k)=2\), and the last-iterate sequence does not converge. Thus ergodic convergence or an ergodic gap bound does not, by itself, imply last-iterate convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating between two bad saddle points can average exactly to the solution, so an ergodic gap may vanish while every last iterate remains nonconvergent and suboptimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(\bar x_N,\bar y_N)=0\) for even \(N\), while \(G(x_k,y_k)=2\) for every \(k\).

notation.meaning: Cesàro average of the first N iterates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic counterexample is correct and the counterexample kind fits the leaf, but no inspectable source is cited. The plain statement also incorrectly calls the alternating points saddle points; they are nonsolution iterates.

children.title: Momentum Instability
children.top_down_role: Instability attributable to inertial game dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Momentum Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Schur-stability boundary for scalar heavy-ball iteration on a strongly monotone linear operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(z)=\lambda z\) with \(\lambda>0\), consider \(z_{k+1}=z_k-\alpha F(z_k)+\beta(z_k-z_{k-1})\). Its characteristic polynomial is \(p(r)=r^2-(1-\alpha\lambda+\beta)r+\beta\). With real parameters, both roots lie strictly inside the unit disk exactly when \(-1<\beta<1\) and \(0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\). Equality places a root on the unit circle; violation gives a root of modulus at least one and permits nondecay or divergence for a suitable initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar heavy-ball dynamics are stable only inside an explicit step-size–momentum region; crossing its boundary produces a nondecaying or divergent mode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{|r|:p(r)=0\}<1\iff -1<\beta<1\text{ and }0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta).\)

children.title: Adaptive-Scaling Instability
children.top_down_role: Instability attributable to changing coordinate scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Scaling Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-metric forward iteration can diverge when the effective step lacks a uniform upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(z)=z\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) and apply the scaled update \(z_{k+1}=z_k-\alpha m_kF(z_k)=(1-\alpha m_k)z_k\), where \(\alpha>0\) and \(m_k>0\). If \(m_k=m>2/\alpha\), then \(|1-\alpha m|>1\), so every initialization \(z_0\ne0\) diverges geometrically although \(F\) is strongly monotone and Lipschitz. Thus positivity of adaptive scaling is insufficient; stability requires control of the effective step \(\alpha m_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even on the identity operator, a positive adaptive scale can make the effective step exceed two and cause geometric divergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_k=m>2/\alpha\Rightarrow |z_k|=|1-\alpha m|^k|z_0|\to\infty\) for \(z_0\ne0\).

notation.meaning: positive scalar metric or adaptive scale

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Acceleration Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral failure diagnostic for momentum applied to a coupled saddle operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(z)=Az\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and consider \(z_{k+1}=z_k-\alpha Az_k+\beta(z_k-z_{k-1})\). With state \(w_k=(z_k,z_{k-1})\), the recurrence is \(w_{k+1}=C_{\alpha,\beta}w_k\), where \(C_{\alpha,\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}(1+\beta)I-\alpha A&-\beta I\\ I&0\end{pmatrix}\). If \(\rho(C_{\alpha,\beta})>1\), some initialization diverges geometrically; if \(\rho(C_{\alpha,\beta})=1\), uniform linear contraction fails. Coupling between rotational eigenmodes of \(A\) and momentum therefore creates a stability boundary not determined by either parameter alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration of a coupled saddle operator is stable only when the companion update matrix is Schur stable; rotational modes and momentum jointly determine failure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(C_{\alpha,\beta})>1\Rightarrow \exists w_0:\|w_k\|\text{ grows geometrically}.\)

notation.meaning: block companion matrix of the accelerated recurrence

knowledge_statements.title: Hyperparameter-Sensitivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform heavy-ball stability region over an interval of positive operator eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a linear self-adjoint positive-definite operator has spectrum contained in \([\mu,L]\), where \(0<\mu\le L\). For the heavy-ball recurrence, each eigenmode \(\lambda\) obeys \(r^2-(1-\alpha\lambda+\beta)r+\beta=0\). Uniform Schur stability over all \(\lambda\in[\mu,L]\) holds exactly when \(-1<\beta<1\) and \(0<\alpha<2(1+\beta)/L\). Consequently, parameters close to \(\alpha=2(1+\beta)/L\) are sensitive to errors in the estimated upper spectral bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For heavy-ball dynamics, the largest eigenvalue fixes the uniform stability boundary, making near-boundary step sizes sensitive to spectral-estimation error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(C_\lambda)<1\text{ for every }\lambda\in[\mu,L]\iff -1<\beta<1\text{ and }0<\alpha<2(1+\beta)/L.\)

e0\), the supremum term is infinite; if \(y
e0\), the negative infimum term is infinite. Hence \(G(x,y)=+\infty\) for every \((x,y)
e(0,0)\), making the global gap unusable as a finite progress certificate on this unbounded domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Small Residual without Global Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth nonconvex example where a zero first-order residual occurs at a nonglobal stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=(x^2-1)^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), and use the first-order residual \(R(x)=|f'(x)|\). Since \(f'(x)=4x(x^2-1)\), one has \(R(0)=0\). However, \(f(0)=1\), whereas \(f(1)=f(-1)=0\). Thus an arbitrarily small, even zero, stationarity residual does not certify global optimality once convexity or monotonicity is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero gradient residual may identify a nonglobal stationary point in a nonconvex problem, so residual smallness alone is not a global certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(0)=0\quad\text{but}\quad f(0)>\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}f(x)=0.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonconvex stationary-point counterexample is correct and appropriately classified, but the record has no source citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-Below Differentiable Functions Have Arbitrarily Small Derivatives

knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Certificate Miscalibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of nominal residual confidence bounds when their moment assumptions are violated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be independent standard Cauchy observations, and suppose a certificate treats \(\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) as a mean residual with uncertainty shrinking proportionally to \(n^{-1/2}\). The Cauchy law has no finite mean or variance, and \(\bar X_n\) has the same distribution as each \(X_i\). Therefore the asserted uncertainty does not shrink, and any nominal Gaussian confidence certificate based on finite-variance asymptotics is miscalibrated. Moment or tail assumptions are essential for such statistical certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Cauchy noise, averaging does not reduce uncertainty, so Gaussian residual confidence bounds claiming square-root sample improvement are invalid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar X_n\overset{d}{=}X_1\), so its uncertainty does not decrease at rate \(n^{-1/2}\).

notation.meaning: empirical average used by the certificate

children.title: Loss of Monotonicity or Lipschitz Regularity

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Monotonicity or Lipschitz Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two scalar examples isolating failures caused by loss of monotonicity or global Lipschitz control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the forward iteration \(z_{k+1}=z_k-\alpha F(z_k)\) with \(\alpha>0\), loss of monotonicity permits immediate divergence: \(F(z)=-z\) gives \(z_k=(1+\alpha)^kz_0\). Monotonicity alone also does not ensure fixed-step convergence without Lipschitz control: \(F(z)=z^3\) is monotone but not globally Lipschitz, and whenever \(|z_0|>\sqrt{2/\alpha}\), one has \(|z_1|=|z_0||1-\alpha z_0^2|>|z_0|\), with subsequent magnitudes increasing. Standard fixed-step guarantees therefore require appropriate monotonicity and regularity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping monotonicity can cause linear divergence, while dropping global Lipschitz control can make a fixed step explode even for a monotone scalar operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(z)=-z\Rightarrow |z_k|\to\infty\), and \(F(z)=z^3\) admits divergent initializations.

notation.meaning: operator used by the forward iteration

children.title: Empty, Nonunique, or Unbounded Solution Sets

knowledge_statements.title: Empty, Nonunique, or Unbounded Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar variational inequalities realizing empty, nonunique, and unbounded solution sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) and operator \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(S=\{x\in C:F(x)(u-x)\ge0\text{ for all }u\in C\}\). If \(C=\mathbb{R}\) and \(F\equiv1\), then \(S=\varnothing\). If \(C=[0,1]\) and \(F\equiv0\), then \(S=[0,1]\), so solutions are nonunique. If \(C=\mathbb{R}\) and \(F\equiv0\), then \(S=\mathbb{R}\), which is nonunique and unbounded. Thus existence, uniqueness, and boundedness require separate hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple scalar variational inequalities show independently that a solution set may be empty, contain many points, or be unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\varnothing,\ [0,1],\text{ or }\mathbb{R}\) in the three stated examples, respectively.

notation.meaning: solution set of the variational inequality

children.title: Persistent Oracle Bias
children.top_down_role: Failures driven by systematically biased stochastic information.

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Oracle Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant bias shifts the limiting solution of a strongly monotone saddle operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(F(z)=z\), whose unique zero is \(z^\star=0\). Suppose an oracle returns \(\widehat F_k(z)=F(z)+b\), where \(b\ne0\), and consider \(z_{k+1}=z_k-\gamma\widehat F_k(z_k)\) with \(0<\gamma<2\). Then \(z_k\to-b\), so \(F(z_k)\to-b\ne0\). Thus even for a strongly monotone operator, persistent additive oracle bias prevents convergence to the intended saddle point; the asymptotic distance is \(|b|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant oracle bias moves the iteration from the true solution to a displaced fixed point, creating a nonzero asymptotic error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_k\to-b\ne z^\star\) and \(\lim_{k\to\infty}|z_k-z^\star|=|b|\).

children.title: Nonvanishing Inexactness
children.top_down_role: Failures driven by persistent computational or oracle error.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonvanishing Inexactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent deterministic evaluation error can produce oscillation instead of convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(z)=z\) on \(\mathbb R\), let \(0<\gamma<2\), and use the inexact iteration \(z_{k+1}=z_k-\gamma(F(z_k)+e_k)\) with \(e_k=(-1)^k\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). The sequence converges to a two-cycle satisfying \(z_{2m}\to \gamma\varepsilon/(2-\gamma)\) and \(z_{2m+1}\to-\gamma\varepsilon/(2-\gamma)\). Hence bounded but nonvanishing inexactness need not permit convergence to the zero \(z^\star=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating error of fixed magnitude makes a contractive inexact iteration approach a two-cycle rather than the true solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_k\) does not converge and \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}|z_k|=\gamma\varepsilon/(2-\gamma)>0\).

children.title: Bias–Inexactness Accumulation
children.top_down_role: Combined error behavior across repeated iterations.

knowledge_statements.title: Bias–Inexactness Accumulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted bias and deterministic errors enter ergodic gap bounds without cancellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a normed vector space. Suppose a saddle-point method produces an averaged iterate \(\bar z_N\) and a nonnegative gap satisfying \[\mathcal G(\bar z_N)\le \frac{D^2+C\sum_{k=1}^N\gamma_k^2}{2S_N}+\frac{D}{S_N}\sum_{k=1}^N\gamma_k(\|b_k\|+\varepsilon_k),\qquad S_N=\sum_{k=1}^N\gamma_k,\] where \(D>0\), \(C\ge0\), \(\gamma_k>0\), \(b_k\in B\), and \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\). If the nominal term tends to zero and \(\rho=\liminf_{N\to\infty}S_N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N\gamma_k(\|b_k\|+\varepsilon_k)>0\), then the right-hand side has limit inferior \(D\rho\). Consequently, this estimate alone cannot certify convergence of \(\mathcal G(\bar z_N)\) to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bias and nonnegative inexactness magnitudes accumulate through their step-size-weighted average; a positive limiting lower average prevents this bound from certifying a vanishing gap.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a normed vector space, \(b_k\in B\), and \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed right-hand side has limit inferior \(D\rho>0\), so this bound does not certify \(\mathcal G(\bar z_N)\to0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct interpretation of the stated perturbed ergodic-gap inequality

children.title: Error-Floor Regimes
children.top_down_role: Accuracy limits imposed by persistent error sources.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Floor Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform perturbations of a contraction yield a sharp invariant error neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((Z,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed space, let \(T:Z\to Z\) satisfy \(\|Tz-Tw\|\le q\|z-w\|\) with \(0\le q<1\), and let \(z^\star=Tz^\star\). If \(z_{k+1}=Tz_k+d_k\) and \(\|d_k\|\le\eta\), then \[\|z_k-z^\star\|\le q^k\|z_0-z^\star\|+\eta\frac{1-q^k}{1-q}.\] Consequently, \(\limsup_k\|z_k-z^\star\|\le\eta/(1-q)\). The radius is sharp for \(Z=\mathbb R\), \(Tz=qz\), and \(d_k=\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contraction with uniformly bounded persistent perturbations approaches an error ball of radius at most η divided by one minus the contraction factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|z_k-z^\star\|\le\eta/(1-q)\), and equality is attainable.

children.title: Uncontrolled Variance
children.top_down_role: Failures associated with insufficient variance control.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Variance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Growing oracle variance can overwhelm a diminishing-step stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(F(z)=z\). For \(k\ge2\), set \(z_{k+1}=(1-1/k)z_k-\xi_k/k\), where \((\xi_k)_{k\ge2}\) are independent random variables satisfying \(\mathbb E[\xi_k]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\xi_k)=k^2\), and let \(z_2\) be deterministic. Then \[z_{n+1}=\frac{z_2}{n}-\frac1n\sum_{k=2}^n\xi_k\] and \[\operatorname{Var}(z_{n+1})=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{k=2}^n k^2.\] This variance grows on the order of \(n\). Thus unbiasedness alone does not ensure mean-square convergence when oracle variance is uncontrolled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with unbiased independent noise and diminishing steps, variance growing quadratically with the iteration index makes the mean-square iterate error diverge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(z_{n+1})=n^{-2}\sum_{k=2}^n k^2\to\infty\), so \(z_n\) does not converge to zero in mean square.

notation.meaning: additive stochastic oracle noise at iteration k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: corrected explicit variance calculation for a scalar stochastic approximation

children.title: Heavy-Tail Noise
children.top_down_role: Failures associated with weakly concentrated oracle noise.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tail Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-variance noise invalidates variance-based convergence and concentration guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the oracle be \(\widehat F(z,\xi)=F(z)+\xi\), where \(\xi\) has the standard Cauchy distribution. Then \(\mathbb E[\xi^2]=\infty\), and the average \(N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N\xi_k\) of independent copies has the same Cauchy distribution as each \(\xi_k\). Hence averaging does not reduce its scale, and neither a finite-variance mean-square bound nor a sub-Gaussian \(N^{-1/2}\) concentration guarantee applies to the ordinary sample-mean oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Cauchy oracle noise, averaging preserves the noise distribution, so variance-based and sub-Gaussian accuracy guarantees fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N\xi_k\) is standard Cauchy for every \(N\), and \(\mathbb E[\xi_k^2]=\infty\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stability of the Cauchy distribution under averaging
