children.title: Robustness Breakdown Regimes
children.top_down_role: Noise regimes where standard stochastic safeguards become unreliable.

knowledge_statements.title: Robustness Breakdown Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The empirical-mean oracle has unbounded sensitivity under arbitrary contamination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\ge1\), \(d\ge1\), and \(g_1,\ldots,g_N\in\mathbb R^d\), and define the empirical-mean oracle \(\bar g=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N g_i\). Replace one sample by \(g_j'=g_j+Nv\), where \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) is arbitrary. The resulting estimate satisfies \(\bar g'=\bar g+v\). Because \(\|v\|\) is unrestricted, contamination of one sample can move the oracle estimate by an arbitrarily large amount. Consequently, without bounded samples, tail assumptions, clipping, or a robust aggregator, no uniform finite contamination-error bound exists for the empirical mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One arbitrarily corrupted sample can shift an empirical-mean oracle by any chosen vector, so its worst-case contamination error is unbounded.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i\in\mathbb R^d\) are aggregated by their arithmetic mean
The contaminated sample is not norm bounded
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{g_j'\in\mathbb R^d}\|\bar g'-\bar g\|=\infty\).

notation.meaning: arbitrary displacement caused by one contamination

children.title: Rare-Event Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of iterates or certificates to extreme samples.

knowledge_statements.title: Rare-Event Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A centered oracle can hide large errors in low-probability events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(p\in(0,1)\), \(M>0\), and a step size \(\gamma>0\). Let \(\xi=M\) with probability \(p\) and \(\xi=-pM/(1-p)\) with probability \(1-p\), so \(\mathbb E[\xi]=0\). Among \(N\ge1\) independent oracle calls, at least one positive spike occurs with probability \(1-(1-p)^N\). If an unclipped update contains the additive perturbation \(-\gamma\xi\), then such a spike produces a perturbation of magnitude \(\gamma M\). Since \(M\) is arbitrary while unbiasedness is preserved, expectation-level unbiasedness alone gives no uniform pathwise bound against rare oracle shocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unbiased noise may contain arbitrarily large rare spikes, so an unclipped fixed-step update can suffer an arbitrarily large perturbation despite zero mean.
assumptions_latex: The \(N\) oracle noises are independent copies of \(\xi\)
The update uses the additive noise without clipping
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A perturbation of magnitude \(\gamma M\) occurs within \(N\) calls with probability \(1-(1-p)^N\).

notation.meaning: positive step size applied to the oracle noise

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit centered two-point noise construction

knowledge_statements.title: Dependent-Sample Correction Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Corrections derived for independent samples may become biased under sample dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a correction requires estimating \(\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y]\) by the same-pair average \(N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N X_kY_k\). This replacement is unbiased only when \(\mathbb E[X_kY_k]=\mathbb E[X_k]\mathbb E[Y_k]\). For the dependent choice \(X_k=Y_k\), where \(X_k\) are independent Rademacher variables across \(k\), both marginal means vanish but \(X_kY_k=1\) surely. The correction therefore has bias one. Dependence must consequently be incorporated through conditional expectations, mixing control, or independent resampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A correction that substitutes a same-sample product for a product of expectations can have fixed bias when its two samples are dependent.
assumptions_latex: The target correction term is \(\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y]\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y]=0\) but \(N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N X_kY_k=1\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: paired samples used by the correction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Rademacher calculation correctly exposes bias from a same-pair product, but no source or concrete saddle-point correction model establishes that this generic estimator represents the intended terminal topic.

children.title: Spurious Stationary Points
children.top_down_role: Stationary targets lacking the intended minimax interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Spurious Stationary Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity need not imply a local min-max saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the smooth min-max problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}\max_{y\in\mathbb R} f(x,y)\) with \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\). At \((0,0)\), \(\nabla f(0,0)=0\), so the point is stationary for the associated saddle operator \((\partial_x f,-\partial_y f)\). However, for every nonzero \(y\) near zero, \(f(0,y)=y^2>f(0,0)\); thus \(y=0\) is a local minimum rather than a local maximum. Therefore \((0,0)\) is stationary but not a local saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the game with payoff x squared plus y squared, the origin is stationary but fails the maximizer’s local optimality condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(0,0)=0\), but \((0,0)\) is not a local min-max saddle point.

children.title: Non-Nash Stationary Points

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Nash Stationary Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous first-order stationarity does not ensure unilateral local optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a two-player game on \(\mathbb R^2\) in which player one minimizes \(J_1(x,y)=-x^2\) over \(x\), and player two minimizes \(J_2(x,y)=-y^2\) over \(y\). At \((0,0)\), \(\partial_xJ_1(0,0)=\partial_yJ_2(0,0)=0\), so the game-gradient field is stationary. Nevertheless, either player can unilaterally choose an arbitrarily small nonzero action and strictly reduce its cost below zero. Hence the stationary point is not a local Nash equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both players’ first derivatives vanish at the origin, yet each can lower its cost by a small unilateral move, so the point is not Nash.
assumptions_latex: Both players have action space \(\mathbb R\)
Each player minimizes its own cost
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The origin is game-gradient stationary but is not a local Nash equilibrium.

children.title: Stationarity–Equilibrium Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Structural gaps between first-order stationarity and game equilibrium.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity–Equilibrium Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equilibrium requires unilateral optimality conditions beyond vanishing game gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let each player \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) minimize a twice continuously differentiable cost \(J_i(x_i,x_{-i})\) over an open Euclidean action set. An interior local Nash equilibrium \(x^\star\) necessarily satisfies \(
abla_{x_i}J_i(x^\star)=0\) and \(
abla^2_{x_ix_i}J_i(x^\star)\succeq0\) for every \(i\). Game-gradient stationarity imposes only the first family of equalities. Thus a stationary point with \(
abla^2_{x_ix_i}J_i(x^\star)
ot\succeq0\) for some player cannot be a local Nash equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing player gradients is only first-order stationarity; a negative-curvature unilateral direction rules out local Nash equilibrium.
assumptions_latex: \(x^\star\) is interior to an open Euclidean action set
Every player minimizes its own cost
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
If \(
abla_{x_i}J_i(x^\star)=0\) for all \(i\) but \(
abla^2_{x_ix_i}J_i(x^\star)
ot\succeq0\) for some \(i\), then \(x^\star\) is stationary but not a local Nash equilibrium.

children.title: Local-Stability Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Local dynamical behavior used to distinguish stationary target types.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Stability Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linearization diagnostic for stationary points of continuous-time descent–ascent dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(U)\), where \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) is open, and define the descent–ascent vector field \(V(x,y)=(-\nabla_x f(x,y),\nabla_y f(x,y))\). At a stationary point \(z^*=(x^*,y^*)\) satisfying \(V(z^*)=0\), let \(J=DV(z^*)\) and \(\alpha(J)=\max\{\operatorname{Re}\lambda:\lambda\in\sigma(J)\}\). If \(\alpha(J)<0\), then \(z^*\) is locally asymptotically stable for \(\dot z=V(z)\). If \(\alpha(J)>0\), it is unstable. When \(\alpha(J)=0\), linearization alone is inconclusive and higher-order or invariant-set analysis is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Jacobian spectrum diagnoses a stationary point: strictly negative real parts imply local asymptotic stability, a positive real part implies instability, and a zero spectral margin is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(DV(z^*))<0\Rightarrow z^*\) is locally asymptotically stable, while \(\alpha(DV(z^*))>0\Rightarrow z^*\) is unstable.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the vector field at the stationary point.
Largest real part among eigenvalues of the Jacobian.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical linearization criterion for a hyperbolic equilibrium

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linearization criterion is mathematically standard, correctly scoped to a finite-dimensional C^1 vector field induced here by a C^2 payoff, and condition is an appropriate content kind for this diagnostic leaf. However, the record has no citation or inspectable locator supporting the stability and instability implications, so it cannot pass source review.

children.title: Limit Cycles
children.top_down_role: Periodic attracting or persistent game trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Limit Cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic-orbit definition for autonomous continuous-time game dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) and let \(V:D\to\mathbb{R}^d\) generate the autonomous dynamics \(\dot z=V(z)\). A limit cycle is a nonconstant periodic solution \(\gamma:\mathbb{R}\to D\) having a least period \(T>0\), so that \(\gamma(t+T)=\gamma(t)\) for every \(t\), whose orbit \(\Gamma=\{\gamma(t):0\le t<T\}\) is isolated among periodic orbits: some neighborhood \(N\) of \(\Gamma\) contains no periodic orbit distinct from \(\Gamma\). The cycle is attracting if trajectories starting in some neighborhood of \(\Gamma\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(z(t),\Gamma)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A limit cycle is an isolated, nonconstant periodic orbit of the game dynamics; it is attracting when all sufficiently nearby trajectories approach its orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma\) is a limit cycle precisely when it is the orbit of a nonconstant periodic solution and is isolated among periodic orbits.

notation.meaning: Least positive period of the periodic solution.
Closed orbit traced during one period.
Distance from a state to the periodic orbit.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes a limit cycle from an arbitrary periodic orbit by requiring isolation, and definition is the appropriate content kind for this leaf. The attracting-cycle clause is also standard under the stated local-uniqueness assumption. No source reference or specific locator is supplied, so authoritative support for the exact definition remains necessary.

children.title: Recurrent Game Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Repeated nonconvergent behavior beyond strict periodicity.

knowledge_statements.title: Recurrent Game Dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise recurrence for an autonomous game flow on a metric state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((Z,d)\) be a metric state space and \(\Phi_t:Z\to Z\) an autonomous game flow for \(t\ge0\). A state \(z\in Z\) is recurrent if for every neighborhood \(U\) of \(z\) and every \(T>0\), there exists \(t>T\) such that \(\Phi_t(z)\in U\). Equivalently, there is a sequence \(t_k\to\infty\) with \(d(\Phi_{t_k}(z),z)\to0\). The dynamics exhibit nontrivial recurrence when such a recurrent state is not an equilibrium, meaning that \(\Phi_t(z)\ne z\) for at least one \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A game state is recurrent when its trajectory returns arbitrarily close to it at arbitrarily late times; recurrence is nontrivial when that state is not an equilibrium.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi_t\) is a well-defined autonomous flow on the metric space \((Z,d)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\) is recurrent if and only if there exist \(t_k\to\infty\) such that \(d(\Phi_{t_k}(z),z)\to0\).

notation.meaning: Time-t evolution map of the game dynamics.
Sequence of return times diverging to infinity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The neighborhood and sequential formulations of pointwise recurrence are equivalent on a metric space, and definition fits the terminal container. A source is required to establish the intended recurrence convention and to resolve whether the one-sided family indexed by t>=0 is meant to be a semiflow rather than a two-sided flow.

children.title: Cycle–Equilibrium Separation
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between recurrent sets and equilibrium sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle–Equilibrium Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bilinear zero-sum game separating stationary equilibrium from last-iterate convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the unconstrained zero-sum game \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}} f(x,y)\) with \(f(x,y)=xy\). Its continuous-time simultaneous descent–ascent dynamics are \(\dot x=-y\) and \(\dot y=x\). The unique stationary point is \((0,0)\), but along every solution the quantity \(x(t)^2+y(t)^2\) is constant. Hence every initialization with \((x(0),y(0))\ne(0,0)\) traces a periodic circle of period \(2\pi\) and never converges to the stationary point. Thus equilibrium stationarity does not imply last-iterate attraction under simultaneous descent–ascent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the bilinear game xy, descent–ascent rotates on circles around the sole stationary point, so nonstationary trajectories cycle instead of converging to equilibrium.
assumptions_latex: The dynamics use simultaneous continuous-time gradient descent–ascent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x(0),y(0))\ne(0,0)\Rightarrow (x(t),y(t))\) is periodic and does not converge to \((0,0)\).

notation.meaning: Payoff minimized in x and maximized in y.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: directly checkable canonical bilinear-game counterexample

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bilinear calculation is correct and counterexample is the proper content kind for a leaf separating equilibrium from last-iterate attraction. The orbit circles are periodic but are not limit cycles in the standard isolated-orbit sense, so the listed Limit Cycles prerequisite should not be interpreted as classifying them as limit cycles. No source or inspectable locator supports the game-dynamics example.

children.title: Recurrence Detection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation by observable forms of repeated trajectory behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Recurrence Detection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact, asymptotic, and finite-tolerance predicates for detecting trajectory returns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a trajectory \(z_k\) in a metric space \((Z,d)\), recurrence may be tested at three resolutions. Exact recurrence occurs when \(z_{k+p}=z_k\) for some \(k\ge0\) and integer \(p\ge1\). Asymptotic recurrence at \(z_0\) occurs when \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}d(z_k,z_0)=0\). Given a horizon \(N\), exclusion lag \(L\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), finite-tolerance recurrence is detected when \(\min\{d(z_j,z_i):0\le i<j\le N,\ j-i\ge L\}\le\varepsilon\). The finite test is observational and does not by itself certify exact or asymptotic recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recurrence can mean an exact repeated state, arbitrarily close late returns, or an epsilon-close return observed within a finite horizon; only the first two are intrinsic.
assumptions_latex: \((z_k)_{k\ge0}\subseteq Z\), where \((Z,d)\) is a metric space.
\(N\ge L\ge1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) for the finite test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed predicates distinguish exact periodic return, asymptotic return, and finite-resolution detection; finite detection alone implies neither intrinsic predicate.

notation.meaning: Distance tolerance for a finite observed return.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is a reasonable content kind for detection predicates, but the proposed three-regime taxonomy is an uncited operational convention. Moreover, z_{k+p}=z_k at one pair is a repeated state, not necessarily an exact periodic return for an arbitrary sequence; periodic continuation follows only when the trajectory is generated by deterministic autonomous evolution. A source is needed to determine the intended definitions and required assumptions before a reliable replacement can be made.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Maximization Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity may select an inner minimizer rather than a maximizing response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\max_{y\in[-1,1]} f(x,y)\) with \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\). The interior point \((0,0)\) satisfies \(
